EScande, A Coon Sw1MMER.-The schooner Margaret from Kauai, picked up. on Friday morning last. at a dis lance of some six or eight miles from Barber's Point, a native boy by the name of Kamoeope-a deserter from the whale ship Franklin I'd which left this port on the preceding day. Kamoeone. it seems, had felt a little homesick when he saw the green noun tains of Oahu growing dim in the distance. and at about half past seven o'clock on Thursday evening, he jumped overheard and struck out for the land then about twenty miles distant, as he thinks. He swan all night, and at daylight vas within half a mile of the shore. Here, however, he was opposed by a strong current ; and after buffet;ng the W ayes for q while in a vain endeavor to reach the beach, he discovered a sail in the distance, several miles to leeward. He accordingly changed his course for the vessel. and at nine O'Clock on Friday morning was standing upon her deck, apparently but little the worse for his fourteen hours swim. CONGREGATIONAL SINGING. = Rev. MIR. Corwin preached a sermon upon thedesirability of congrega- tional singing in our churches, on Sunday evening last. This is one of the best methods of social wor- ship-the way in which the hearts and voices of the whole congregation can unite in songs of prayer and praise to the great Giver of all blessings. Choirs are entirely done away with now, in many churches "a IL Cttc II COukE tnooiO in their stead-the congregation, or those of it who care to, meeting round occasionally, at different houses. for practice. 1t should be remembered, how ever, that it is not necessary that congregational singing should be unanimous only general and those who have neither ear or voice for music, should leave the matter to others better qualified. We have known the harmony of church music to be married. Sabbath after Sabbath, by the harsh voice of u single man, who sang, not because he thought he could i'm prove the music, but because he considered il q duty to do his share. - MISPLACED SYMPATHY.-A lau ghable incident oc- CURED in kaahumanu street a few days since. A gentleman passing through the street, observed a fine looking terrier dog, lying PROSTATE and appa- rently dead, in the path. His limbs were relaxed, his eyes closed and his tongue protruding-a victim evidently. to the ravages Of strychnine. poor fellow!'' exclaimed our kind hearted friend, giving him a little kick in the side, when to his great establishment the dead dog came suddenly to life, with a hoarse growl, and seized him firmly by the toe of his boot-while a merry laugh, aud a cry of "sod, sold, from a neigh boring corner announced that the would be sympa- thizer, if not the dog, had been :" victimized.' Cullen, the president of the Reading Railroad Company, has consented to enter into an ar rangemeut by which in few days through passenger and freight trains will be running over his Lebanon Valley Branch, and East Pennsylvania Railroad, from Jersey city and Elizabethport to all the points in the West and Southwest. This is new route and certainly very important oneto New York. A fire at Brooklyn, n. V, on Wednesday, destroyed the cordage factory of Lawrence & Waterbury. The works were making up an average of $50 bales of Manila week, besides Russia and Kentucky hemp. BY this fire over 80 men, boys and girls are thrown out of employment. The loss Is es- t.mated at from $4,000 to SlOO,OOO, on which there is an insurance of about 60 per cent. The fire originated from spontaneous combustion. A letter in the Richmond Dispatch from Lynchburg, Va, says:-"There are FIVE to- bacco warehouses in this city, in which are stored two thousand five hundred hogsheads of tobacco, weighing in the aggregate up wards of two million five hundred thousand pounds! In addition to this, there are large quantities of loose tobacco piled in the diff ferent warehouses, which would make quite an accession to the above aggregate" The Department Of State has received in formation that, through the exertions of our minister at Rome, Mr.. Stockton, the Roman government has paid TO Mr.. Perkins and his party three thousand three hundred dollars in full compensation for the injuries they suffered from the soldiers during the re- cent commotion at Perugia. Mr.. Perkins il fully satisfied with the arrangement. Ex-Mayor Wood, Of New York, has au- thorized the New York News to state emf phatcaly to all concerned that MIR. Wood, if he lives, will be the Democratic candidate for Mayor of New York, next December" and to add that there is no compromise, and that could induce him to swervc from this purpose. Lately, an English lawyer succeeded in proving his innocence of II crime for which he had been sent to the penal settlement, publicly whipped, and kept for some time in chains He spent S5U,IWO in litigation, in proving himself the victim of foul con- spiracy. aud has been awarded by Parla- ment, S25, 900 rs L settlement of the matter. Rather tardy and cruel justice. Two little children, Alice and Mary Welsh, aged respectively nine and twelve years, ar rived at Hannibal, Missouri, day or two ago, having accomplished the whole journey from Ireland. without any other protection than their helplessness and their own brave hearts. Their father had preceded them by Il year or more. The famous Empire Club" of New York, which did so much to help elect "Polk and Dallas" but which has been out Of ex- istence the few years past, is re-galvanized. Captain Rynders is not to be com mander, az of yore, but James Irving, esq, gentleman not unknown to fame, in pugilistic as well as political circles. A Baltimore bully, giving the euphonious name Spruel, has got himself into trouble at Norfolk, by entering a public house, and, BIZ way of amusement, knocking down the inmates and smashing things generally lie was, however, promptly arrested, and IN default Of $500 bail, committed by Mayor Ferguson to Jail. Written for the Pioneer and Democrat.l THE GOLDEN YEAR, To the far.otf Colchian shore, the Argo Crept Ger the storm-grey sea to touch the Fleece Which goldenly cleaned out upon the deep; And when the sun went down, strained eyes did gaze To where the glittering ripple touched the wave, And marked the goal of long and dreary toll. As Jason sailed to grasp the Golden Fleece, So, cycles LATER toiled new Argos filled With hearts expectant of the fancied joy, To where the Western sands tossed in the spray Their more than Atran wealth, and where the land Glowed with the throbbing veins of virgin gold So men for years have sought the Golden shore, A few to grasp the gold, and more to fight Alternating want and danger dark, Aud some to stretch in death their wearied limbs, In savage wilds, adding their ghastly bones To the grim thousands there. Thus ever men Have wasted youth and strength in distant hopes, The while the earth they spurn behind them far, Cradles brighter gold and surer yield, Than sun -scorched sands reveal, through dewy toll. In truth, Gods earth doth bitterly reproach The wandering race /; for every year she calls For human toll to ease her of her wealth, And where man toileth not, she pants beneath Her own wild wealth of bloom and waving grass. there, Thank God! that man has learned the lesson And surely found the gold beneath his feet. Daily the full, golden sheaves, royalty Roll to the sheltering barns, mid joyous song, Like glittering conquerors, victorious borne Into the bosom of imperial Rome. For every field of grain hath poured its tide OF waving affluence to the sun.browned hands, And loved the stronger hearts of those who toiled, And braved the fervid sun for daily bread. Gods sun and shower have dressed the MUIR murinp land with With ripping smiles have met the thankless God.like hand of grace and kindly look: Have poured golden tide of wealth and bread Upon the universal man, and left HIM no complaint. And yet the Good Right Hand Which nursed these fields of bread and watered them With tenderest care-bringing the kindly sun To breathe his warmth and stir the germ OF life, Till tn inert grains sprang into merry stalks This Good Right Hand works on, by man ignored. Remember you who murmur bitterly, Because you suffer for yonr own mlsdeed, In looking every where but unto God; Remember evermore this Golden Year; Remember how the earth hath smiled with God, And let her smiles flow through thy thankless heart As the soft flow of summer waves upon a flowery shore, or as the pleasant sound OF summer wind among the summer trees. ALROY. ROSE TOWNSHIP, Sept. l, 1852

THoMAs.-The last news via Iehuantepec mentions that the Island of St. Thomas, one of the West India group, has been ceded by Denmark to the United States We find the following reference to the Island in the Lippincott Gazetteer: SAINT THoMAs-One of the Virgin Islands, West Indies, belonging to Denmark, 3s miles east of Porto Rico. Lat. (E. entrance of Fort Christain) lSo 26f 24/< n, Ion. Gao So 45H W. Greatest length from east to west, seventeen miles; greatest breadth, about four and half miles. Area forty five square miles. 1t has a rugged and elevated surface, which attains its greatest height towards the center, and descends sometimes gradually but often abruptly, to the shore. 1t was once well wooded but the cut ting down of the trees has laid it open to the full force of the suns rays and it now suffers much from a deficiency of water. The soil being sandy and by no means fertile, the far greater part of it remains uncultiyated. The area under crop is only about $500 acres, of which nearly half is planted with sugar cane. The whole island enjoys the privileges of free harbor, and the trade is very extensive, Saint Thomas being depot of goods for many of the neighborng islands. 1t has its central locality at the capital, Charlotte Amalie, which is annually visited by about 5000 vessels from Europe, North and South America, and also from the other West India Islands. In Europe the trade is chiefly with London Liver pool Glasgow, Bordeaux, Hayre, Marseiles, Genoa, Hamburg, Bremen and Amsterdam. Saint Thomas is principal station of the West India mail steamers from Southampton, for which large steam packet leaves it every fortnight. Population is estimated at $500. The views constantly varying and shifting that it would require pages for an adequate description Of the rich variety of celestial scenery then exhibited. The prevailing characteristic Of the display was the constant streaming up of the auroral light from all parts of the visible horizon and forming brilliant crown in the zenith This light was constantly vary ing from white to straw color and purple, with now and then geenish tinge, and appeared rs distinctly from the southern from the northern portion of the horizon. It commenced Immediately after daylight had vanished and continued until day break. An OBJ in this village informs us that the display about three O'Clock in the morning better than ut any other time. 1t then light enough to see to read coarse print. The cocks crowcd the signal for rising the hens left the roost and it appeared us if the sun was about to arise in the east. The LATE FRosTs.-Last week was re- markable for Borealis and Frosts. In some portions of Wisconsin and Michigan the frost was hard enough to damage veg etables and Buckwheat. In Wisconsin some fields of corn on low ground were in jured. The drought in Wisconsin is also very severe, no rain having fallen for sew eral weeks. Corn and potatoes very light. There were two or three frosty moru- ings last week in and about Aihtabula, but nothing suffered. In Somerset, Lawrence, Armstrong, Venango, Indiana, &c, coun- ties of Pennsylvania, slight dry frosts oc- cured every night of the week. Not much damage was done TO the growing crops.-- The unusually cool atmosphere at this sea- son of tho year is believed by many to Aave as yet unexplained relation, either Of cause or effect, with the recent displays Of what Humboldt calls the exhibition of a magnetic storm" ' Cleveland Leader.

The AURoRA.-At Boston, on the night Of LIST inst, the Aurora Borealis was SO brilliant after midnight that ordinary print could be read by its light It considerably impeded the working Of telegraph lines, and its effects were continued up to noon.of the ed. The au- roEal current from east to west was so regular that operators on the Eastern lines could send messages to Boston without the usual batter les being applied The same extraordinary eff feet was apparent on the telegraph wire be- tween Philadelphia and Pittsburg.

In one of his speeches, while canvassing Texas in his capacity of independent can didate for governor, General Houston had for portion of his auditory a fine collec- tion of females. They who do not fully appreciate the many excellent traits in the gallant old soldier and statesEan's charac- ter would hardly expect to hear him de- claim such beautiful and ennobliny senti- ments as are contained in this eloquent ex. tract. No wonder he is a favorite of the gentler sex. and no wonder that he is the Governor elect of that widespread and thrifty young State: Ladies, | know that politics are always uninteresting to you, yet believe you have in their general result an abiding interest. Ii Is always qualification 10 me to behold my fair countrywomen in assem5lages of this kind. 1t is a guarantee that their hus- bands and fathers and brothers are men of intelligence and refinement, who appreciate their mental capacities, and desire their countenance In their un lertakings Your presence exercises calming influence upon those antagonisms which are too often engende"ed in the heat of political con- tests. All parties desire your approving smile, and therefore all are encouraged by your presence. | know that in the direct administration of political affairsyou have no share; but yet, reigning as you dc,sspreme IN the realm of love, your influence often controls the destiny of nations. Woman's love is the great lever which arouses man to action. The general, as he plans his strategic combinations which are to insure victory, looks forward to a recompense dearer than the laurels upon his brow; the soldier, as he trudges along on the weary march, or mingles in the scenes of the bat tie field, even with death around him, for gets awhile the Carnage, and turns his thoughts to the fond girl he left behind him; the mariner, tempest tossed, driven by rude waves, sings merrily aloft as he thinks of the cottage by the shore. where his wife and dear ones await him;-tfe statesman, as he devises, amid deep and painful thought, plans of government which are TO tell upon his own and his country's fame. never loses sight of the joys which await him when cabinet councils are over, AS he enters the portals of home; the sentinel, as he PAGES his weary watch, loves the moon light tramp, that be may look beneath its rays at the dear momenIa of mothers or sisters love- Over man, in all his relationships, the influence of woman hangs like CHARM Deprive us of your influence, which digni- fies US and stimulates us to noble deeds, and We become worse than barbarians Let it be ours, and We can brave the cannon's mouth or face danger in ten thousand forms You stimulate all that is good. You check in us ignoble purposes. You have also an ! important influence upon posJerity. Tie early impressions which the child receives from you, outive all the wisdom of latter days. Sages may reason and philosophers rlay teach, but The voice which we heard IN infancy will ever come TO orr ears, bear ing a mothers words and mothers com sells. Continue TO iGstiI into your children virture and patriotism. Imbue them with proper yeneratiOn for the fathers of liberty. Learn them to love their country, and to labor for its good, as the great end of their ambition. Bid them proudly maintain our institutions. Point them to the deeds of their ancestors. Make these their escutch- con, and bid them hand it down to their children as free from stain as It came to them. Do this, ladies, and your influence will not be lost in the future. In The Ian guage of the poet. it will srl be said: Woman is lovely to the sigLt, As gentle as the due of even As bright as mornings earliest light, And spotless as the SHOWS of heaven

back on the soft hay; her child slept, too and all her troubles faded away in heavy unconsciousness, till she was again ava kened by her husbands grasp, to fine that dawn was gathering it's light roseate feeces in the east, and that their flight was for the present stayed at the door o1 a tavern, lonely and rude enough, but welcome to Hittty as place of rest, il only for moment. The sullen mistress of the house asked no questions and of fered no courtesy, but, after her guests had eaten their breakfasts, rapidly pre- pared, she led the way to a bedroom in the loft, where Abner Dimock flung him. self down upon the straw bed and fell sound asleep, leaving Hitty to the undis. turbed care Of her child. And occupa. ton enough that proved; for the little fellow was fretful and excited, so that nc hour for thought was left to his anxious and timid mother till the dinner-bel] awoke her husband and took him down. stairs. She could not eat, but, begging some milk for her boy, tended, and fed and sung to him, till he slept; and then all the horrors of the present and future thronged upon her, till her heart seemed to die in her breast, and her limbs failed to support her when she would have dragged herself out Of doors for one breath of fresh air, one refreshing look at a world untroubled and serene. So the afternoon crept away, and as soon as night drew on the journey was resumed. But this night was chill with the breath of a sobbing east wind, and the dim stars foreboded rain. Hitty shiv- cred with bitter cold, and the boy began to cry. With fierce curse Abner bade her stop his disturbance, and again the poor mother had hands and heart full to silence the still recurring sobs of the child. At last, after the midnight cocks had ceased to send their challenges from farm to farm, after some remote church clocks had changed one stroke on the damp wind, they began to pass through a large village; the lights burned in the windows, but white fences cleaned through the darkness, and sharp gable ends loomed up against the dull sky, one after another, and the horses hoofs flash ed sparks from the paved streets before the church, that showed it's white spire, spectre-lke, directly in their path. Here by some evil chance, the child awoke, and, between cold and hunger and fear, began one of those long and loud shrieks that no power can stop this side of stran- gulation. In vain Hitty kissed and coax ed, and halfcboked her boy, in hope to stop the uproar; still he screamed more and more loudly. Abner turned round on his seat with an oath, snatched the child from its mothers arms, and rolled it closely in the blanket. "Hold on minute, Bent" said he to his companion; :this yelp must be stop ped;" and stepping over to the back of the wagon he grasped the wife tightly with one arm an with the other he drop ped his child into the street. ''Now drive, Ben," said he, in the same hoarse whisper,-"drive like the Devil!" as her child fell, Hitty shrieked with such a cry as only the heart of mother could send out over newly-murdered infant. Shrek on shrek fast and loud and long, broke the slumbers of the village; moth ing Abner could do, neither threat nor force, short of absolute murder, would avail,-and there was to much real estate remaining of the Hyde property for Alb ner Dimock to spare his wife yet. Ben drove 6end-fashion; but before they pass ed the last house in the village, lights were glancing and windows grating as they were opened. Years after, I heard the story of such midnight cry borne past sleeping houses with the quick rat tie of wheels; but no one who heard it could give the right clue to its explana- ton, and it dried into legend. ~. The occurrence ol aurora boreais Ou- men boreale) in the zenith, on Sunday night has suggested reflections i'll the mind of spectator, which it is supposed at least, have the merit of novelty to recommend them to the attention of scientific inquirers. Without considering the hypothesis hitherto advanced for the occurrence of these pheno- mena, which my hypothesis, to say the least are defective and unsatisfactory, may it not be a philosophical conclusion, that both au- i rora borealis and rains, are caused by want of electricity in the atmosphere. That such as electricity exists is evident from certain known effects. Assuming the theories of Franklin and SPINNER, that it is an ETHEREAL fluid having certain fixed properties--that ii pervades the universe and that the heavenly bodies are great reservoirs of it, is not import ant to the purpose to inquire whether it may or may not be the agent of transmitting power from planet to planet, or of regulating the motions of the heavenly bodies. 1t is suffi- cient to know that il materially affects the condition of bodies on the surface of the earth. / 70 what extent these are affected by il is an open field for investigation; and, subject to the correction Of discovery and demonstration, the ensuing theory is propounded 1t is .af- irmed- 4 First, that electricity is compound prin- ciple. Second, that it has the properties of heat, permeability elasticity, or expansion and con- traction. Third, that it is uncomfortable and invisi- BILE. Fourth, that ii is fixed or free. Fifth that it has attractive, repellent and medium relations or properties. Sixth, that it is doubly positive and doubly negative. That it is compound principle is evident from the opposite properties which il possess / SEES. That it has properties of heat and permea- bility; that it is fixed or free, imponderable and invisible, and that it has affinity these are sufficiently evident. That il is doubly positive and doubly mega | tive, is assumed from the consideration that if it had not these properties the north and south poles of the earth would exhibit entire ly opposite conditions /; while il the north | positive attraction was identical with the south positive attraction, the compess would he detected towards either pole, and be turn ed round in passing the equator. | That it is elastic is predicted from the fact of its accumulation in the Leyden lar, and from other manifestations of its action. From the properties Of the elasticity and affinity of electricity, the following PROPOSE tions are deduced - | First, That gaseous and mineral exhalations from the surface of the earth are accompanied by a certain amount Of electricity, which neu- tralzes their property of density, and keeps / them suspended in the air. 1 Second, That when there is an accumulation of fixed electricity i'll the air, it is subject to condensation, in which free state il takes a direction, either back to the earth or TO the superior regions, according to the presence of means of conduction, while the bodies which it held in suspension, regaining theirde fall to the earth in the case of rain, or are at tracted and separated from earth in the case of borealis. Third, That one condition of electricity is attracted to the equator, and another condition to the poles. From these premises the con clusion is drawn, that rain and borealis are produced from the same cause, which consists OF the separation and condensation of cleo triety. Fourth. That rain is the effect of electricity leaving the atmosphere and descending into the ground, and that borealis is the effect o + electricity ascending into the superior regions of the atmospherer perhaps, attracted by other planetary influences. In support of these positions, it is to be re4 marked: FlFst. IHat tne amount OF rain is greatest at and towards the Equator, and the occur rance of boreais, is nearly limited to fifty de- grees from the poles. Second. That the occurrence of both is I'M der nearly similar conditions of atmospheric density. Third. That rains and borealis are nearly opposite elemental condit ions the one con- sisting of showers of water descendant; the other of showers of fire or of incandescept heat ascending. Fourth. That the effects of loss of heat by the atmosphere and its ratification are results common to both. There is one important difference, however, which would seem TO give to the borealis more the character of the agency of rositire cleo tricity, and to rain that of negatire electricity. viz. that rain is of an aberrant character, moving about, creating, and influenced by the wind whereas, borealis is fixed, having n pole of attraction at its apex and, what is more extraordinary, occurring in calm weather and creating no wind. Another popularity, or ditlererence is, that rain is generally fol- lowed by residue of clouds whilst the borealis, at its termination, leaves the sky clear, cloudless and rarihed. During the operation of perfect borealis, however, there is dense cloud in the nadir, which seems like sediment that it deposits, and is probably the grosser particles that are not attracted to the zenith.

From one slippery rock to another she made her way, until at last she stood upon the bank of the river. / Oh, how black and terrible was that toss ing waste of water! The foam-capped waves leaped up madly against the rocky shore, and the roaring of their voices was like the muttering of distant thunder There were brave hearts around the hills OF Pentland-but few would have ventured the passage of Mad River that night. Uttering one wild prayer for strength, Rachel unbound the ropes which held the frail raft used for crossing the stream to the giant oak upon the bank and then depos- iting her lantern and basket upon the barque. she stepped on herself, seized the long han died oar and pushed off! Oh, but it was a fearful conflict between the dreadful waters and the stern courage which lent strength to the arms of that he roic girl Once her heart grew faint with womanly fear, but thought of what she went to accomplish, nerved her on, and she cast all fear away. like velocity-then the raft glided smooth ly and gently-again, in the embrace of a trcacherous whirlpool it was nearly engulp ed-but at last, oh, Joy lit struck violently point of land! With few vigorous dry upon the beach, and seizing her basket the ruined bridge. 1t was as she expected. The whole vast structure had been torn away, and the wa ter dashed through the fearful gorge with appalling rapidity. She shuddered as she gazed for a moment down into the boiling black depth-what if she were too late She fancied that even then she heard the whistle of the coming locomotive, and caught the CLEAN of the great lamp upon its front. But no, it was only her imagina- tion and piling the faggots upon the track, she applied the light from her lantern. 1t did not ignite She was frantic with ter ror lest the dampness had rendered the wood incombustible, to the heat which she was a. BILE to give. She tore off her cotton shawl and cast it on the pile. A faint stream of light shot up, then broad lurid glow, and almost instantaneously the fire laid hold on the turpentine of knots, and the whole country was illumined in the radiance. Thank God ~ burst involuntarily from Rachel's lips. She brought brush wood from the forest and piled upon the fire +; and as the red tongues of fame rose higher and higher, SO the stream of thankfulness in the girls bo- som flowed freer and stronger up to that Power whose instrument she was. | Patiently she stood in the cold and wet the rain beating heavily on her uncovered head and shoulders, and dripping down the wavy masses of her soft, brown hair. 1 10 no al, I'D he thing combustible upon which she could lay she heard afar off the shrill whistle Of the approaching train. On it came, that black-winged monster, rumbling and snorting up the rugged val ley, with its vast freight of human life be- hind The speed was frightful, and for a moment Rachel feared that her signal would not be noticed; the next instant the sharp whistle of alarm rang out loud and clear the kissing steam rushed forth hot and fiery, the engine was reversed, and with shock like that of an earthquake, the train was brought to dead halt on the very brink of the gorge From these long, dark cars hundreds of human beings came pouring out, alarmed by the sudden stoppage, and perhaps wa kened from sound sleep by the violence of the shock | Oh, but there was deep horror on their faces. and strange trembling at their hearts, when, gazing down on that black abyss, they saw the grave which had been theirs but for the efforts of that pale-faced girl. Oh, how they crowded around her with their warm admiration-how enthusiast cally they thanked and praised her for what she had done what fervent blessing they called down upon her head Women S beautiful faces streamed with tears at the thought of her brave daring and swarthy mems heart beat quicker and stronger as, in fancy, they saw her tossing out on frail raft at the mercy of that furious river to save them from destruction. The old weather beaten engineer, who was | scarcely ever seen to exhibit emotion at anything, crowded his way to Rachel's side, and taking her hands in both of his, he lookedripto her face with q tear in either "God bless you ~ he uttered, impetuous- ly, and then rushing away he was lost in the crowd. The passengers were to return to Hart stein; and very earnestly they besought Ra- ming, when the swollen waters would have abated, and the passage of the river might be made with safety. "No," said she, ''that cannot be. I have little sister at home, and now that have done alr could, my duty lies with her God helping me shall cross the stream once more ~ AT this juncture a fine looking young man, wearing the undress uniform of a lieutenant in the navy, stepped forward, removing his cap said Lady, with all due respect, I declare that if you cross Mad River tonight, shall go with you have been on the water oc- easionally, and think can be of some as sistance in your voyage. Will you trust me 90 Rachel gazed up moment into the noble face Of the young lieutenant, and Offering him her hand, said, simply 81 can trust you" And so amid the cheers and acclamations of the people whom she had saved from death. The seargulls -infallible barometers- gath cred along the shore, and were lazily floating on the water. preening their feathers as they always do before sstorm. We had not made more than few miles offing, when the little scattered patches of white fleecy cloud that come in the van of the northcrs, made their appearances and fitted across the sky with extraordinary rapidity, and in less than two hours afterwards the sea was one seething, kissing expanse of foam, swept by one of the fiercest northers ever encountered. The New York Post notices the Scenery Of the Heavens ON Sunday night at length We quote: The ruby crown, gemmed and fringed by sparkling stars, retained its proud position in the zenith, and the tremulous waves of light hoated and quivered downwards like some imperial train waved by the cool night winds. At times it suggested mighty hand and an outstretched arm, bound ut the wrist with bracelet of ruby and diamond with the open palm held US if in benedction over the earth, while the fingers of light reached almost to the distant horizon. Soon, rs Everett has beautifully spoken Of Il somewhat similar scene, tho hands Of an gels shifted the glorious scenery Of the heav ems The mass Of apparent red cloud to fading, while the corresponding red cloud on the West seemed to sink into "a chaos Of dark cloud, that, with fringe of blue, skirted the Western horizon. While these changes we're taking place in the East and West, the wondrous crown above, moved u few degrees and then gradually faded. Flashes Of light covering many degrees. slowly condensed in to mi ghty luminous cloud, with its top near the zenith, this cloud gradually altering its shape, assumed forms both singular and suggestive. At one time it bore striking resemblance to an eagle, and then the slightest, almost impcrceptble change, transformed it into a tortoise. Then again it seemed to sweep across the heavens, presenting the appear ance of Il confused procession Of beings clad in ghostly shrouds, and reminding one of the dim heroes of Ossian. For about half an hour these remarkable changes took place, and then the lights gradually disappeared. In Il short time, however, they were resumed. Sheets OF the same white luminous cloud again Illuminated the sky. producing about the same amount OF light ~ the full moon, and the night became almost as the day. Ii must have been much like those de- scrbcd by DR.. Kane, Bayard Taylor, and other Northern travellers. OF the extent of the phenomena we have some idea, from the fact that the Geographic wires were affected by it in every direction.

Western Boundary Of Minnesota. WASHINGTON, Sept 10. Advices received by the General Land Of fee announces the completion on the 18th ult. of the survey of the western boundary of Minnesota, and the placing of the corner stone at the intersection of the northern and south ern divisions of the western boundary of that State. -Messrs. Hutton & Snow were the con- tractors to run and mark the western bounda- ry. The northern section of the boundary line is formed by the Red River of the North and its tributary, the Bots des Sioux river, which heads in Lake Traverse; and thence through that lake to its head. Here the sur, veyor work commenced across the short land portage to the head of Big Stone Lake, the source of the Minnesota river. Their instruc- tons were to mark the line distinctly between these two lakes, and plant iron monuments at the starting points at the head Of each lake. This appears by the despatch to have been DONE The boundary line then continues down through Big Stone Lake to where the Minnesota river issues from it. At this point another monument is placed, and then the western boundary of the State is line drop ping due south to the State of Iowa, the north ern boundary of which State at 43 deg. 80 min. of latitude, forms the base line for our western boundary

The March night had darkened down upon the little New England village of Ashdale.-- It was pretty place in Summer, lying be- tween two hills, on whose summits the ash trees lifted their green arms to the sky, all the long bright days, as if imploring Q benedic- tior, or spread them out lovingly over the white houses nestled round the one church in the vale below. But tonight it wore different aspect. A storm was upon the hills. A little snow and hail were borne upon it's wings, but not much. Chiefly it was the force of rushing winds j; shaking the leaflcss ash trees, hurling against closed windows swinging the bell in the old church tower, till it gave forth now and tLen, a dirge-like peal, as if the dead were tolling their own reqniems. Many homes there were where the wild scene without seemed but 10 heighten, by the force of contrast, the blessed calm within homes where smiling infants slept warm and still, through the twilight, in the soft hush of mother-bosoms, and happy children gathered round the knee of father or grandsire, to hear again some simple story or thoughtful ones looked into the fire, and fashioned from the embers brave castles, ill which they were to dwell in the coming time, with over all, the sunshine of youth and hope. Twenty years from now they would look into the embers, and see these fair castles, in which they had never come to abide, with ruined windows and blackened walls 'The twilight memory over all, And the silence of death within But in one house no stories were told to gladly listening ears--no soft evening hymn husbed slumbering babes to rest-no chicren's eager eyes looked into the embers. It was the stateliest house, by far, in the little village "a lofty mansion, gleaming white through the trees, with the roof supported by massive pillars. No where did the evening fire burn brighter, but into it looked only two old peo' ple, worn and sorrowful, with the shadows of grief and time upon their shrivelled faces two who had forgotten, long ago, their youths fair castles who looked back over waste fields of memory, where not even settling sun rays gilded the monuments built to their dead hopes They sat there silently. They had sat si 1 lently ever since the darkness gathered. Int lofty. we'll furnished room was lighted only bJ the wood-fre's glow, and in the corncr strange shadows seemed to gather, with beck 1 onipg hands and white brows gleaming spec 1 trally through the darkness. Towards them now and then. the wife looked with anxious searching gaze then turned back again t. the fire, and clasped her hands over the hear that had learned through many trials the har lesson of patience.

LISA guarantee that their husbands and fathers, and brothers are like men of intelligence and refinement, who appreciate their rental capacities, and desire their countenance in their undertakings. Woman's love is the great lever which rouses men to action. The general, as he plans the strategic COM binations which are to insure victory, looks forward to recompense dearer than the laurels upon his brow; the soldier. as he trudges along on the weary march, or min giles In the scenes of the battlefield, even with death around him, forgets awhile the carnage, and turns his thoughts to the fond girl he left behind him; the mariner, tenn pest-tossed, driven by rude waves, sings merrily aloft as be thinks of the little cot tagc by the shore, where his wife and dear ones await him; the statesman. as he devi- ses. amid deep and painful thought, plans OF government which are to tell upon his own and his comntry's fame, never loses sight ofthe joys which await him when cabi- net councils are over, and he enters the por- tails home; the sentinel, as he PAGES his wea- ry watch, loves the moonlight tramp. that he may look beneath its rays at the dear memento of mothers or a sisters love. - Over man. in all his relationships, the inau- ence of woman hangs like charm. De- prive US Of your influence, which digniies US and stimulates us to noble deeds, and we become worse than barbarians. Let it be ours, and we can brave the lannon's mouth Or face-danger in ten thousand forms. You stimulate all that is good. You. check in us lgnoble purposes. You have also an i'm portant influence upon posterity. The ear ~ impressions which the child receives from you outliye all the wisdom Of later days. Sages may reason and philosophers may teach, but the voice which we heard in in fancy will ever come to our ears, bearing a mothers words and mothers counsels.- Continue to instil into your children virtue and patriotism. Undue them with proper veneration for the fathers of liberty. Teach them to love their country, and to labor for its good, as the great end of their ambition. Bid them proudly maintain our institutions. Point them to the deeds of their ancestors. Mark these their escutcheon, and bid them hand it down to their children as free from stain as it came to them. Do this, ladies, and your influence will not be lost in the flu ture. EDTroR.-It is not our desire to appear before the public, in print, for renown, but sim ply to relate few incidents relative to Union Sabbath School celebration in New Jefferson, on Saturday, September 10th, of the present year. We were by the nature Of our business, en- abled to be present on the memorable occasion, memorable to all who were assembled, either as spectators or participants of the exercises OF the day. The morning was cool and threatened rain, which increased the anxiety of those engaged in the affair. But when the time came, few drops of rain pattered on the face ofOld mother earth, ond then ceased-leaving the good peo- pie of Jefferson to enjoy their festival, unmoles- ted by the aqueous element of nature. At IL O'Clock the Sabbath School met in the German Reformed Church, and were very appropriately addressed by Revs. McKirahan and Mcfarland. The school was then escorted, with sweet mu- sic, by the Jefferson Brass Band, to the western part of the village, where beauty and the lux | ~N~--N attractive. Without fattery we may safely say, that the people OF Jefferson and vicinity have nice discrimination in getting up an af- fair of that kind. The children were stationed around the table, which presented pleasing sight, when they, with great eagerness, and in nice order and decorum, despatched the escu- lents to their complete satisfaction. The spec tators were then invited forward, and the table was cleared as if by magic. We cannot forego the opportunity of speak ing few words in commendation Of that beau tiful table, groaning as it were, beneath its great load of luxuries It was 80 feet long, so many arches, stood up in bold relief, which graatly augmented its beauty. Vases and sma IL wreaths were lavishy distributed, which gave it the appearance Of desert splendidly decora- ted with flowers, shedding their "ambrosial sweets around" Methinks the fairies would not deign to sport amid such an array of beau ty. In the middle stood an object Of peculiar attraction. 1t was an artificial representation Of a mound, having for its drapery grape vine, full of beautiful, dark blue grapes. Indeed, it looked like an Eden, where the nsetul and beautiful, combined to beguile old time, and like phantom, drive loneliness away. The committee of ladies' who superintended the de- coration OF the table, and the ge tting up Of the splendid cakes, are entitled to praise for their indeatigable exertions the taste and style they exhibited in their laudable enterprise. Their success speaks nobly of their ideas of the fanci- full. We were favorably impressed with the fact, that the young ladies and gents, with an ambition and spirit equal to the task, took very interesting and active part in all the exer- cises. In conclusion, suffice it to say, that the chill iren were escorted back to the Chnrch, and dismissed in good order and the whole affair was conducted in a manner in perfect conformi- " to the cause of Sabbath School interests Young ladies and gents you are engaged in and responsible duty. The good you do here in the Sabbath School, will be called by angels with infinite delight Though vour work is begun here Oh earth, it will rise, ,loom and bring forth fruit in eternal felicity, where there will be banquet of celestial lux lrics set before you, the constituents of which will be eternal happiness. EDITOR DEMocRAr:-For the first time within the memory of the present gene ration, Suutherners, in this latitude, have been treated with the magnificent spectacle of genuine aurora boreakis, or polar light. Such phenomena are com mon in more Northern climates, and at. tract but little attention generally among the masses Of the people. The present season, however, they have ap- peared with more than usual splendor in all parts of North America, owing to the unusual heat of the summer and fall, and, as consequence, the superabund- ance of electricity with which the at mosphere is charged. 1t is probable that the present autumnal equinox will present very interesting meteorological phenomena, accompanied in some places with unusually destructive storms-a , legitimate result of the thcrmo-electrical condition Of the atmosphere, and not as one whilome, politico-military parson, Col. Dick Stewart, would have us be- lieve, Goods silent messengers, warm ing men that the great day of His wrath will come" It is evident from the COM munieation of the Col. in Sundays Delta, that his attention has Of late years been directed more to earthly than to heaven ly objects =; hence his attempt to- ex- plain celestial phenomena, shows that he is surrounded by terrestrial fogs, which have to him the appearance of luminous atmosphere. The Col. denies that the spectacle witnessed on the night of the 1st inst. was real aurora boyealis for the reasons, lst: 1t made its appear ance at too late an hour of the night! That was done on purpose to CRAFTY the more fashionable portion of the commu- nifty who keep late hours. End and 3rd: The aurora of the LIST presented lurid red colors, and features of terror repul- sive to the mind; whereas, the true aurora is always beautiful, soft and inviting to the intellectual mind" These objections onl y go to show that the con- dition of the mind of the observer was out Of order, and not in unison with the spectacle. The n. Y Journal Of Commerce Of the 29th ult., contains the following de- scription Of a similar phenomenon wit messed in that city the previous even ing. Strange that it should excite no feelings of repulsion and terror in the minds of the wicked Gothamites: Shortly after sunset last evening, the Northern Heavens were illuminated by a display of the Aurora Borealis which / in brilliancy and magnifccnce has sell dom been surpassed in this latitude. At about eight o'clock, persons up town looking from the street Northwards over the tops Of the buildings thought that an extensive fire was raging in that quarter. Between nine and ten, when our attention was called to the spectacle, rose-red corona had formed at the zenith, which seemed to distri- butte its arched streamers of light in all towards the East and West. Red tinges like great clots Of blood, overspread at times large portion Of the sky. The Pickering streamers or | brushes Of light diverged from the Au- rora towards the zenith; their active and beautiful motions dazzeled the eye, while the brilliancy and rapidity with which the corruscations appeared in va rious parts of the armament filled the spectator with feelings Of admiration and wonder. We hope to see some ac- count Of this interesting phenomenon scientifically reported. At midnight the main arch was still visible. QUITE A ROMANTIC AFFAIR. The traveller who has been fortur ate enough to sit beside an unknown beauty in railway car riage, and had his conversational powers brought into play by her socability, can comprehend the bliss off good-looking bachelor, whose car adyen- ture We are about to relate: This worthy gentleman was a passenger on the Central R. road Monday last and happened to be in a car that pretty well stocked with humani- ty. He had managed to retain seat from the commencement of the journey, until the train reached stopping place, where a fresh supply of travellers entered it, when he gallantly surrender ed it to an old lady, and made up his mind to stand awhile. Now it happened that young and stylish lady noticed the act and so pleased was she to an old woman treated politely, that she at once removed her carpet bag from the end of the seat she occupied and invited the gentleman to take its place. Nothing 10th, our hero accepted the modest invitation, and was engaged in a friendly conversation with the belle of the train. They chatted in lively style until ''the shades of night were falling fast when the ladys utterance grew slower, then indistnct, then altogether ceased, for she was asleep. Not being disposed to follow her example, the gentleman amused himself by watching his fellow passengers, and was reminded of his companion s presence by her head touching his shoulder Morpheus had her completely in her folds, and by a series of graceful mods she unconsciously sought the support of her railway acquaintance. The bachelor delighted with the first gen. tie touch, but his pleasure, when in the sweet abandonment of sleep, her form nestled down until its whole weight rested OH him, battles de- scription The better to support his lovely bur- den, he placed his arm around her waist and then gave himself up to the delirium of the moment. After passing the next station, gentleman en- tered the ming the persons above referred to, and commenced examining the face of each oc- cupant as though he was in search of some friend In tie darkness of the hour he passed the sleeper and her supporter without noticing them, and it was only when he turned to retrace his steps that the scene attracted his attention. In moment the shade of anxiety on his fea- lures was succeeded by frown, and he stepped quickly to the side of the fair sleeper. As his hand descended heavily upon her should er, she started opened her eyes and sprang to her feet "blushing celestial rosy red" Before the bachelor could speak, the new conner politely in formed him that he would take care of his own wife, if be had no objecti ons, and straightway led the lady to another seat. The explanation that cnsued unfolded the fact that the young lady had been on visit for some time, and was returning to the faithful husband, whose mpa.ience led him to meet her half way Eager to meet her he entered the car only to find her asleep in the arms of a stranger! OF course the stranger told how it happened but the frown did not pass away from the brow Of the husband until they left the car Ladies should be careful how thew fail asleep on the wrong vest pattern.

The Mountains. There is nothing SO simple and apparently as are mountains. And yet there is no variety in tree, in plain, in river or lake, that can be compared to mountain vari- ations. Upon nothing else does the atmos- phere work such wonderful effects. We do not refer to those vast heights whose snow and ice.clad SUBMITS play with such witching effects with light and color but to our lower and home-bred mountains. This one, behind us, not two thousand feet high, is solemn necromancer, forever putting forth new fam cies. Itwears one face in the morning; it chan ges its countenance at noon it surprises you with still another at night. 1t has one face for heat, and one for cold. 1t shags and boards Itself with mists, looking down upon you venerable as hoary seer. Then it drives away every vestige of cloud, and re- veals to the eye each line, every depression, every crease and crevice, with such plainness that it changes the whole mountain express sion, and you doubt whether you have ever before seen it. A new picture stands before you every day, and yet its identity is pre- served, !so that it maintains its old associa- tions with new sites of beauty. Not cloud can come near without paying some tribute. Sometimes you shall see vast range of white, glistening clouds, piled up in banks and brilliant bouders, one upon another silently rising up behind the green mountain, that thus appears but foreground figured upon this magnificent range Of air-mountains. A. other times, fleets of clouds are seen plotting their way quietly through the air, and letting down their shadows upon the mountain side, as if to anchor there. But both cloud-ship and cloud-anchor move on, dark below and white above! 1t would seem as if the smile of the cloud was the ilown OF the mountain. | But all these are mere fancies, compared with the grandeur of mountains when storms make them their walking-ground. After long heat and dryness, the mountains seem to shrink back, lose distinctness, and become al most insignificant. The summer, which shrivcls vegetation with long drouths, seems to parch and shrink the very rocks. But, suddenly, from the South there come up the tokens of thunderstorm. Storms especial ly love mountain highways, and walk upon their SUBMITS with a majesty unknown in lowlands Upon such theatre, the specta- Gle, lifted up above you, exhibits itself with a grandeur that recalls the noble old concep- ton, that God rides upon storms, and taber- naces himself in clouds upon mountain tops. Indeed, we never see that haf-sacred motion of cloud-tolds rolling out from the interior, as if there were an inner presence which drove forth the terrified mists, and justified their fear by headloug thunder bolts and fierce lightning-Aashes, without an irresistible inn preston of a real living agency at work within the storm; and that clouds arc but the hiding of the Divine Presence! Nor is the Imagination lessened when the murky splendor passes on, and the mountain lifts up its cleansed head and sides with such vivid green, and in such clearness and exquis- lite beauty, that you feel as if they had been in communion with superior influence, and had received baptism from on high. This never seemed more striking than yesterday While in church, in the morning, there came came on sudden dash of rain and hail. We rode home with the mountains before us wear ing robes of clouds, and grand with flying storm. 10 look at these tops, and recall all the passages Of the Old Testament which speak divnely of mountains, would be SER mon more impressive than any from the living voice.--Reu. Insurance Against Fire. There is a subject to which We wish to call the especial attention of every reader of The AHeghanian, and it is the subject of INSURANCE. Amongst all the various institutions of the day, it looms up as one of the most important and useful. Modern times have furnished to mankind variety Of inventions and means for improving their condition, but certainly none of them can better or more worthily excite our admiration or gratitude than the system of Insurance. 1t has become a part of our civilization, and gives unmis- taxable evidence of the wise policy and constantly progressive spirit of our people We live in an age of progress, and Insu- rance is one of its concomitants. 1t is not a new system, comparatively speaking, but it is one which has recently been developed and properly brought before the people. The benign influence which the system Of Insurance exerts upon our present So cial organization, should commend it to the patronage of every property-owner in the land, and to the encouragement of every philanthropist, whether an owner of property or not. There live but few individuals who would care to part with property, without some fitting equivalent either in present or in prospect. There are few, no matter how rich in this world goods they may be, who have property that they feel able to lose, even though that property be trifing and of little val ue. And yet, how often do we find it that many who are enjoying the comforts of hard-earned home-many who are fast pressing onward to independence, are nearly if not entirely ruined by their neg lect to insure. The earnings of whole life may be swept away by single fire, and the party neglecting to indemnify himself against such calamity be plunged into state of hopeless destitution- Thrown upon the cold charities of the world, his youth and energy gone, he perhaps seeks consolation from the intox- icating bowl, and drags out miserable existence, rendered still more SO by the consciousness of his own folly and neglect Perhaps, too, he may have family. If so, how bitterly must he realize the truth OF the saying, "If a man provide not for his own household, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infdel." What change is thus wrought in the social position of that household! Home and its endearments gone, husband and faith er unable to provide for their necessities, the mother untitled to earn a livelihood the children without education-and all without hope-they too are cast upon the cold charities of the world-they too are made to feel the bitter pangs of penury and want This is sad picture truly. but not overdrawn. Its counterpart MIGHT readily be produced but comparisons are | odious. Against reverses like these, Insurance furnishes adequate means of protection. 1t has been well said, that ga stitch in time saves nine,' and nowhere does the maxim better apply than to insurance upon property. But small pittance from your income is required to secure yourself against the probable loss of your house or your barn. Natures Song in the Night. Night hath its songs. Have you never stood by the sea at night and heard the peb- bles sing and waves chant Gods glories ? Or have you never risen from your couch and thrown up the window of your chamber and listened ? Listened to what ? Silence, save now and then low murmering sound, which seems sweet music then. And have you not hncied that you heard the harp CT God playing in Heaven Did you not conceive that yon stars that those eyes of God looking down on you were also mouths of song-that every star was singing Gods glories, sing as it shone its Almighty Maker, and his lawful well-deserved praise Night hath its songs We do not need much poetry in our spirit to catch the song of night and here the spheres as they chant praises which are loud to the heart, though they be silent to the ear-the praise of the mighty God, who bears up the unpillared arch of heaven, and moves the stars in their courses

Many months ago in the neighboring town of Belchertown young man sought and received the promise of the hand of young lady, whose home was in the lap of luxury, whose mental and personal attractions made all pleasant around her. Examining Bottoms of Wells. 1t is not generally known, we think, how easy matter it is to examine the bottom of a well, cistern, or pond of water by the use of a common mirror. When the sun is shining brightly, hold mirror so that the reflected rays of light will fall into the water A bright spot will be seen at the bottom, so light as to show the smallest object very plainly. By this means we have examined the bottoms Of wells fifty feet deep, when half full or more of water. The smallest straw, or other small OBJ ject, can be perfectly seen from the serface.- In the same way one can examine the bottoms of pounds and rivers, if the water be somewhat clear, and not agitated by winds or rapid motion If well or cistern be under cover, or shaded by buildings, so that the sunlig ht will not fall near the opening, it is only necessary to employ two mirrors, using one to reflect the light to the opening, and an other to send it down perpendicularly into the water Light may be thrown fifty or a hundred yards to the precise spot d esired, and then reflected downward. We have u.s. ed the mirrors with success to reflect light around field to a shaded spot, and also to carry it from a south window through two rooms, and then into cistern under the north side of the house. Halfa dozen reflec- tons of the light may be made, though each mirror diminishes the brilliancy Of the light. Lei any one not familiar with this method try it, and he will find it not only useful, but pleasant experiment twill perhaps reveal a mass of sediment at the bottom of well, which has been little thought of, but which have been fruitful source of disease, by its decay in the water.

Over the wide, deep sea, where roll the great pillows of years, | can see the beautiful land of hope and youth, from which / embarked many long years ago, glad and happy. Life prom ised me much, and fearlessly l steered over the bounding waves. Why should fear! Love and joy encompassed me; there were light barks beside my own; the sky was sunny, and the unmeasured depths If the grand ocean that lay be- fore me danced merrily in the sunlight. All? the dawn of my life voyage was royalty fair. Wealth, hope, hoane, and love crowned my spirit with uuspeakable glory, and Harry Icons ahianced bride, the idolized child of wealthy parents, the darling of gay social circIe-what | could [ have to wish for? But there came changes such as must come to re- mind us Of our mortality, our weak ness. 1t needs not now to tell how death and change, those cold iconoclasts, took, one by one, every idol of my life, and left me desolate, wrecked, hopeless, ere yet eigh- teen summers had matured their blossoms and ripcned their fruits for me. 1t was a wild, wild struggle. All the pillows of agony rolled over me. Ny ruddcrless bark beat about wildly under sky in which there was no light, neither hope O. any brightness. I prayed to die, bu death came not; many months | strug- gIed feebly with gloom; and then, cold, passive, inactive, l was not made perfect through suffering; was crushed. Two years moved lstlessly through the halls of our city manson-alas! it was mine only now. received the visits of my nearest acquaintance, and opened my stately halls for theil pleasure, but all the while waited-oh! so YEARLY. I could not rally from my great grief, and when they brought Harry Icons gold haired bride to me, | only turned my dark, sad eyes upon them both, and then I left them. l could not speak calmly to the woman who had supplanted me in the heart of the only man that could ever be loved by me. Not that l loved him then-oh! no, po-but for lis sake ] mourned a broken trust, and on him, al unworthy, had wasted love that could never be recalled. At last, one day, as 1 was weeping over the grave Of those be- loved ones whom we laid in Gods keep ing, thought, new and interesting, came to me. For many days [ searched through the haunts of the great city, and one day very much astonished my good house-keeper by giving into her charge s little girl of three years, with the request that she should be cleaned and dressed and sent to me. Mrs. Arden never ques toned, and an hour later the golden-hair ed little girl who sat on my lap, hsped out my name, and laying her dimpled lips on mine, lisped. Il am your May, Mamma Flory." did not heed the innuendoes anc sneers of the world in which l had lived but sold the old city mansion, and sen the books and the pictures to the deal country home-sweet Riverside. Thith Ell, with May Leslie, [ migrated, and there for many long years we lived together And truly she was my May, my morn ing, my sunbeam, else how could [ hav' borne the old associations of Riverside But when l sat with May on the sea where years before Harry Leon hac pledged me his truth, where he had rea( and sang, and talked with me, her sof voice and her strange questioning brough me away from the bitter past, from tn staenant waters where my dear hopes haC been wrecked, to the duty of the present There were times when 1 would hav' been alone to have mourned cor the low which had lived its glorious but brief lif at that country seat upon the HUDSON But by-andby l learned to love it'll May as l had never thought to love an, earthly thing again. 1 would teach her she should be perfect in soal as in form but how, how might I, sorrow-crushed sinful, teach Aers And so, feeling, "Too great for me the task. to lead soul Unscathed through earthly fires / learned to pray, and laid my burden a the feet of the Infinite. Once upon a time-and IA very long time ago it was, for Ruric was the son of Holder who killed Balder, son of the god of Odin- | once upon time, when Ruric reigned over Denmark, the province OF Jutland was gov erned by two brothers, in the capacity of | joint yice-roys. One OF these, named Hor- wendil, slew the King of Norway in single | combat, and presented so large share of | Norwegian booty to Ruric, that the grateful | monarch bestowed upon him the hand of his | daughter Gerutha. on this marriage Hamlet was the result. Fengo, the other viceroy. instead of re- joicing at his brothers good fortune, muir | dered him out Of sheer envy, and married Gerutha himself. To account for this singu- lar proceeding, he explained to King Ruric, | that the deceased was in the habit of NAL | treating his wife to such a degree that his murder was absolutely necessary, in order to relieve most charming and inotfensive lady from an exceedingly disagreeable position. | King Ruric, who tenderly loved his daugh | ter, found this explanation perfectly sat | siactory, and confirmed the second mar | rage. Thus, for time, the matter blew over; but, | in the meanwhile the boy Hamlet, thinking | that he might be murdered in his turn, be | gan TO feign idiocy, that he might thus APP | pear too insignificant for his uncle's suspi- cions. He jabbered a great deal of nom | sense; he contrived that his ngure should | approach as nearly possible To that of | scarecrow, and he smutted over his face, so that his features were scarcely disccrnible. | However, when he made certain wooden | hooks, and having baked them in the fire, concealed them carefully, saying that they | were arrows for his fathers murderer, the more shrcwd persons OF the court, notwith- standing the laughter OF the fools, deemed | there was some method in bis madness" ! and communicated their doubts to the vice roy. Fengo, therefore, determined to watch his nephew closely, and, on one occasion when Hamlet took Il ride into the woods with some youths of his own age, it was expected that his true character would be revealed. But his foster-brother warned him that he was surrounded by spies, and accordingly, to sus- tain his character for imbecility, he mounted 4 Aan1 IL Al,<s =. which he used as bridle--thereby causing much laughter and diversion. Had Hamlet lived at the end of the seven teenth century instead of flo arshing at the commencement of the year nothing, we should have concluded that he framed his sham character on the model of Charles the Second as described by that famous epigram, which says that the Merry Monarch s'never said a foolish thing, And never did wise one" Since, while by the excessive. stupidity of his acts he maintained his reputation for insan- ity, he constantly shook the very belief he wished to establish by sayings of remarkable shrewdness. Thus, on the occasion of the notable ride into the wood, wolf happened TO cross his path What's that?" said Hamlet. "A young foal," replied one of the attend ants winking, no doubt, at the resi-. Aha quoth Hamlet, there are many such foals at Fengo's court" Ere the sting accustomed by this SARCASM had quite ceased to Jingle, the party arrived at the sea-shore, where the rudder of wreck ed ship was the first object that met their gaze. The graeeless youths, intending once more to poke their fun " at the demented prince. exclaimed: Look, what big knife we have foundr' But Hamlet reflected for a while, and then said, gravely: "Of IA truth the ham must have been large, that such a knife was iuten- ded TO cut" thereby referring to the sea- and possibly the satin, S. thereof But, not quieted by this sharp retort, his facttious comrades proceeded to explain to him that the sand on The shore was flour, and that the pebbles were greats But Hamlet said: /" Such -four a. that has been ground by the storm and the WITHDRAWING pillows" These jokes may not appear very brilliant now, but they made great sentiment in The year nothing, and the court of King Ruric was often convulsed with laughter on hearing of .Hamlet's last" Indeed there Is no doubt that Hamlet and Yorick were historically one and the same person. He, therefore. by the counsel OF a friend, feigned to leave the country on some urgent matter, that during his supposed absence, Hamlet might hive an interview with his mother. at which the same friend engaged 10 be present, un- seen. Naturally enough something began TO move beneath the straw, aud that somelhing-which the reader may, If he pleases call Polonus-was immediate ly transfxed by the sword OF Hamlet Queen Gerutha, shocked at this new manifestation OF madness, began to weep aloud, but Ham let. dropping the mask, read her severe lecture on the improperly OF her position. His words seemed to have an effect as, indeed well they might, for they were marked by ruffianly coarseness which could not be ex- ceeded, and Of which Shakespeare does not convey the slightest idea. This is 4 phenomenon, we are assured, which has never before taken place, even among the many freaks on the telegraph wires. Wake mournful muse, and touch thy saddest string -,- a~-a-s-ss Breathe forth in words of plaintive melody A dirge for the departedl Not for him The fallen hero of the battle field, Whose name is waited on the wings of fame, Till echo sends it back from distant shores; Not for the dead Whose dust arrayed in all the pomp of state, Is borne in solemn grandeur to the tomb. Nor vet for her, the maid in beauty's bloom, With brightest charms of youth and love entwined, Torn ruthless from affections fond embrace, 3 And sent away to feed the loathsome worm. Oh not for these awake the mournful lyre For nought is lost to earth when these depart. The riven heart soon heals, and wealth and fame Bequeathed; descend to crown new brows, and fiIl With other forms the momentary void. A deeper grief demands a sadder strain! An honest man has left the shores Of earth! One of the noble uncorrupted few Who firmly trod the devious walk of life, With open brow and heart that dared the light. Whose steadfast virtue needed not the fear Of future vengeance to sustain its strength; One who calpd God, his Father, and all men His 6rofhers--and no brother ever wronged. Oh is not earth the poorer for the void! Is not humanity loser by his gain? A state may lose its head millionaire Lie down in shroud of gold, and none shall feel Their presence wantlng-yet for such as he True hearts shall weep, and build his monument Within the spacious hall of memory, And w.'eathe it round with virtuous resolves. Of such as Mee our brother, earth has none Too many; and we feel loneliness Thy vanished presence never more shall fill. Yet there is sweetness in the tears we shed. And in our solemn mourning there is joy. For while we miss thy genial spirit here Shading its cheerful influence DER our hearts, And while we sigh for thy untimely fate We hear a whisper from the higher sphere Saying, God reigns, and doeth all things we'll !" Beyond the shadowy mist encircling earth Faith sees glorious land of fadeless flowers; Trod by the pure in heart; no stormy sky, No dark ming night-no blight of joy is there; No sundering of natures dearest ties; No ehangeful friendship and no tickle love, But every aspiration of the soul fufll'd And full fruitiop of hopes brightest dreams. There is thy home-wc cannot wish thee hence; But humbly pray for heavens assisting grace, To walk with footsteps firm, the path of night Till death shall ope' for us the door to life, And bid us enter and rejoice with thee. FLORENCE. Keelersville, Sept. 18th, 1859.

THE AURORA BOREALIs. The New York Times furnishes the follow. ing account of the Aurora of Sunday night week. The same phenomenon was viewed in this city, but on a less splendid scale, probably owing TO the fact that no clouds were visible to reflect the transient glory of the heavens: The present generation have listened with wonder and admiration TO the stories their fathers and mothers have told, them of. auroras and meteors. They have opened ears and mouths and eyes as they heard of stars falling from the heavens like rain, of the sky at night becoming red as with blood, and in the day time of its being so darkened that stars were visible. Few have had opportunities of wit Messing these sublime displays but on Sunday night the heavens were arrayed in drapery more gorgeous than they have been for years The phenomena then witnessed are worthy re. cording, and comparing with previous appear ances OF like character, as they will be refer red to hereafter among the events which occur but once or twice in a lifetime Sunday was very much such day as could be expected at this season of the year. Per haps it may have been trihe cooler than usual but this was attributed to the rain which fell in the morning. With the change of wind to the west, the temperature fell notceably toward. evening, until it seemed like that which more appropriately belongs to the middle or latter part of September. Soon after sunset, the streamers which mark every appearance of the Aurora were visible in the north. As the twi light deepened, the merry dancers ventured from their hiding-places and played along the horizon as though successive sheets of impal pable flame were sweeping over the sky. Then they shot up to a point nearer the zenith, and | ,a,p Al al - and west. The flashes from the south were fewer and less brilliant. The appearance Of the horizon in this direction was in striking contrast with that towards the north. Then a bright arch, spanning nearly ninety degrees sprang up, supporting and apparently origina ting three floating, quivering sheets of fire. TIC | the south, the sky was of q dark leaden.colored hue, which contrasted oppressively with the surrounding brilliancy. At first, the light was of that peculiar whitish tinge which all have observed IN similar displays on winter nights | This became deeper and more intense until il | lighted up the night as though the moon were shining. With this, beautiful tint of pink finally mingled. The clouds of this color were most abundant to the northeast and northwes of the zenith. There they shot across one another, intermingling and deepening until the | sky was painfully lurid. There was no figure the imagination could not find portrayed by | these instantaneous flashes. The beautiful ceronal of light which was first exhibited north of the zenith point, was gradually thrust further and further to the south, until it became sta | tionary at point the definite locality of which the astronomers must settle. Between 10 and l02 o'clock, the display was overpoweringly brilliant and beautiful. After that, II gradual | ly faded. Now and then there were light flashes, but the pink hue gave way almost en-, tirely to the yellow. 1t was remarkable as in. dicating the perfect transparency and lumin. BUSINESS of these sheets of flame, that the stars whose light was not eclipsed by this superior brilliancy, were distinctly visible through their covers of light. Such was the Aurora, as thousands wit messed it from housetops and from pavements Many imagined that they heard rushing sounds as if Eolus had let loose the winds Others were confident that a sweeping, as if of flames was distinctly audible; but if these same indi viduals will but listen this or any other evening as attentively as they did Sunday, they can satisfy themselves that the identical sounds are always perceptible on a quiet night. Undoubtedly, the watchmeD of the skies were on guard in all the observatories through. out the land, and to these the scientific obser vations must be left. When the Scientific As us shall remember this Aurora as a thing OF the past, we shall be favored with detailed &C. counts of the time of its exact appearance, OF the precise locality where it was brightest, and finally, long discussions as to the cause will follow. "Some account of similar phenomena in times gone by will undoubtedly be of interest in this connection. "Pliny and Aristotle record phenomena iden- teal with those which later times have wit. messed. The ancients ranked this with other celestial phenomena, as portending great events. In 1860, historians state it appeared in London, in the shape of burning spears, similitude which would be no less appropriate now than it was then. Frequent displays are recorded during the fifteen years following that date. During the latter half of the seventeenth century, the phenomena were frequently visible, oftentimes being characterized by remarkable brilliancy. After l745, the displays suddenly diminished, and were but rarely seen for the next nine years. The last century, until within the last twenty years, has been favored in a remarkable degree. One of the most interest ing periods of the display of the Aurora was during the years 1885, 1886, and 1887, the last exhibition of special interest occurring on No vember IL. Astronomers tell US that the light centres around the magnetic pole when the display is of sufficient brilliancy to define the curve, and, taking this point as that of measurement they have attempted to calculate the height of the sheets of light above the earth. Various OBJ servations made by Prof. Olmsted, in conjunc- ton with Prof. A. c. Twining, of New Haven, fix its elevation, on different occasions, at 423 100, IA, and 100 miles. Prof Olmsted claims that it is rarely less than 20 miles from the earth, and never more than l60 above it. "What is the origin of this remarkable phenomena? The ancients asked the question, and the moderns reply by repeating the inter rogation. The most popular theory attributes it to electricity, but that agent has been made responsible for everything which men did not know how to account for otherwise. The late Prof 0lmsted maintained that Its origin was cosmical, or, in other words, that the earth, in revolving on its orbit at certain periods, passes through nebulous body, which evolved this strange light in more or less brilliancy, as the body was larger or smaller. To support this the. DRY, he attempted to establish that there were fixed epochs for its display in the highest degree of brilliancy. He fixed the length OF these peri. DDS at from 60 to 50 years, and, if we remember Alright, named 1890 as the time when we might look for another appearance. The remarkable display of Sunday night gives those who have so strongly contested this idea strong argu. ment against it, and launches astronomers who have anchored TO it upon the sea of conjecture again. Sabbath geaaing. The Empire of God. Prof. Mitchell, in closing his series Of lectures on Astronomy, said Now, my friends, must close this long course of lectures. We have passed from pIannet to PLANETS, from sun to sun, from system to sys- TEN. We have found other island univer- ses sweeping through space. The great unfn- ished problem yetremains, Whence came this uni verse? Have all those stars which glitter in the Heavens been shining from all eternity Has our globe been rolling around the sun for ceaseless ages Whence, whence this magnif- cent architecture, whose architrayes rise in spen dor before US in every direction? Is it all the work of change? | answer, no; it is not the work of change. Who shall reveal to US the true cosmography of the universe by which we are surrounded?
