New York Letter. New York Letter. From our Regular New York Correspondent. New YORK, Sept. 2, 1859. Our cool and breezy days and nights, soft ly illumined with the rainbow lights of the North, invite back the wandering children of Gotham. Preparations are making to receive the returning flock with open arms the closed and dusty blinds are opened and refreshed with showers Biddy withdraws from the parlor to the kitchen again, signing that she can no long receive her gallant lowers on the crimson brocade, commonly held sacred to the guests of misses" The schools and churches are being repaired for reopening; the theatres also are making ready to begin the fall campaign, with bril- liant programmes and freshly cushioned seats. Young men who have gone seedy for months together because there were no ladies In town, feel the necessity of fresh invest ment in the articles which make so much of the man in this part of the world. Soon Broadway will be gay with the fall fashions. Our men, in their business suits, are quite as gay looking as the fairer promenaders. Scarlet cravats, high colored vests, and wool suits, woven of divers colored yarn, make quite pleasant contrast to the dead black and white uniform in which only a man is supposed to be dressed. Somebody has said that he could distinguish New Yorker anywhere by the " cut of his ib." Our Broadway tailors cultivate certain jaintiness of pattern which is quite their own. Just now, the city is fuller than ever of strangers, buying goods to sell through the TALL and winter to the four quarters of the United States. An immense amount of business will be done with the South, and it is hoped now that the Western trade will begin to improve. The northern cities and manufacturing districts will undoubted en- Joy prosperity and buy goods freely, as they will have the advantage Of low prices for wheat, with good employment for their manufacturing establishments at fair range of profits. Large failures are being made in the stock market by brokers who have been attempt ing to control important stocks. The public are beginning to see through this sort of gambling, and are not so easily de- ceived by made-up "rise" or d" fall" as was formerly the case. The time has been when it was possible for parties owning but a few shares of railroad stock, to depress or elevate the market at pleasure by fictitious sales-thus playing with the property of their neighbors for their own gain; but the palmy days of the bulls and bears are over. The losses have been chiefly made, not by operators, but by business men rot very thoroughly acquainted with the stock market, who can easily be induced to take flyer" but this class Of people are better posted. The whole system of " time sales " of stock is vicious one and ought 20 be broken up. 1t draws money from the banks for the purpose of carrying stocks, thus Tightening the money market on regular and good business men and this is one of the least of its evils. The faro gamblers may make as much money as they please it will not carry them into society; but the stock gamblers are among the "pillars of uptown institutions. BRANCH cannot be extinguished He bazes forth again this week in the " Daily Hand," his newly established organ, six inches by four, which is quite as recherche a literary curiosity as his previous efforts The style of the Branch school has not as yet provoked imitation. BRANCH is with. out followers but there is certainly some thing thoroughly unique in his style of rhetoric. People read his rawlings with un- diminished curiosity; the Hand" was to be seen in many hands yesterday, the first day of its publication, and its libels on BUCHANAN, TIEMANN, and other notables appear to be well relished. There ought to be an asylum for the class of people who are commonly known as halfcracked." There are numbers of persons in the world who are not insane enough for an asylum of the severe kind, who, nevertheless ought to be under some gentle restraint. They annoy their neighbors, mortify their friends and bore the public generally and there is no way of escape. 49,. .... -a" A stroll along the docks this week reveals an immense amount of business going on in the shipment of goods to the interior. The southern steamers and the railway and canal freight Offices are crowded. This is the halcyon time of draymen, who make extra wages for getting in their goods in advance of others. This, of course, induces some fierce competition. The freight agents of the railroad lines are running in all direc- tons, recommending the merits OF the rival roads. The Custom House officials are also kept busy entering foreign goods, which | still continue to come, though the cry was, short time ago, that the importation was through for the season. The cause, effect and composition of what is called the Aurora Boreals' have not been demonstrated by modern science. Several imperfect theories have been put forth at times, quiet unsatisfactory in their details. The peculiar electrical phenomena of these auroral displays, however, are at tracing the attention of scientific men generally, and comparison Of the obser Vations and experiments in different parts Of the country may lead TO the develop ment and discovery Of their nature, and the laws which govern them. A reduced temperature Of the atmosphere is also OBJ. served as an accompaniment Of the auro raj light. Professor Henry is said to be devoting his especial attention to this sub, Ject, and it may result in throwing light upon the cause and effect of the Aurora Borealis, so long a subject Of discussion among our savans.

The following estimate Of New England is made by The London Atheneum in a rc- view Of Palfrey's History Of New England New England may be considered the soul Of the great Republican eonfederaey. IL is not the mos, wealthy part Of the Amer. lean territory. II is not, perhaps, the mos, picturesque. IL il certainly not the most noisy. Neither the capital Of trade nor the capital OF politics i. built within It's hounda- rics. IL has not more roads. railways. ships. ;olegraphs, canals. than ITS neiehbor nor more prosperous commcrce or a no. bier agriculiure-its history is not more chivalrie, nor ITS connection with great events or splendid men more close. Sections Of country further South may boast II hav. ing sent Up more noticeable men to the great assemblies OF the country. Virginia Ia. more romantic past, New FORK more gor- geous present. Yot within the territories loosely designated New England. are found the intellectual and moral forces which make the Union what it Is In the eyes Of Europe. There lies the spirit Of perma. nant dominion. New England is to tie ,liw and serious part Of the States, as the coun. try TO the south is the plastic, volatile, and frivolous. Boston is Edinburgh, ns New York !, Paris, and Philadelphia is Geneva. New England is, in fact. Old England. "Peopled by some OF the very best men ever sent on; from the moth,rland. IL has renamed pure in motive and in blood. Scarcely any admiSture has taken place. No Lord Chief Justice Pophams ever pour. ed into this territory the refuse oi jail. and stews. Few emigrants Of foreign stock ever turned into IL. The climate !. dry and sharp. the Landscape is no, brilliant, the soil il not rich. Thus the same causes which had drawn the Pilgrims to Plymouth as refuge, KEEP, away from the bleak rock their more worldly followers in the wake of emigration. No wild vines. or palmetto fruit, or dazzling birds allurcd the naviga- tor Of It's inhospitabe coast. No tabled gold mines-no reported pearl hsheriss- drew the daring who made haste TO be rich. The sky looked cold and dull. The soil barely promised corr. and maize. To step on its shore was to encounter toll. want and care in every shape which savage nature presents at first interview to man. But the settlers who threw themselves on the rock sought in their new home not fortune, but irccdom-not gold and pearls, but God. They came alone, they remained and multiplied 'lone. In the three or Tour mil lions which a few years ago made up the population Of New England, no foreign cle- men, was visible in name or vintage. The thousand. had in six or seven generations, multiplied into millions; but multiplied without mixture OF race or transformation Of character, just rs they might have done IN Yorkshire or EAs, Anglia. While New York, under the influence ola immense ir. ruption Of Irish, Franks, and Germans, con. tinued without. pause like the first lowing Of tho SaIons into Britain, sunk into luIu- ~ or rose into crime, the les snowy coun. try TO tho north remained in,act-kept IL, own moral boundarie'-and preserved the rigid and fcrVent character Of it, people re- markedly free from change or stain. Thus a nation, as it were, simple, solid, and sta. bic, grew up within another nation open to infinite fluctuations Of thought. obcying ey- cry impulse Of tho moment. splendid, eI. perimen,al, and productive in its march OF more snowy events and exceptional men. Bot wha, is gained in speed is los, in pow. er. The solid mass OF New England char. acter weighs far more in the des,lnies OF America than tbs noisy smartness and eph. emeral success Of New York"

These flashes followed one another almost in stuntauously aud in less than seconds time would move from the horizon to the zenith. 1t was in these particulars the most remarkable display have ever witnessed. Friday evening the operators above named after noticing the recurrence Of the disturbance in the electrical currents cut of the wires Of that line from the batteries, and worked their wires for about hours on the Au.o current; better than with the batteries connected. N. de Ia Rive, the celebrated French astron. mer, explains the production of the aurora bore alis in the following manner When the sun, having passed INTO the south. ern hemisphere, the 5queous vapors which have accumulated during the summer in this part of the atmosphere begin TO condense, the kind of humid cap enyeloping the polar regions ex- tends more and more, and facilitates the passage Of the electricity accumulated in the upper portions of the air But in those elevated re- gions, and especially at this season of the year, tue aqueous vapors must frequently pass into the state of minute particles of ice or snow floating in the air, similar 10 those which give rise to the halos they form, as it were, a kind of semi transparent mist. These half frozen fogs conduct The electricity to the surface of the earth, near the pole, and are at the same time illuminated by these currents or electric discharges. In fact all observers agree in asser- ting that aurora borealis is constantly preceded by mist, which rises from the pole and the margins of which, less dense than the remain der are colored the first and indeed it is very near the pole in the wint MONTHS and espes cially in those where there is an abundance of vapor in the air. Mr.. Merriam, the Brooklyn meteor-wise, has pronounced his opinion of the Boreal lights He says ''the Aurora( electricity discharged from the craters of volcanos) either dissolves in the atmosphere, and is thus diffused through space, or concentrated into gelatinous substance form. ing Reteors, called shooting stars. These me teors dissolve rapidly in atmospheric air, but sometimes reach the earth before dissolying, and resemble thin starch" Merriam is easi. ly humbugged if not humbug, for he claims to have a bit of the Aurora in his possession, which so resembles silk that he styles it the silkery of the skies" The auroral display at Boston after midnight on the ID, was so brilliant that ordinary print could be,,read, and considerably impeded the wor- !; =, Of the telegraph up to noon of the 2d. At times the current from east to west was so reg ular that messages could be sent over the lines without the usual batteries being applied The operators in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia transmitted auroral messages to each other, and at intervals kept up lively chat by the same medium, the galyanic batteries being cut off and the instruments worked exclusively by means of the auroral electricity. 1t was exact ly similar in its effects, though differing in kind, to that generated in telegraphic batteries or what is known as common atmospheric elec tricity. The Pittsburgh Chronicle says; This, it is believed, is the first and only in stance on record, where the Aurora itself--beau- tiful, glorious and mysterious as it has always been considered in its brilliant manifestations has actually been harnessed up and been com pelleI to do the errands of man. And thus it is that science is ever achieving fresh and i'm. portant triumphs over nature and those phe- nomena, which in former times. when the laws, general and particular, that govern our earth, were comparatively unknown, were but objects of dread, or of drelul omen, are now noted with interest, recorded with precision, and utill- zed and employed so as to render glory to God, and do the bidding of man. |...

We are this day called upon to exercise ct the polls the FIRST privilege Of American citizen ship--the elective franehise-and in the action Of to-day momentOus issues are involved. The question is not merely. who shall hold position and Gil ONCE for few years; but il is cur ver- diet and judgment upon the national policy Of the present Administration; our Interpretation of the Democratic Platform Of 1856; our voice for the Platform upon which we give battle in 1860. Into the contest Of to-day we fearlessly enter with the old and tried leaders Of our par ty; with she men who bore the standard Of De- mocracy when they we're feeble and few who followed it. Their political history is the guar anty of their fidelity, and with such champions the principles for which we contend must tri- unph. b.a aa And our opponents, who are theyi The re- fuse Of Know Nothing lodges; the hirelings Of Federal patronage; time-serving politicians, and Custom House sweepiugs, with the shifting policy Of q vascilatiDg Administration as their platform, and the proven falsehoods of last years campaign nailed to their standard. These are the reptiles that gnaw at the party in 1859, which they could not overthrow in 1856. kAruRALIzED CITIZENS, to the polls, for you have indeed vital interest in this contest. The Know Nothing element which in 1855 would exclude you from our shores and our brotherhood, again raises its head. 1t now stands in high places, and speaks with the voice Of power; it returns you forsworn traitor to the monarch whose allegiance you have denied, 10 the land you have abjured; it strips you of the proud habilimen!s of freemen and freedom, and leaves you on the soil of liberty an alien, subject. and serf. REMEMBER THEN, and let your vote and your this day act be felt in 1860, that it may then restore you to that high position Of American citizenship from which base policy would de- pose you. To all, we say, be up and doing. In the next election the nation are actors, and let us this day rouse the echoes that since 1856 have slumbered in these hills, and send them pealing East until with the united voice of the People, they shall find in 1860, the response and recognition in our National Capitol, that THE PEOPLE ALONE ARE SOVEREIGN.

TIE NORTHERN LIGHTs.-Ihere was, on Sunday evening, an exhibition OF the aurora BJreaHs or Northern Lights, thai surpassed in beauty and extent any thing of The Kind that has been seen here for many years. 1t was first observed quite early in the evening, presenting the appearance Of a phosPhoTescenI globe over the whole northern section OF the heavens, and reaching from The eastern to the western horizon. In the course Of The next three hours it passed through a diversity Of changes, ending in splendid display Of rich roseate lightin the east and west, with coruscalons Of a paler tint slboling up from time TO time in the North. The brightness of the phenome non during the whole evening, was such as to render our streets very light. The Aurora Boreais is doubtless Of electric origin, but how high it is above the earlh's surface, is considered matter Of question. Dalton estimates the sum- nit Of the auroral columns. al about one hundred and fifty miles, but other obser' ers differ widely from this indeed Phi losophers are not al all agreed as 10 whether it is within or beyond The limits of our atmosphere, for owing TO its fnul and changing character it is almost impos- sible 10 Identify any particular beams, by different observers; indeed The same beam may present very different appearances when seen from different points of view, which would of course tend TO prevent its recognition. The Aurora generally affects the mag nelic needle. One OF the finest aurOral displays ever seen in, this country. ap- peared on the evening of November l4th, 1887. Ii attracted the attention Of great numbers Of observers, ard was largely commented upon in all quarters. M. de la Rive, the celebrated French astronomer, explains the production of the Aurora Bo- reals, in The following manner - "When the sun having passed into the southern hemisphere, no longer heats our atmosphere. The aqueous vap"rs which have accumulated during the summer IN this part of the atmosphere begin 10 con- dense, the kind of humid cap enveloping the polar regions extends more and more, and facilitates the passage of electricity accumulated in the upper portion OF the ! air. But in this elevated region, and es pecialIy at ihi, period OF the year, the aqueous vapors must most frequently pass into the state Of minute particles OF ice or snow floating in the air, similar TO those which give rise TO the halos they form, as it were, a kind of seml-transparentI mist. These half frozen logs conduct the electricity TO the surface Of the earth, near the pole, and are al tie same time i Illuminated by these currents or electric discharges. In fact, all observers agree III asserting that the aurora borealls is con stan,ly preceded By mist. which rises from the pole, and the margin Of which, less dense than the remainder, is coIored the first and indeed it is very frequent near the pole in the winter months. and especially in those where there is an abundance Of vapor in the air."

LEIGH HUNT.-"Ielgh hunt, lne popular author, died in London on the 18th day of Au- gust, in the 18th year of his age" This item of news comes to us from England, by the steamer Anglo Saxon. There are a great many persons in this country in whom it will revive crowd of recollections associated with what they know of him through his essays and poems. He wrote some of the most exquisite essays in the language; and those who have read the "Story of Rimini" should know very well what he was as poet. We mention the Story of Rimini, not because we deem it the best of his poems, but because it has probably been more circulated and read in this country than any other. He was one of the brightest richest, and most genial writers of his time. Leigh Hunt was born at Southgate, Eng land, October 49, 1854. His father, who was educated in this country, married in Philadel phia, settled in that city, ridden in cart there for the sin of toryism, and at last driven to England by the revolutionary storm, finally became clergyman of the church of England The poet gives in his autobiography most readable account of his family, his school days, his early friends and the beginning of his liter airy development. There is, or has been en- couraged in English schools something like brutality. He says 1.-THE sight of boys fighting from which l had been so anxiously Withheld, frightened me as something devilish." He was timid and shrunk from their brutal ways; but this drew upon him general hos. tility and he was compelled to cultivate cour- age, else, as he says, "there was an end for ever, as far as l was concerned, Of all these fine things that had been taught me in vindica- ton of right and justice" He found in him. self all the courage necessary to resist ana endure successfully. And herein the 'child was father of the man." In his early manhood he became a gallant champion of the most liberal style of English politics; and sometimes this championship was inspired by zeal which could not pause to be prudent As chief writer for the London Ex' aminer he appears to have kept the tories in a state of continual wrath. In 1872 he was pub licly prosecuted for truthful but terribly Sc we're article on that despicable wretch the Prince Regent, known in history as George Fourth OF course the decision was against him. He was sentenced to pay fine of f1000 and be imprisoned two years. Then followed an offer of delivery from the penalty ifhe would no more attack the Prince; but he refused it and went to prison, where he was followed by the unwearied kindness of many friends. This connection with the Examiner hinder ed his literary reputation and kept it I'M der cloud for long time. Not until he had passed on toward old age, was he fully recognized as one of the brightest and most permanent lights of English literature. In the earlier part of his life he spent considerable time in Italy. He was there with Byron and Shelley. His last days were spent at Ham, mersmith, near London; and all who have found access to him there describe him as a rare specimen of beautiful old age. GLOW like he seemed to his own glorious Abou Ben Ad- hem" says one of his latest visitors. Is itnow too much to hope that some publisher will is sue complete edition Of his works for Ameri- can readers

The Philadelphia Ledger speaking Of the complaints that have sprung up within a few years, in reference to the treatment OF seamen by their captains, says, that the mum. Der Of such complaints have become formi- dable. Nor are the complaints all on one side-conspiracy on the one hand, mutiny on the other; so that in foreign ports all over the world our Consuls have more such cases on hand than they know how to dispose of. "They are of so general character as to indicate far more than local or personal cause. They show that sailors on the one side are getting, as q class, to be incensed against what they conceive the tyranny OF officers, and the officers arc becoming habit ually estranged from, and suspicious of, their crews. 1t is no longer private and individual matter, but an estrangement of classes Of men who have got in some way to work together under penalty of the de- struction Of our whole commerce." This condition Of affairs looks gloomy enough. The Ledger asks a question and gives it sensible, practical answer GLOW the matter is to end it is difficult to see. We are in a transition state. The sal lors have got the ideas Of liberty belonging to New England whaling ships, and the captains have got the ideas of authority be longing partly to the Navy and partly to foreign lands. Neither party is at home in the use and workings Of these new ideas. The best practical way is for each captain to get good name, and then he can get good crews"

Rachel Wharton sat by the fire, holding in her lap the sleeping form of her little sister Grace. The two girls were alone in the house, their parents having gone down the river two days before, to dispose of their little stock of butter and cheese, and bring back in return, groceries for winter con- sumption. Far away from all human habitation the cottage of the Wharton's stood but Ra- chel was brave girl-born and bred among the wild hills-and she felt no fear. Tonight, for some reason which she could not explain to herself, she had failed to retire at her usual hour and now her eyes were bright and wide open gazing fixedly into the glowing fire. Suddenly she rose up, and putting her sister upon a bed in a corner of the room, she threw her apron over her head and went out into the night. 1t was pitchy dark, and the frigid gusts of wind pierced through her thin clothing but she did not heed-for rising above all the din of wind and waters came to her ears the crash of timbers and the clanking of iron chains! She listened with strained nerves and hushed heart again there was a low, heavy rumbling in the distance-the solid earth beneath her feet quivered-a mo- mentary pause, and then the dull, dead shock of some heavy object falling from a great height She understood it now; the railway bridge which spanned the river mile below in the valley, Fad been swept away ; and the de- struction of the huge pile of masonry and the falling of the chained timbers, had occa- stoned the strange sounds to which she had listened. She had scarcely time to arrive at this conclusion, when another thought struck her. PETERSBURG, Va, Aug. 2. am just in from the great new State of Minnesota, having travelled the sixteen hun dred intervening miles in the almost incredi- bly, short period of three days and half Though so far distant, the trip thither, or back, is so pleasant and cOmfortable-and at a moderate cost, too-that it really amounts to nothing, considered as Journey The routes are many, and all of them agreeable !; for speed, comfort, beauty of scenery and economy. On the morning of the third day after leaving your city, the passenger is land ed in Chicago to breakfast. The same even ! ing he arrives at Lacrosse, on the upper Mis- sissippi, about one hundred and fifty miles below st. Paul, and before noon of the fourth day, he stands upon the levee of that rapidly growing and enterprising city. He stands there wondering at the vast extent of our great country, (the centre of which he has not reached and at the skill, enterprise and capital which have accomplished for him such a speedy trip ! All along the route his atten- ton has been engaged with views of the rich est agricultural country, and the finest natur- al scenery, which the country affords. The nights he has spent in sumptuous sleeping cars, affording better facilities for rest than any steamboat your correspondent has ever met with, and, at appropriate times during | the day, he has stopped at first-class hotels, and has been allowed unusually ample time to partake of the excellent meals prepar- ed for him. He may make the trip through, including every expense, for about $40 for first-class, or about S29 for second class pas. sage. am surprised that this trip is not more generally favorite with pleasure seekers than it is. But few, as yet, have discovered its advantages, and those few assert that to breathe the pure and celebrating atmosphere of Minnesota to wander about amongst it's crystal lakes, rolling prairies, and lovely Laughing waters" falls y to visit its yet lingering Indian settlements, and to study the habits and manners of the natives, to say nothing of the splendid picture. scenery of the Upper Mississippi, which far exces that of the Hudson, is worth all the "mountain breez- es" and humbuging sulphur waters that even our own beloved Virginia affords. The time is not far distant, surely, when it will become the great resort of the Southern and Eastern summer travel but those who go first, and see and enjoy it before Art has despoiled the beautiful works of nature will be amplest re- paid. There is no more beautiful country in the world. Minnesota is appropriately named the State of the ''Sky-Tinted Water" for it is difficult to say whether its surface presents more of land than water. Every few miles the traveller meets with lovely lakes of clear spring water, transparent to the bottom, and rejecting from their surfaces sky as soft and beautiful as that of Italy. These charming lit tie seas, varying greatly in size and extent, all seem to be thickly inhabited by the finny tribes of the very best species, and bordering as they do in some sections of the State, upon nearly every "claim," they are of immense advantage to the settlers as well for their use as their beauty. Moreover, at the proper sea- sons, their bOSoms are covered with very fine qualities of wild ducks and geese. One is struck with the quantity of these lakes on looking at the map, but the map present not one-hundredth Of them-only the very large ones. These lakes separate sections of the richest and most beautiful rolling prairie land to be found in the whole Northwest, with magni- ficent supply of excellent timber, scattered here and there over the face of it. The soil, which is now being rapidly broken up, is a rich black Gas your hat,) sandy loan, varying from four to fifteen and twenty feet deep, with "sub' which, when fixed with it, makes it even richer than itself, and the whole perfectly inexhaustible. The crops are such as we are accustomed to in Virginia, only spring wheat does better than winter, on &C count of the scarcity of snow. Corn, wheat, rye, barley and oats make up the grain crop the two first particularly. But there are some Virginians around Belle Plaine, on the st. Peters River, which is the richest part of the State, who are cultivating an excellent ar ticle of tobacco, and ground peas also, with great success, and assured me, tho they had been at it for several years, they had not yet seen fly or worm-it only needed to be succored. Sweet potatoes also do admira- bly,. There is nothing, indeed, to prevent Min. nesota from becoming one of the first agricul- tural States in the Union, and as she is per- fectly accessible to the Mississippi and the lakes, she is destined to enjoy an immense commerce. And when the great Pacific Rail road is extended, one branch at least of which must lie through this State, her influence in every department of civilization, will be felt throughout the country and throughout the world. She is very young yet, but already blossoms as the rose," it must resemble that of the original Eden for no one ever gets sick, and invalids, particu larry consumptives, come from every part o. and are not disappointed. One inhalation invest you with a quantity Of oxygen that and drive you at least five years farther or the course of life than you can possibly g by any other route. II r e.. Life is but deaths vestibule; and our pilgrimage on earth buta journey to the grave. The pulse that preserves our being beats our death march, and the blood which circulates our life is floating it onward to the deeps ofdeath To day we see our friends in health to morrow we hear of their decease. We clasped the hand of the strong man but yesterday, and to-day we close his eyes. We rode in the chariot of com. fort but an hour ago, and in a few more hours the last black chariot must convey US to the home of all living. Tho west winds blow, and, singing low, hear the glad streams run; The windows Of my soal throw Wide open to the sun. No longer forward nor behind look In hope and fear; But, grateful, take the good l find, The best of now and here. Iplough no more desert land, To harvest weed and tare; The mamma dropping from Gods hand, Rebukes my painful care. break my pilgrim staff, lay Aside the toiiing oar; The angel sought so far away l welcome at my door. The airs of spring may play Among the ripe ming corn, Nor freshness of the flowers of May Blow through the Autumn morn. Through fringed lids TO heaven, And the pale aster in the brook Shall see its image given; The woods shall wear their robes of praise, The south wind softly sigh, And sweet, calm days In golden haze Melt down the amber sky. Not less shall manly deed and word Rebuke an age Of wrong; The craven flowers that wreath the sword Make not the blades less strong. But smiting hands shall learn to heal, To build as to destroy; Nor less my heart for others feel That the more enjoy. All as God wills, who wisely heeds To give or to withhold, And knoweth more of all my needs Than all my pray ers have told! Enough that blessings undeserved Have marked my erring track That wheresoe'cr my feet have sweryed, His Christening turned me buck That more and moro a Providence OF love Is understood, Making the springs Of time and sense Sweet with eternal good That death seems but covered way " hich opens INTO light, W herein no blinded child can stray Beyond the Fathers sight That care and trial seems t last, Through Memcry' ss sunset air, Like mountuiR-ranges overpast, In purple distance fuir- That all the jarrng notes Of life Seem blending in psalm, And all the angels Of its strife Slow rounding into calm. And 80 the shadows fall apart, aud so the west winds play; Aud all The windows Of my lisart | open 10 the day.

PEARL HUNTNG.-In many parts of the east or section of our country, during the past year or two, people have found rare pleasure and some profit in hunting for pearls not. we fear, the pearl of infinite price, but the kind yielded by mussels, or common fresh water clans. For many years, it is well known, they have been found in plentiful quantities in New Jersey Some very valuable ones have been obtain d from this source. But that State is not the only one in the Union where pearls have been found. Several years ago some very handsome ones were found by some truant boys, in II small stream in New Hampshire we never heard. however, that anybody ever made business of hunting pearls in that State, renowned for at least, her granite hills,-we will not add and also for the great men she has produced That has been said times enough. In Vermont pearls are found in various localities but in and near Montpelier the beautiful capital of that magnificent State, magnificent, spite its politics,) they chiefly abound. Several have been found there by la dies, and even by small children, that were of great value. Indeed, Montpelier pearls have already become celebrated, and a commerce is now carried on in them. Numerous elegant pearl rings, of this origin, deck the delicate fingers of ladies in Chicago. 1t has been our good fortune to examine a very costly pearl necklace, from the same quarter, which is now owned by the wife of u wealthy banker in q neighboring city. A set of these pearls have been estimated tn be worth $500. The pearls, as we have intimated, are hunted mostly by ladies and children, and exciting sport they make of it. When found they require but very little polishing, and are mounted tastefully and richly both in Montpelier and Boston. We have seen, recently.a pearl breast pin, which Montpelier, and which is highly priced by its owner. The pearl is large and whole, and its lustrc equals any of the New Jersey, and many of the Panama pearls even some of the oriental pearls do not excel it.-Chicago Times In the case Of the election of field officers in the Sd regiment of Vermont militia, which wal claimed to be invalid, adjutant general Kellogg has decided in favor of their validity. Those officers holding commissions in the Vermont militia merely, without the addition of " Uni formed in the document, have no sort of in terest in the present regimental organizations Their position is but nominal one, and fol present the three regiment organized last yea ale to report only to the adjutant general, ant are expressly ordered to recognize no superior authority but his. Correspondence Pac. Commercial Advertiser Letter from Sam Francisco. lcorrespondence pac. Commercial AdvertiserI Letter from Sam Francisco. SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 2, 1859. Mr.. EDITOR Two more mining towns have been DESTROYED by fire, since the date of my last letter "Murphy's'' and '.Campo Seco." both Aourishing towns, have been added to the long list of ~confagra- tons. In both cases, the work is supposed to be that of an incendiary. This week, Columbia came very near sharing the same fate. The devouringe element was, however, conquered, after some twenty houses had been destroyed. Vallecito and Murphy's are being rebuilt in better shape than ever, with that energy which is peculiar to Californians. Horace Greeley having strongly urged a fusion of the Republicans and Anti-Lecomplonites Of this state in order to defeat the administration party, at the next election. the leaders of each party manifested a desire to act upon the suggestion. Accordingly. the central Committee of these two parties met in this city, and also in Sacramento, for several days in sue cession, but they have failed to agree upon a basis of fusion. Still, it would not be surprising if the adj ministration party will be defeated. A more general interest is manifested in political matters by all classes, this year than ever before. The merchants Of this city have agreed to close their places of bust ness on the eth inst, election day. A movement is being made in the southern part of the state, to separate the counties of San Louis Obs po, Santa Barbara, San Diego, Los Angeles, San Bernadino, and part Of Buenp Vista, and to erect them into a territory. The proposition meets with no favor in this part of the country and will probably be defeated. No good could possibly result from such a separation. There seems to be a good prospect of an extensive trade springing up between this coast and the AMOR River. Otto Esche, Esq, formerly a merchant of this city, who has been established some time at Nico- layeffsk, a city near the mouth of the river, has chartered the schooner Caroline E. FOote. and sails for that place, with a full cargo of goods in a few days. The Manchoors, inhibiting Southern Manchoo- ria number several millions, and are said to be much wealthier than the Chinese They obtain their sup plies from Canton, by way of Peking, and as goods can be imported thither by the Amoor and ~Songhary rivers, at a much cheaper rate, it is probable that a brisk trade will spring up with them, through that channel. Mr.. Burling, of this city, is now at Niso- layeffsk, putting together a small steamer which he brought with him thither for the river trade. The Russian steamer .Amoor, which visited Honolulu on her way out, is still running on the river; and it is said that the Russian Government is having four steamers built at Hamburg for the same trade. The lower part of our city is now supplied with water hom the reservoirs of the Bensley Water Co., very much in the way that New York is supplied by the Croton Works, and in a few weeks, the whole city and suburbs, will be amply supplied with this great luxury,-pure water. The works of the company are constructed on a large scale, and when fully CON- pleted. will cost about $3.50, 900. 1t is estimated that the people of this city expend $5OO,OOO Fer year for ,cafer alone! The completion of the water works will enable them to enjoy the same luxury in greater abundance for one-third of the expense. AS another example of home enterprise, we might cite the wooden factory now being erected near Fort Point. This will give employment to about 95 hands. 1t is intended, for the present, merely to manufacture blankets. 1t will commence operations early in November. The affairs of the Louisiana Tehuantepec Co. are in a sad plight. Their property on the isthmus has been seized for debt, and their agent had to escape imprisonment by fight. This company has been hampered by debt from the beginning, and European capitalists did not take hold of the business, as it was hoped they would. Our communication with New Orleans via Tehuantepec will cease October 1st. The sale of the Collins steamers to the P. NJ. S. s. Co. was confirmed by last mail. They will commence running Immediately on the other side, and will be a vast improvement on the vessels formerly employed between New York and Aspinwall. Fights, murders, robberies, sc. &C., compose the burden of the news. The Indian difficulties still continue in Utah. An engagement had taken place near Camp Floyd, be- tween a body of U. s. troops under Lieut.. Guy, and 1000 Indians. Four Mormons were found among these Indians, instigating them to bloody deeds. They were killed in the battle. The brig EAenita. Capt. W. q. Hayes, which has been advertised for Australia for some time past, has very mysteriously from our harbor. Capt. STARTLING ELECTRICAL PHENONENoN- This morning, one of the most startling as well as singular electrical phenomena, occurred on the telegraph lines through. out the United States, that has ever taken place in this country. 1t has been mani Tested on the various telegraph lines throughout the country during all this forenoon, thereby causing much annoyance to the operators. 4 series of currents OF electricity, entirely independent of the batteries, seem to have taken possession Of the wires, and to such an extent that the National Telegraph line was actually ena- bled to send messages from New York ia Pittsburg, Pa, correctly without the use of a particle of galvanic battery, using this Independent electricity of the air in the place of that supplied by the ordinary batteries! This is a phenomena, we are assured, which has never taken place, even among the many pranks an unseen power Is dai- ly practicing on the telegraph wires. As has been stated. the extraordinary freak is doubtless owing to the Aurora Borealis, as the wires were paralyzed during their shining on Sunday night. As these same lights were shining brilliantly after one o'clock this morning it is fair to presume that the phenomena of to-day may be at tributed to the same cause. The Cincinnati Consnercal, Of last Monday, has the 0llowing in relation to the display Of Northern Lights" on Sabbath evening" The display Of Northern Lights" last night, was Of extraordinary brillianee. There was q wierd magnificenee IN the illumination Of the North and East. There was a CHASTITY SPLEEN dor over the horizon OF the North, from which fantastic spires oflight shot up, and rosy glow extended, like a vapor tinged with fire, TO the zenith. The spectacle presented was Of mar. velous though spectral beauty-and a rarely vivid exhibition Of the phenomenon Of the Nor thern Aurora for this latitude. Those who see in these revelations of the handiwork of the Creator, Signs and wonders are furnished a fruitful theme for speculation. The northern lights, which formed so mar kable a spectacle last night, between eight and ten o'clock, interrupted telegTGphic communion. ton at al points. Reports were received in this city that the effect of the Aurora was noticed at New York, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Columbus. and was the SAME rs that experien- ced in a thunder storm. There were strong currents OF electricity observed on the wires to which no batteries were attached, and some ex- traordinary electrical phenomena, difficult Of explanation, noticed. The wires in operation norGh of New York, were interrupted in a greater proportion. Business was at last sus- pended. A similar Interruption was observed IN 81 or '52, when all the wires in the country were interrupted, so that business was entirely suspended. The Cincinnati G,sete, OF the same date as the Commercial, has the following article on the same subject A SPLENDID AURORA BoREALIs.-We had, last night, one of the most brilliant auroraE manifestations we have ever known in summer. 1t began about eight O'Clock, before the twilight had fully gone, and at twelve it was still bril- liant. At the time it began, there were dense masses of black clouds in the West, reaching halfway to the zenith. These disappeared be- fore the Aurora, which soon overspread halfthe sky, at the "zenith of the magnetic dip" which phrase may be thus explained. If a magneti- zed needle be suspended in a vertical plane on a pivot, the northern pole will point to the earth, but not in a vertical line, and the angle of variation from the v~erticle line is called the magnetic dip" The zenith of this is the point in the sky to which the south pole OF the needle points. The colorS Of TIE Aurora were g%recning yellow, and the complimentary shade Of red. When the Aurora was at its height I've SOIOiS WIZ very DIliIldht' AdbCl III t'S night the blush was confined to the north, and did not reach more than one-fourth the dis lance to the zenith. The Aurora is supposed 10 be caused by the illumination, through electrical influences, of particles of sleet, in the higher regions of the atmosphere. We have seen it several times in summer, and have almost always noticed that it followed a sudden lowering of the tempera- ture after rain. Last evening the mercury sank rapidly, at twelve O'Clock it was more than probable that we should have frost before morn ing. Although, as we say, we have several times seen the Aurora in summer we never saw so brilliant a manifestation but once before, and that was mo!e than fifteen years ago, in this city, when the diffusion was as great and the light msre brilliant than last night. The southern part OF the heavens seemed pur- pie by contrast. In the east and northeast the lights were green, of various shades, min gIed with yellow, while in the northwest they were of a brilliant rose tint, likes the flames from burning buildings. And over the whole Of the sky thus illuminated, away up to to the crown of the arch and beyond, ever an anon ran tremulous waves oflight, not unlike the flashes Of lightning. Tha light was so intense that our hand held near a wall cast a shadow, and we read by it solid minion type. p. S.-Aboat one O'CLOCK this morning the aurora assumed a form Of extreme beauty Commencing with an arch in the North, which was green above, and beneath Of the ~intensest purpletstreams of light green shot up to the zenith Of the magnetic dip, from fully half the circum cerance of the horizon. These united making a sort Of crown. Beyond this there were banks of greyish green light.

The village bank, of which he was director, gave him the names of the bankers whose check were for warded every three months, and he set on foot questions which elected the information he desired She had no wealth Of her own but was understood to be sole heiress of something like half a million that belonged to her grandfather, who was still living - This was sufficient, and he proceeded to prosecute his suit. But he knew too we'll, by family experience. the danger Of attempt ing runaway marriage with the expecta- ton Of receiving money with his bride, and he accordingly determined to commence his negotiations III person with the parents of the young lady, who were then abroad Steamers were just then commencing their trips, and he proceeded to France. where he had reason to anticipate meeting with them, though they were represented to be moving from place to place. In small cabaret on the road from Paris Ito Lyons, somewhat celebrated in those days for the perfection Of its cuisine and the elegance Of its miniature arrangements, a gentleman and lady who were travelling post had ordered dinner, and were waiting its appearance while their horses were chang ed. The gentleman was about seventy years of age, tall erect, and stately in his appear ance. His hair was silvery white, and flow ed over his back in large locks. His dress was purely French, SO that he might rsadi- y be mistaken for marquis Of the old reg ime. Such, doubtless, the host supposed him to be, If his obsequiousncss were any proof. While they waited. gentleman arrived, travelling in the other direction, by post al 50, and the old gentleman approached the window and saw him dismount from his carriage. Turning back suddenly, with a start, he exclaimed, "Keep back, Kate ; keep back !" '.Why, who is it, father p cit is he !" "John % "Bromley." Strange! What can he be here for Father, mean to see him. Do you think he would recognize US? We are, surely, much changed, and our disguise is perfect Mrs.--did not know us in Paris what think you 7" 1t would be curious Perhaps 1t will be as well. And if he does recognize US, what is the harm, after all. It will disturb our quiet for while, and then all will run on again in the old channel" The landlord entered with card. ''Mr. Bromley hearing that Mr. Carlton and Mrs. Carlton were at the inn, desired leave to present himself It was granted. Full Of his object, John Bromley never dreamed Of recognizing them in their Iis- guised appearance, and they saw that they were safe on that score His proposition startled them, and they exchanged glances rapidly. OF course they could neither ac- cept nor decline it now. They must have time to consider. they would be in Amer- lea within few months, when he should have their answer meantime, he must rot attempt to see her. These and sundry sim liar provisions enabled them to be rid of his for the present, and the direc- ton of their travel was changed, and they fastened to America. When Bromley arrived at his home after an absence Of about ninety days, he learned that rival was in the field in the shape of his own cousin, Frederick Bromley, the son of his elder uncle, and promising voting lawyer in the country He had already ex- perienced the severity of his cousins enmity in the contests he had about his ill-gotten estates, and this was the worst blow that could have been inflicted. 70 say the truth he had boosted over his wine that he had been successful in his foreign trip-a boast that reached the ears Of his younger rival, and elected from him smile Of contempt An accidental meeting, a slight service rendered, few words exchanged, these were the incidents which commenced an &C. quaintance that had ripened into love, and in two months the young lady had accepted him, without thinking it necessary to refer the matter to parent or teaher. But rumor reached the ears Of John Brom- ley that her mother was in America. and had knowledge Of this new engagement, and had approved it. Just at this time had thunderbolt fall en- at his feet, he could not have been more startled than he was at an action in parti- ton, commenced against him by Frederick Bromley on behalf Of an unknown person, as grantee of Kate Cameron, Of one-fourth of the estate finer grandfather. The name startled him. He had not heard it for years. He had not seen it written in more. It seemed strange that it could appear in such papers as these. so formally, so mixed ed up with law phrases and technical terms. He had never thought of it for years except as the young queenly girl he had loved, had deceived, and forsaken. The old law pro- ceedings had been discontinued when she left her home, and he had forgotten them. His first impulse now was one Of exceed ing tenderness for moment he thought of abandoning all to her claim. Her very name had magic power at that instant, as the names of the once loved ones must have, if we have left them and they have not for saken us.

CAUSE OF THE AURORA BoREALIs.-M. de la Rive the celebrated French astronomer, ex plains the production of the Aurora Borealis in the following manner: when the sun, having passed into the southern hemisphere, no longer heats our atmosphere, the aqueous vapors which have accumulated during the summer in this part of the atmosphere begin to condense, the kind of humid cap envelop- ing the polar regions extends more and more, and facilitates the passage of electricity accu- mulated in the upper portion of the air. But in this elevated region, and especially at this period of the year, the aqueous vapors must mCst frequently pass into the state of minute PARTICLES of ice or snow floating in the air. similar to those which give rise to the haios, they form, as it were, kind of semi-trans- parent mist. These half frozen fogs conduct the electricity to the surface of the earth, pear the pole, and are, at the same time. Illuminated 10y these currents or electric dis charges. In fact, all observers agree in as serting that the aurora bOrealis is cons antly preceded by mist, which rises from the pole, and the margin of which, less dense than the remainder, is colored first; and. in deed, it is very frequent near the pole in the | winter months. and especially in those where there is an abundance of vapor in the air."

She dreamed, and her vision was of a garden, where each bright flower seemed to outvie in beauty its gay compeers; birds of dazzling plumage, insects with golden wings, fitted from flower and shrub, and filled the air with their gay songs and dreamy cummings. But strange, cold blight came DER the scene: the flowers withered, the bright birds dropped their colored pinions, and their glad songs were mute Slowly all faded from her straining sight-naught but misty void remained-while voice spake words of sad meaning: "Child of the Ocean spirit of the deep trust not to Aeeting earth for per- manence Mark we'll this passing vision, and lay it to thine heart. Child of the Ocean! thou art in misty dream, following cheating phantom, which lures thee on to bitter woe and disappointment" With a sob, she woke, and flung her arms around the neck of him who held her, "Thou dost love me still2" she cried, "and thy love shall last2 Oh! l have had dream, dashing the cup of happiness from my lip, and offering in its place bit ter draught of sorrow. The love of him she loved so well grew cold; the dull blight came in that; his words of soothing kindness ceased, and frigid courtesy, or scarcely that, usurped their place-there fell the blight again. She sought to chase the growing mist far from her, but it crept on and on, shrouding her in its damp, death-like GOODNESS. Her cheek, her bright young cheek, be- came pale and wan with grief, and her dim eye betokened naught but sorrow, and he the idol she had worshipped with her warm young heart-cared neither for the pallor nor the sorrow. There, in that hour of woe, back to her despairing mind, stealing DER her smarting senses, came low and gentle whisper: "Child of the wave, thou hast built thine house upon the sand, and it has fallen around thee; thou hast placed thy hopes in the heeting things of earth, and in mer- cy those hopes have been destroyed. Z lIou hast but tasted of the fate of all mundane creation-change. She listened and as the angel spoke, she stretched her arms towards heaven to Him who must endure when all things else are gone, crying, Take me to thyself, en- shrine me in thine own imperishable love, let me dwell there, in that which can, and shall, and will endure, when this world with its false and cheating hopes, is gone" And with clasped, outstretched hands, with thoughts and hopes of Heaven spring ing in her heart, and warm and fervent prayers on her lips, she turned her eyes upwards. Then came glorious band, who, with their balmy wings, waited the damp and noxiouS mist away-wafted her woe far from her; waited her earthly hopes, regrets, back to her earthly home. Once more her guide lowered above her. An article on Death in the New Cy- clopadia, has the following:- "As life approaches extinction, insensi- biilty superyenes-a numbness and dispo- sition to repose, which do not admit of the idea of suffering. Even in those cases where the activity of the mind remains to the last, and where nervous sensibility would seem to continue, it is surprising how often there has been observed state of happy feeling on the approach of death. IF I had strength enough to hold a pen, I would write how easy and delightful it is to die. , were the last words of the celebrated Viii liam Hunter, during his last moments Montague, in one of his essays, describes an accident which left him so senseless that he was taken up for dead. On being re- ! stored, however, he says: sMethought my life only hung on my lips; and l shut my eyes to help thrust it out and took pleas ure IN languishing and letting myself GO | A writer in the Quarterly Review records that gentleman who had been rescued from drowning, declared that he had not experienced the slightest feeling of suffoca- ton. The stream was transparent, the day brilliant, and, as he stood upright, he could see the sun shining through the wa ter, with dreamy consciousness that his | eyes were about to close on it forever. Yet he neither feared his fate nor wished to "a vert it. A sleepy sensation, which soothed and gratifed him, made a luxurious bed of watery grave" 1t is striking fact. the dying never weep. The circle of sobbing, agonized hearts around produce not one tear. Is it that the dying person is insensible and stiff already in the chill of dissolution That cannot be- for he asks for his fathers hand, as if to gain strength in the mortal strug- gle, and leans on the breast of mother, brother, or sister, with still conscious af- lection, and just before expiring, after a long converse with the angel of Summons, he says to his brothers or sisters--the last audible good night of earth-''kiss me- kiss me!'' 1t must be because the dying have reached point too deep for earthly crying and weeping. They are face to face with higher, holer beings, with the Father in Heaven, and the angel throng, led on by the Son himself; and what are the griefs of a mourning, tears of dying farewell, be it that they are shed by the dearest on earth in that vision bright of immortal life and everlasting reunion?

In one of Cooper's best nov els, the Pioneer, prodigal laughs at the owner of the village property, for desir- ing to save trees, as if such common af- fairs could have any value, or possibly become scarce. The feeling of indiffer- ence to such economy was all but uni vcrSal, not many years ago. Now, how ever, the destruction of our forests has brought people to practical knowledge of the value Of lumber. Hemmed in among a chain vi bills that reach the skies. lhe quiet water Vt Champan, Like molten silver lies While on its tranquil breast, A thousand sails are spread. AURORA BoREALIs.-There was very brilliant display of Aurora Borealis, last even ing, between the hours of eight and ten o'clock, and, at the time of its brightest illuml- nation, covering nearly the whole heavens. The phenomenon began to appear soon after dark, increasing in brillancy and intensity till nearly ten O'Clock, when the whole sky was overspread with sheets and streamers of light, varying from the usual pale color to deep and brilliant crimson. The colors were brightest in the east and the west, and paler In the north From all these and the intermediate points were many-colored rays shooting to the zenith forming at one time kind of irregular corona, and at others disappear ing in waves or flashes of light, following each other with great rapidity. In some parts of the heavens the sheets and rays Of light, OF various shades of crimson yariegated with white, had only vibratory or tremulous mo- ton, while in others they were continually flashing with the rapidity of lightning. Later in the evening and during the early hours of the morning the aurora was exceedingly Drill liant in the north, while other parts of the heavens were Hinged with softer and more delicate crimson hue. Broad rags of light, less eccentric than at first, but still strikingly clear and distinct continued their majestic march toward the zenith, till near the approach of dawn. For many years the "merry dancers" have not presented in our heavens so beau tiful and striking spectacle.

This light pro- cee1ed from the Aurora Borealis. which shone with more brilliancy Sunday night, than it has since March, 1882, when its light was very dazzling. and overspread the whole hemisphere. Our telegraph dis patches inform us, that the light had most extraordinary effect upon the wires and it was with much difficulty that some 400 words of the news brought by the Indian was teleg aphed from Farther Point. At one o'clock, the line utterly gave out, and the operators were obliged to suspend op erations. The oldest operators on the line say that they never experienced anything Of the kind before. The night was indeed beautiful one and we shall long remember how bright and beautiful everything appeared.

AURORA BoREALIs.-There was another atmUs- pheric exhibition yesterday morning, which, COM mencing about one o'clock, lasted until near day light and, while it lasted, filled the heavens with spiendor, and lit the city as with the light of raging fire. owing arch of flame seemed to be thrown across &c zenith, extending from east to west, from the top crown of which long spears and streamers of red light were thrown far down the southern sky, giving to the whole heavens the ap- pearance of being illumined with the glare of an immense confagration. To the north there were comparatively few clouds, and over the broad and clear expanse, the light seemed to go and come like bushes upon woman's cheek-now glowing into deepest intensity, and then palng into the faintest flush. To the south there were clouds which, catching and rejecting the light, gave to that portion of the heavens more brilliant though perhaps less beautiful appearance than that just de- scribed as belonging to the northern sky There was light breeze stirring at the time, and the at mosphere was pleasantly cool. We understand that the different lines of telegraph in this vicinity were so much affected that it was several hours af ter they were opened before they were in perfect working order. The Prince, the mighty Conqueror, the highborn genius, as we'll as the lowly, for saken and the down-trodden slave of the earth-all meet at the grave, and pay COM mon homage to the ghastly king Of terrors and skeleton monarch. All know that they will have to lie down in the grave; but how few there are that give it one serious thought How few there are that tell by their actions that they have the grave in view A man comes into the world he COM mences a swift race for glory, knowing it will end in the grave. He begins the jour ney Of life as one blind on a race course, when there is yawning guilt at the end. He walks the earth with as firm, assured footsteps as if it were his eternal home-as if there were no gloomy grave-no darker world beyond the shores of time. Yonder 60 the youthful, with thoughts only of life; with eyes sparkling with an ticipated joys, and fixed upon that fatal mirage that rides upon the floating wing Of time. Hope hoyers over him with gilded wings, urging him onward till he makes his last grasp at the shadow of life, when lrv geth0sea tLs- .vindine shoot and sinks in to the grave. Yonder 90 the aged and the infirm, with heads bleached by the dews of three score years, and bodies almost to spectres turned; even now their hearts are swelling with hopes Of earthly joys; but how soon will the deceptive crust of earth beneath their feet sink under them and drop them in the grave! No doubt, in youthful days, they thought to turn from vanities in time TO redeem their souls from death. But DELAY is the thief that steals mems souls away, and gives the victory to the grave The grave who is there that does not grow chilly at the thought? Even the christian may shudder when nearing th' dark portals Of the tomb and when th' gloomy shades of that last, long night begiI to gather around him, may shrink at tn long leap in the dark. If the Redeeme of man would pray for the cup to pass iron him, how may not the most devout chris tian feel when about to enter the marrow passage to the eternal world? If the chris tian may shrink at his dissolution, wha will the ungodly feel when he finds tn sting, for him, still left in death, and tn grave with the victoryl When he trun a searching glance beyond the gulf of time and the last glimmer Of hope dies away i his breast, what then must be his agony How many there are that thus lie down j the grave How many there are thu stand on the line between life and deatl and scan the darker world beyond, anC then, with one long howl of despair, cntC the eternal gloom! There stands the hero-the mighty col oueror-beneath whose tread empir' shrank away. with blood stained bann, fluttering in the breeze upon the prou battlements Of warriors fame, and wit his name written upon the highest apex earthly glory. Worms are now feasting on frame, and time corroding his glory. The proud Philosopher, whose scienti mind ranges the distant fields of space, a. steps from star to star, and numbers worlc lies down in the grave with the comm menial from whose dull mind was new born a thought. CAUSE OF THE AURORA BoREALIs.-M. de la Rive, the celebrated French astronomer, ex- plains the production OF the Aurora BorealiS al the following manner 20 When the sun, having passed into the southern hemisphere, no longer heats our atmosphere, the aqueous rapOrS which have accumulated during the summer in this part of the atmosphere begin to condcnse, the kind Cfhumid cap envclopng The polar regions extends more and more, and facilitates the passage of electricity accumu- lated in the upper portions of the air. But in this elevated region, and especially at this period of the year. the aqueous yapOrs must most frequently pass into the state of minute PARTICLES of ice snow floating in the air, similar to those which give rise to the halos : they form, as il were, 4 kind of semi-transpa- rent mist. These half frozen fOgS conduct the electricity to the surface of the earth, near the pole, and are, at the same time, illu- minated by these currents or electric diScbar- ges. In fact all observers agree in asserting that the aurora borcalis is constantly preceded tT a mist, which rises from the pole, and the margin of which, less dense than the remain der, is colored the first; and, indeed, it is very frequent the pole in the winter months, and especially in those where there is al abundance of yapor In the air.

From Tait's Edinburgh Magazine. THE OCEAN CHILD. The sea in its great stiffness seemed one huge sheet Of glass, rejecting from its gent ly-heaving bosom the suns warm, glisten- ing rays. Heaven spread her canopy of deepest azure, whereon white, feecy, gold tipped clouds foated Ike tenant specters of the air, sporting erewhile in mimic chase, and then vanishing into an essence more ethereal than themselves. Nothing of earth-dull earth--was visi- bic: not one trace of land to dim the bright ness of the glowing scene, not one being of human mould-nothing of earthly life to mar the lonely beauty of the ocean soil tude. Yet there was life, and beings of life foated on each ripping wave-danc- inc on the creamy foam Life strange, unknown life to poor blind mortals-life of the spirit kind, dwelling in rare cabinets of beauty; for there were nymphs with float ing locks of gold and snowy skins, and beaming eyes Of fatal brilliancy, which woo-and win-and promise-but to curse The sisters of the deep kept holiday, as frequently they sported on the surface of their world They touched their harps of shell with fairy fingers, and in sweeping cadence drew forth rich tones of melody; and then they sung and laughed, and sung again. in very mirth and mischief son, to the emerald of the ocean, on" and away they sped, that merry crew, borne on great dophins' backs-on to that spot which, with truth, they styled the en- nrol1 81 Al, iclonI cNanly of earth an oasis Of beauty in that great desert Of the waters Tall pines grew from the messy turf, which seemed but floating in the clear green deep-tall pines of mel ancholy form. and moulding, looking as though they were the tenements of disem- bodied spirits imprisoned there-so the mind would Suggestion some dim error of the past. Thither the water spirits fed-thither, to hold their festival; and their songs and gIeesome mirth rang in wild music over the broad expanse of ocean. But one being, and she the lovelieSt of them all, rested, so sad and silent, no melody springing from her harp, no mirth dwelling on her ruby lps-her eyes cast down, and pearly tears imprisoning the heavy lashes to her cheek her hair, even her hair seemed to hang in sadness, and shroud in gloom the beauty Of her fairy loneliness. "Eola"-and the gay sisters clustered round her, and linked their arms, and dane ed, she in the midst, like pure marble. "Eola, ever, ever sad; come Join with rs, and cast off this dull garb of grief, which better fits the stolid children of NOR tality than oceans fairy daughters" Then Eola unused, and unused, and then repeated their light words again-repeated them as dreaming Of their import, forgetful Of Their utterer. Stold children of mortality" she said, can those be dull whose outward form en- shrines the precious diamond OF a soul the gem which sparkles through the whole tenor OF the lifeY-a never-dying, never ending Soul-a spirit reaching through all space and time! O blessed fate to be more than mere bubble-more than a thing of foam, breath, vapor r And now she stood alone, for her CAV companions, wearied of her mood. had left her. Then balmy air spread round her, waving her golden tresses, lifting them from her snowy skin; and looking, she saw descending on his outstretched pinons the radiant form Of one of the great spirits of the air. Eola,' he said, as alighting he stood be- s s her" EOla, to Heavens great dome NY words have fed, betokening high, spring dream in thy poor, perishable, . JlndiesS form. Speak now, and say why suOQldst thou wish to be more than thy say companions, or pine for ought more

THE AURORA OF SUNDAY NIGHT We copy 'front.' the Euening Post, the following description of the brilliant display of the North- ern Light as it appeared in New York city: We copy from the Eueaing Post, the following description of the brilliant display of the "North- ern Light as it appeared in New York city, THE SCENERY OF THE HEAVENS. Last night one of the most magnificent atnios- pherlc exhibitions that has ever been witnessed in this latitude took place. A display of the Aurora Boreals, of surprising extent and beauty occupied the heavens, producing the most singular effects and exciting the admiration and awe of the thou sands that witnessed the wondrous sight. The day previous had been unusually cool for the season, and the sky cloudy. 1t rained for short time uring the middle of the day, but in the after noon the clouds dispersed, and the sun set in un- clouded brilliancy. 1t was observed that the twilight appeared of I'M usual length About eight O'Clock it perceived that the prolonged light, instead of being legacy OF the sun, emanated from singular luminous cloud that swept in long trail of white light across the western part of the heavens, extending about half way to the zenith. The stars were not visible through the denser part of this cloud which retained its position and appearance for some time 1t then gradually shifted, and extended, assuming new phases of beauty. At about o'clock the atmospheric DISPLAY SEEM ed 10 reach Its elimination and its aspect seen from elevated positions and housetops commanding a full view Ell the horizon all sides, was such as to arouse the most overpowering emotions At the zenith, directly above the spectator appeared large clrcet OF white and red, dotted with stars While from this coronet radiated in every direction spears and currents of quivering light both white and red Most of these shoots Of light were trans parent, and the stars beyond beamed through with unobstructed beauty. To the east and to the west lay huge fields of luminous Clouds tinted with bright rosy flush, wholly unlike that produced by the rlslngsun, and, If possible even more beauti- 1ul. For some ten minutes this climax remained The ruby crown, gemmed and fringed by sparkling stars, retained its proud position in the zenith and the tremulous waves of light loated and auivered downwards like some imperial train waved bv the cool night winds at times it suggested mighty hand and an outstretched arm, bound at the wrist with bracelet of ruby and diamond, with the open palm held if in benediction over the earth, while the fingers OF light reached almost to the dis tant horizon Soon, Everett has beautifully spoken of somewhat similar scene, "the hands Of angels shift ed the glorious scenery of the heavens" The mass OF apparent red cloud to the east moved away south ward, gradually fading, while the CORRESPONDING red clouds on the west seemed to sink into a chaos OF dark cloud that, with fringe of blue skirted the western horizon. While these changes were taking place in the east and west, the Wondrous crown above moved few degrees and then gradu- ally faded Flashes of light, covering many de- grees slowly condensed into mighty luminous cloud, with its top near the zenith. This cloud gradually altering its shape, assumed forms both singular and suggestive. At one time it bore striking resemblance to an eagle and then the slightest, almost imperceptibe change, transformed it into a tortoise. Then again 1t seemed to sweep across the heavens presenting the appearance of a confused procession of beings clad in ghOstly shrouds, and reminding one of the dim heroes of Ossian. For about half an hour these remarkable changes took place. and then the lights gradually disappeared. In a short time, however they were resumed. Sheets of the same white lu- minous cloud again illuminated the sky, producing about the same amount of light as the full moon, and the night became almost as the day.

DIXON Twas early dawn, while dewy and bright The flowers were smiling in the day-god's light; And far from its home in the orange vale, Came the bamy breath of the southern gale. As looked from earth toward the azure sky, saw two clouds that foated on high, And crimson and white with the hues of morn Seemed the blushing herads of the dawn, Which the sun had surprised ere they hasted away From the glorious lustrc of his kindng ray; For they chung to each oherall beauteous and bright AS clothed in their drapcry of crimson and white They slowly hoated through ether and air, And seemed two angels lowering there. So, as gazed, a sky-mk upward driven, BY quiyering wings, toward the steep of Heaven, Opened his beak in a carol Of praise, As he shook his wings in the morning rays; And bent his flight toward those forms so fair Those beautiful clouds that hovered in airl | watched him still, and still he upward flew, Til lost, he seemed, in Heavens ethereal blue But alas his daring flight was all for naught, For the fairy forms which he hopefully sought, Were scattered and broke by the fcryid rays OF the morning sun, and dissolved in his blaze. As he sunk to earth ana hushcd his hymn, His eyes so bright with tears were dim; For the lowering forms which hc soaled to greet Had vanished forever away Thus, HETTIE, methinks we all are but larks, Forever pursuing ephemeral sparks; Forever by shadows decoyed astray, Forever allured by things which decay Pursuing unweariedly through lifos desert way Hopes shadows and clouds which dissolve in the ray OF sorrows sun, and leave us to mourn in despair, That visions so bright are empty air! The Stars that Fade. FROM THE FRENCH OF BERANGER. Shepherd our star, such is thy tale, Rules our days and shines in the skies; True, my child, but with her veil The night conceals it from our eyes. Weep Not For Her. weep not for her the pure, the good, Who from our midst is gone; Twas ever thus since mortal man This earth was placed upon: Our dearest objects pass away The cherished droop and die; The hopes that highest upward soar The soonest PROSTATE lie. Weep not for her-to mother dear A higher boon was given, In grace immortal now she treads The sapphire streets of Heaven. With crown unfading on her head, She chants the Savior's praise With myriads who in concert sweet Their angel voices raise. Weep not for her-she's better off For one so mild and meek: This earth was not a fitting place, So barren, cold, and bleak. The sinless light the golden air Of Zion claimed its own, And took her wearied spirit up Unto its native zone. Weep not for her-for "all is WELL" She is an angel now, No more will sorrow sweep athwart Her bright effulgent brow. Nor sin, nor suffering pain her heart This sinful worlds bchest- She lives DER death victorious now, On Heavens eternal rest Weep not for her-for mother dear, Though sadly we're bercft; And though within our circle fond, An aching void is left. Her memory is a sacred shrine sweet endearing theme On which our holiest thoughts may dwell Our calmest slumbers dream. Weep not for her-but let US strive To nerve our spirits up 'Gainst sorrows pang-oh yes, we can Unshrinking drink the cupl And when we've walked life's thorny path y few fleet severing years, Wen meet her in those happy realms Where bought but joy appears. W J. MULLIN.

Elspeth found home in the Mar quis' household, after the good old fashion of these times, which recognized claim on the part of all the helpless and afflicted of the clan to find a refuge with the family of their chief, and Kenelm had to all ap- pearance, escaped with perfect impunity. A writer in the Boston Christian Register gives this account of the last hours of Hor ace Mann. "On Monday morning august 1st) I was allowed to visit him, and my first glance convinced me that the chances were against his recovery. On Tuesday, at FIVE O'Clock P. NJ, the great soul mounted from the fal len tower. l was with him constantly du ring the last thirty six hours of his life, and / must say that I never saw the excel lencies of his character so fully revealed All that was craggy, angular and masculine had already died, and what remained was rich indeed. His real greatness never shone out more than in the death hour When he was told that he had but few hours to live, his brain flashed up with all the glow of his best days, and he talked at least two hours in strain of almost supra mortal eloquence. The members of his family, students remaining here during the vacation, and many of his neighbors were called in at his request, and he had for each some word of warning or cheer. Il was particularly noteworthy that his remarks to each person had some specific pertinency Of adaptation. His ideas, and the language in which he clothed them, were really grand. and amazed US all to silence-nay melted Us ALTO tears A signal of sweetness and tenderness per- vaded every word. Not often in ones life time does one have the privilege of witness ing so great scene. I am forced to con- fess that I never before appreciated the soft ness of the core that this masculine heart contained

Another Display of the Aurora, New YORK, Sept. 2.-Between II and O'Clock this morning the heavens were illum- mated with a display which was in no respect Inferior to the magnificent phenomenon of Sunday night. In the north, northeast and northwest at first there was a light like thai of the full moon, and showing everything i'll the streets as plainly. This light seemed to come in waves, differing in magnitude, velocity and color. At some moments the sky was as deeply crimsoned as on Sunday. At half past one o'clock the strange light showed from all points of the compass, and the deep crimson cloud floating in the south as well us in the north, and the magnetic beams radiated from the zenith, and every moment was unlike the last. A chilly wind was blowing from the north. BosroN, Sept. 2.-There was another dis play of the Aurora last night, so brilliant that about | o'clock, ordinary print could be read by the light. The effect continued through this forenoon, affecting and impeding the work ing of the telegraph lines. The auroral cur rents from east to west were so regular that the operators on the eastern line were able to hold communication and transmit messages over them between this city and Portland, the usual batteries being disconnected from the wire. The same effects were exhibited upon the Cape Cod and other lines.

MISCELLANEOUS. wealthy farmer, named Joseph Smith, re- siding in Kent county, Canada West, having been much annoyed by depredations upon his grapes and other fruit, loaded gun and kept it in readiness for the return of the thieves. On Monday evening, 10th inst, on leaving his house after supper, he directed his servant girl to take the gun and shoot the first person who approached the grapes. On his return, forgetting the injunctions he had given he went to the grape vines, when the girl, not re- cognizing him in the dusk, fired, the charge of shot taking effect in the thigh, and terminal lug his life in few minutes.
