An individual died recently in Paris who. twenty years ago, was one of the most noted men in the French capital namely: Lord Henry Seymour. He has done more in France than any Englishman of the age. He was greater conoueror than We'll ington, for he achieved victory over as stubborn a prejudice existed, viz: the prejudice of frenehmen against pig-skin. By pigskin we mean saddle Before his time French equitation was confined to the regiments of Dragons private citizen no more thought of horseback riding for pleasure than he would now of flying. The "turf" technically speaking, unknown in France ihere had been, 1T is true, on fete days. few races IN the Champ de Mars under the patronage of the Due d Angoueme; but they were what would be called here "scrub" races and English Jockeys ony were hired to ride, for no Frenchnen would risk their necks in this manner, prone though they be to all sorts of risks in public. Lord Sevmour dis covered the Bots de Boulogne-that charming wood, the pride of Paris. He first gave the exam pie of riding, and then of riding outside the Cbamp Elysees to the wood beyond. Previous to this re- markable mans appearance, Parisians never went beyond the barrier; now they have one of the most beautiful drives in the world. And all this the re- suit of an Englishman persistence in the sports and exercises OF his "bright little, tight little sland!" He wasn't genius, this Lord Seymour; bv no means bel esprit. Nothing but a rosv-faced Eng lishman, with rent-roll OF fabulous length, and a stock of health which enabled him to enjoy it, He VISITED VISITED Paris in making the "grand tour which English noblemen only made then, but which all classes make nowadays, and found the town so attractive that he established himself in sunerb apartments, and by lavish expenditure and person al advantages, soon made himself famous fash ionable OF the first water. His equpages were something new to Frenchmen His horses were thorough breds. His carriages, from a Pail Mall mandatory, were quite different from the estab- lishments in which the stiff old fogies of the Fau- bourg ST. German in the habit of airing them selves. He became the mode. The young exuui- sites admired and copied him. He was the Brum- mel of the boulevards He gave the law in every petely changed the social habits of the Frenchman He instituted clubs and drew them away from their cosy, economical cafes 1t was he, much as the chief of police, who broke up the public gambling houses, Frascati's, and those gorgeous "hes' of the Palais Royal. The famous Jockey Club, which is now an institution in Paris, was founded by him and his clique, and it was the pio- neer OF all the superb "cerces" which now dot the Boulevards, and are frequented ny dplomatists, statesmen and warriors, who play such fierce games OF iansquenet and baccarat in spite of sharp-eyed police and a regulation against stalking money games of chance. ,.H f- 49, # The whole social system of France was revolu- tionzed by this Lord Seymour Nobody smoked, nobody took spirits and water, nobody was in club-room, and nobody dared to undertake steepe chase. He brought all into fashion, and they are now characteristics of the people. He was gay YOUTH too and took kindly to the French life with out abandoning some of the agreeable peculiarites of his own country. The widest farceur was Sey- mour, the most interchangeable courier was Sey mour; and never before was seen such cicenr as Seymour. These being all the Gallo synonyms for "fast," were coupled with his name whenever it was pronounced. Everybody in Paris knew him. At the masked balls he was the noisiest and the drollest. With troop Of his boon companions he would bust in among the dancers and draw all at tention upon himself. How TO TEST EaGs.-A correspondent of the Springfield Republican says: There is no difficulty whatever in testing eggs; they are mostly examined by a candle. Another wry to tell good eggs is to put them in a pail of water, and if they are good they will lay on their sides, always; if bad, they will stand on their small end, the large end always uppcrmost, unless they have been shaken considerably, when they will stand either end up. Therefore, a bad egg eau be told by the way it rests in w~ater-always end up never on its side. Any egg that lies fiat is good to eat, and can be depended upon. An ordinary mode is to take them into a room moderately dark land hold them between the eye and a candle Or lamp. IF the egg be good-that is, if the albumen is still unaf- fected-a light will shine through a reddish glow; while, if affected, it will be opaque or dark"

A Young Wife Dies Broken-Hearted. In the obituary department of the Jour nal, published at Palmer, Mass, we find the following announcement: "DIED-Mary, aged 20, wife Of De Witt Clinton Packard, of Providence, II. L." In the editorial column there is sad and touching story, relating to the announce mcnt, which we annex below. 1t is a les son from the tomb, to the young and thoughtless, and told so eloquently that it cannot fail to make an impression for good on readers of every age. 1t says: "ln another column we record the death of young lady who died Of broken heart We do not like to trespass upon the sa- credncss of domestic grief, to unfold the DEATHS of her sad story; but. when the privacy of afiliction become public feeling, it is not improper for the Press to place the events on record. 1t is not necessary to repeat names or relate minute partcu- lars 1t is enough that we draw the out lines ofa picture for the reader to paint with appropriate colors. Many months ago, in the neighboring town of BelohSr- town. young man sought and received the promise OF the hand of a young lady, whose home was in the lap of luxury, whose mental and personal attractions made all pleasant around her. Like too many confding ones of her sex, she trusted mans uAhallowed promise and yielded all to him. From that hour he estranged himself from her, and removed to dis tant State When it became evident that he had exposed himself to the penalty of Il l. Al. L. \ returned to her to fulfill the vows he had long before made They were married in one of those hasty. unceremonious ways, which occupy but little time or attention. Late in the evening they returned to her fathers house, where he left her in the street, promising to return in short time. But that promise was never fulfilled She wrote to him, and received encourage ment that he would soon provide home for her, but delay followed delay, till her letters and entreatics were unheeded and unanswered. At lenght pledge of wo- mans love for her husband came into the world 10 open new fountains OF affection to / the young wife. Still the husband and 7 father came not. at The mother recovered from confn,- ment; but after repeated letters 10 her hus- band found no answer, the idea that she was descrtee-by him forced itself upon her, and she gave way to dcspondcncy and des- pair. The child, partaking of its mother s grief, soon died. There was nothing that she could live for now, and though suf- fering from no disease, .he sank upon a dying bed. Then the swift wing of light ming bore to the distant husband the intel ligcnce that she was dying. He still hcsi- tated, but at length set out to meet his cx- piring wife. Conscious that her hours were few, she only wished to live long enough to see her husband; he was still all to her. Her last words to her friends were: Tell him that | still love him-that died for him. When evening shadowe,l the earth the husband came. AS he ap- preached the bedside of his injured wife he was recognized, and the words. Hes come. burst from her lips. Already had the wing of the death. angel cast its shadow over that dwelling. she was entering the dimness of the dark valley. Next morn ing, in that room, lay the corpse of beau tiful young wife, on which the husband had looked for the last time and departed. Last Sabbath afternoon the funeral OF the young wife took place under her father roof. Her ncighbors and friends to the number of five hundred were present: but the husband who bad left her to die for him was not there. A deeply affecting address was made by her former pastor. and just as thesun was sinking behind the western hills, four young ladies of her ac- quaintance. clad in garments of white, bore her to grave in the garden, where the green turf was laid gently over her. Snch is the story of one who died broken heartcd.- The grave is quiet place for the injured wife. but where in AL the world can there be peace for him who would thus bring sor- row and death upon her? The story has its moral. but we viii leave the reader to apply il; it is full iofwariiing. and we leave the young to heed it.vhlaf "a

A Splendid Aurora Borealis. We had, last night, one of the most bril- | liant auroral manifestations we have ever known in summer. 1t began about eight / o'clock, before the twilight had fully gone, | and at twelve it was still brilliant At the time it began, there were dense masses OF black clouds in the West, reaching halfway to the zenith. These, DISAPPEARED before the Aurora, which soon oversPread half the sky, the arch eliminating, as the Aurora always does when it covers The sky, at the "zeni;h of the magnetic Dip which phrase may be hus explained II a magnetized needle be suspended in vertical plane on pivot, the northern pole will point to the Earth, but not in vertical line, and the angle of vari- alton from the vertical line is called the "magnetic Dip" The zenith of this is the point in the sky to which the south pole of the needle points The colors of the A Irora W ere green:sh yellow, and the compliment tary shade OF red. When the aurora was at its hight the eoiors were very b rilliant. Later in the night the blush was confined to the north, and did not reach more than one fourth the distance to the zenith. The Aurora is supposed to be caused by the illumination, through electrical influen- ces, of particle of sleet. in the higher re- gion of the atmosphere. We have seen it several times IN summer, and have almost always noticed that it followed a sudden lowering of the temperature after rain. Last evening the mercury sank rapidly, and at twelve O'Clock it was more than probable that we should have frost before morning Although, as we say, we have severa times seen :he Aurora in summer, we never saw so brilliant manifestation but once before, and was more than fifteen years ago, in this city, when the diffusion was as great and the light more brilliant than last night. The southern parts Of the heavens seemed purple by contrast. In the east and north east the lights were green, of various shades, mingled with yellow, while in tho nortk west they were of a brilliant rose tint, like the flames from burning buildings. And over the whole of the sky thus Illuminated, away up to the crown of the arch and beyond, ever and. anou ran tremulous waves of light, rot unlike the flashes of lightning. The ligb. was so intense that our hand held near a wall cast shadow, and we read by it solid minion type. p. S.-About ore O'Clock this morning the aurora assumed form of extreme beauty. Commencing with an arch in the North, which was green above, and beneath of the intensest purple streams of light green shot up to the zenith of the magnetic dip, from fully half the circumference of the horizon. These united, making a sort of CROWN bey ond this there were banks OF greyish green light.-Cin. Gaz, 29h u!t.

This man, on IIou- din's showing, had passed through variety of adventures, wonderful as any related by Eu gene Sue or Alexandra Dumas. One of these adventures is related in Hou- din's Autobiography, yet unpublished in this country, and we here take the liberty of throw ing it into our own less attractive words, in order to condense it within reasonable bounds. While in Rome, an invitation reached Tor RIM to exhibit before no less parsonage than the Supreme Pontiff. The occupant of the chair Of St Peter at that time was that very estimabe old gentleman, Pope Plus the Sew enth 1t was not to be thought of, by any con- jurer with a proper pride in his art that only the ordinary tricks should be exhibited before His Holiness. Something new was to be hit upon-something which would astonish, be long borne in memory, and talked Of as Who'll ly wonderful and inexplicabie Without searching for such thing, chance, that inventor of all inventions the most ingeni- Gus, came to aid him. The very evening be- fore Torrini was to show off before the Pope and conclave and other high tligntaries of the church, he happened to be in the shop of one of the first watchmakers of Rome. A servant came in to inquire whether the watch of his Excellency the Cardinal de was mended. The matchmaker replied that the repairs would not be completed until the evening, when he should himself bring it to the CARDINAL and the servant withdrew Taking the watch from drawer, the watch maker proceeded to examine it. Otis hand some and excellent watch,' said the tradesman to the conjurer, "and the Cardinal values it at more than ten thousand francs, because, hav- ing ordered it himself from the illustrous Breguet, he fancies it unique ofits kind Yet, what an odd thing two days ago mad young fellow of this town of ours came to Of fer me, for thousand francs, watch by the same maker, exactly like the Cardinals" This attracted Torrini's attention. He ex- amined the watch, which was handsome one, with several distinguishing peculiarties. An idea struck him. ''Do you think" he asked the matchmaker, "that this person really wishes to part with his watch 2" There was no doubt. The young man was spendthrift, who had gradually made away with his prop erty, and had come down to selling even his family jewels. The thousand francs would be acceptable. Then, said Torrini, "Find this person for me. l wish to make his watch mine but | must have it at once. Buy it for me then engrave the Cardinals arms on mine, so that the two may not be distinguished one from the other. On your discretion de- ponds the benefit you will draw from this transaction" The owner of the watch was easily found, at the Clearinghouse, which he constantly fire. quented. The watch was seen, examined, closely compared with the Cardinals, and pur- chased 1t was duly engraved, duly sent home, duly paid for, and as duly placed in Torrini's pocket, ready for the trick of tricks which was to close his night at the Vatican. Pope Plus VII. was an enlightened man. and turned deaf ear to all hints that Torrini's wonderful effects were produced by sorcery He occupied large armchair on a dais, placed on the foreground. Near him were placed the cardinals, and behind them were the different preates and dignitaries of the church. AS far as that nights teats went, the Pope sat simply like Wondering. elayman, astonished at the skill Of the conjuror. The evening passed off agreeably, for Torrini never performed BETTER and never had more wonder-stricken audi ence." "Then,' las Torrni himself told the story,) "to end it and by way of bouquet went on to the famous trick which | had contrived for the occasion. Here however, had to encounter many difficulties. The greatest of these, with out question: was to lure the Cardinal de to give me his watch, and that without directly asking for it. To gain my point, L had re- course to stratagem. On my asking for a watch, many had been handed to me-but had given them back, on the pretext more or less true, that offering as they did no pecu- liarity in shape, it would be difficult afterwards sietuS, any one among YOU said |, has "a. ther large watch 1.-THE Cardinals had precisely this popularity and would entrust it to me, should accept it willingly as the one fittest for our experiment. The Cardinal piqued himself on the size of his watch having the idea that the works acted more freely in a large case. He hesitated to lend it to Torrini, but did so at the special re- quest of the Pope adding many cautions to IIo IL MI tho NH I'M; amined and admired the watch, and asked nu- merous questions about it by way of bonment- a word used by conf Jurors to denote the pre- liminary talk which is to pass the time and put an audience off its guard, by pre-occupying its attention. Torrin praised the Cardinals watch up to the skies, expatiating on its numerous good qualities. "See, said he, "a first proof of them" And with this he lifted up the watch as high as his face and let it fall on the parquet. There was cry of fright on every side. The Cardinal, pale and trembling, got up. 'Sir!" said he, with illrestraned anger, "what you have done is an extremely bad joker Torrini assured him that this was only done to prove the per- lection of the watch, which would come back to him uninjured by the trials to which it would be subjected. The beautiful Breguet, which the Cardinal believed to be unique, was destined for severer ill usage. Torrini, not content with dashng it down, stamped upon the case, crushed it into a shapeless mass of wheels, springs, and broken hands This he handed around that all might be sure it ,cas the Cardinals watch of watches. All this time the Cardinals rage was at fever heat. He had no small cause for anger. His watch, about the identity Of which there could be no doubt, for he recognized his arms en- graved inside the case, was utterly ruined, and, almost in tears, he declared that it had been unique, and never could be replaced. Torrini's next move was to get the watch the real Simon Pure, for it was his own which was destroyed-into the Pope's pocket. As long as his holiness remained seated, this could not be done. An expedient had to be found for getting him out OF his chair. Torrini was SO lucky as to find one. He asked for brass pestle and mortar, and one was brought up from the kitchen, where it was an implement of the cuisinier. Placing it upon the table, he cast into it the wrecks of the famous Breguet, and began to pound them violently with the enormous pestle. A slight detonation was sud- denly heard and reddish flame arose from the bottom of the vessel, which gave the scene the appearance of real magic Tor RIM, still pounding in the mortar with great fury, eant over it, and pretending to look in, made ordinations of wonder to himself at the surprising things he pretended there to see. The spectators, consisting of Cardinals and their attendants, were dying to know what he was wondering at, but, out of respect to the Pope, no one ventured to rise. AT last excited by curiosity, the Pope approached the table, followed by some Others of the audience. Tor RIM was still pounding away, and still excaim ing. 81 do not know to what am to attribute the bewiderment j feel, said his Holiness "but really cannot see anythingP Neither could that arch imposter, Torrini He, how ever, was too prudent to own it, and begged the Pope to come round the table, next to him self-as the best point for seeing. This was done, and the Cardinals watch was quietly

FROM JAMAICA.-Advices have been received at New York from Jamaica, dated at Kingston on the 10th inst. Trade was exceedingly depressed, with little prospect of revival soon. The sugar crop of the year would not exceed twenty-three thou sand hogsheads, which, with the proportionate de- crease in rum would show decline in the exports amounting to 81 900, 900 in the year. The Governor had left Kingston on visit to the excited district. The weather good. and the public health report is favorable. The local press indignant at the efforts of the Anti-Slavery Society of England to prevent immigration from the East, and the papers assert that Jamaica has fallen in her material pros perity since emancipation. So that, instead OF ex- porting 10000 hogsheads of sugar, as in 1888, she will send out only $4,000 hhds in 1859.

But know in whom have belived,' and leaning on His arm i fear no evil. DO not blame me for keeping even all this from you. How could subject you. Of all Others. to such sorrow as feel at parting. when time will soon make it appa- rent to you! could have wished to live, if only to be at your side when your tins shall come and pillowing your head ON my breast, wipe the death damps from your brow. and usher your departing spirit into its Makers presence, embalmcd in woman's holiest prayer. Yours is the privilege of watch ing through long and drcary nights, for tho spirits final flight, and Of transferring nv sinking head from your breast to my Sa viour's bosom. And you shall share nv last thought, and the last faint pressure OF the hand, and the last feeble kiss shall be yours. and even when flesh and heart shall have failed me, my eyes shall rest on yours until glazed by death, and our spirits shall hold one last communion until gently ia ding from my vicw-thc last Of carth-you shall mingle with the first brigh. glimpscs of the unfading glories of the better world. where par:ings are unknown. Il appears by late advices from the Pacific that the everlasting Oregon Boundary question is again to be.revived. 1t is generally thought however, that the news of actual hostiiities hav- ing been commenced by one of Her Brittanic Majesty's steamers, is not true. Be this as it may, difficulties with Great Britain, in regard to the Oregon Boundary line, are confidently anti cipated. The manner in which the difficulty presents itselfis as follows: By the treaty of June 10, 1876, negotiated by Louis McLane, under in structiOns from Mr.. Buchanan, then Secretary of State, it was stipulated: that the dividing line should run along the 49th parallel of North latitude "to the middle Of the channel" which separates Vancouyers Island from the continent and thence southerly through the middle of said channel and Of Africa Straits to the Pacific. 1t appears now, however, that there are taco channels, between the Island and the continent, both of which lead into the Pacific. By one of these the Island of San Juan will fall to us, and by the other it will go to Great Britain. The British claim that the line should run down the strait of Rosario, as it is the nearest to the main land. The q. S. claim that it should run through what is called the "Do Haro channel" upon the ground, we presume that such line would include all of Yancouyers Island-the Island of San Juan not having been mentioned in the treaty of settlement. The Oregon boundary Question The Main Channel.-The Smithsonian Institute Rockville Fair. .-Fsrenaun's Visit, dc When the United States and Great Brit ian agreed upon :he treaty, that the 49th pa. allel of latitude, should be the Northern boun dary of Oregon Territory, every body sup posed that the question was finally settled. Had this 49th line been extended to the Pa cifc, it would have divided Vancouvers Is land, which it was conceded belonged to Great Britian, therefore the treaty stipulated that the 49th PARALLEL should run only as far West as the main channel, which separated Vancouvers from the shore, then follow the channel so as to exclude Vancouver then due West to the ocean. Now it appears there are two channels between Vancouver and the main land; that of the canal De Haro, which lies between Vancouver and the Island of San Juan, aud the Rosario Straits. lying be- tween San Juan and the main shore of Wash ington Territory. The Americans contend that as the canal De Haro is the widest, deep er and more direct, that it is, therefore, the main channel, whilst the British say the Is land of San Juan has always been considered as an appendage of Vancouver, therefore, the channel referred to in the treaty is the Rosario, SO that the present difficulty in that section OF country rests upon the several in terpretations of the treaty. San Juan has been partly at least, in the possession of our government for several years. aud u. S Of ticers have resided and done business there. Gen Harvey in taking exclusive possession OF the Island acted without positive authority from the Government, and although matters III that quarter look like hostilities between | two peaceful Nations, the question oe boun- dary will undoubtedly be arranged to the sat lsfaction of both parties in peaceful man ner. The exhibition of farm products. vegetables and articles of female industry are spoken of in highest terms The George town Light Infantry were present and went through number of Military evolutions. This is combining the arts of Peace and War in new and yet not Objectionable man ner The American Engine Company of Phila- delphia, will visit this city on Monday even ing, and while here will be the guests of the Franklin Fire Company. Beck's celebrated Band accompanies them, on Wednesday, they take an excursion down the Potomac to Mount Vernon and Glymont, and return home on Thursday. The Sons of Malta are making grand prep arations for their Tournament on the 18th inst. Delegations will be here from Baltimore, Philadelphia, New York and Boston, and it is expected large influx of strangers will be present to witness the exploits of the gallant knights. CarlInc0urt Lowe, an GrOnaut of six years practical experience, and mechanician of uncommon ingenuity, has been for several months engaged in building and perfecting an Ar-Ship of unparalleled dimensions, with which he proposes to undertake the tr ransit of the Atlantic Ocean. This daring scheme has been for many years the pet am bition of many aronauts, who have lacked either the bodness to carry their plans into execution or have not had the pecuniary means to build the proper machinery. Mr.. Lowe, being luckily pos sesSed OF both these requisites, has invested some S22, 900 in the construction of machine with which he is confident he make air-voyages of DAYS or even weeks duration. He planned his machine and even began his work, some eight months since; but hearing that his friend, Mr.. John Wise, had in contemplation the construction of a machine for the transatlantic trip, Mr.. Lowe laid aside his work for SIX months Mr.. Wise having, for satisfactory reasons, given up the project of building his ma chine, MIR. Lowe resumed work on his invention and for the past two months the labor of a number OF persons, numbering at times as many as sixty has been constantly in requsition, and the machine Is now in so great state of forwardness that but two or three weeks more time is required to put it in working order, ready for the great experiment The work has been carried on with so much mys- terry that but few of the many people engaged it have had any idea to what end so much sewing, and netting, and vanishing tended. Most of them imagined that they were working on some sort OF new-fangled tents, or for some patent sails of fashion soon to be introduced certain Government vessels. The scene of operations is about five miles distant from New York, it being necessary to have grassy field of considerable extent on which to varnish and prepare the four five acres of ma terials. The cloth was three times carefully Overhauled by the most trustworthy persons, and every flaw or hole, slight strainng apart of the threads COW cred with a patch of silk stitched down by hand. When the cloth had been cut and stitched into these sections the next operation was to thorough ly saturate them with the varnish before mention ed The first coat of varnish increased the weight of the cloth l,500 pounds; the following ones of course, add much less to the weight. Hayes, which hagqbeen employed some time IN the coasting trade, was advertised . few days ago to sail for Australia, and offered to take passengers and smart Jeremmy Diddler laid in his stores in the most extravagant manner. He bought furniture, carpets. provisions, wines, liquors, and, in fact, everything necessary to the comfort Of a sea-voyage. unIor5u e nately, however, Capt. Hayes forgot to pay for the articles He bought the brig for $500, and PAID $500 on it. He then placed her upon the ways OF Tichenor & Co., and thoroughly repaired her on 9 credit. He then advertised her for Melbourne, anu commenced laying in his stores, without disbursing q cent, so loosely did he manage his cards. His butch err, grocer, market man, and strange to say. even his lawyers, were victimized to the tune OF $oOU. The only man who felt any doubt OF his honest lnten- lions was the man who filed the water casks, and who kbelled the brig for his bill, amounting to $50. The U. s. Marshal had, or was supposed to have had, the keeping of the brig. On Sunday night. Aug; rs, however, there sprung up a brisk breeze, and the Captain being a good sailor, could not resist 1t, and spreading his sails to the favoring gale, he quietly .idrew OUT from the harbor, and cleared the Heads instead of the Custom House, forgetting the little formality of ssthe papers, AS soon as it was ascer- tanned that the brig had gone there was a terrible hubbub. and Marshal Solomon started the steam tug Martin While in pursuit of her, but 1t was like starting a snail to catch q swallow. The steamer re- turned with a report that the brig was non est inren- fus.-Jdha, -4ug. 30. MORE OF THE ELlENrTA.-We yesterday learned q few more particulars relative to Capt. Hayes OF the brig ElLenita, which left this port on Monday morn ing, August %. Mt two o'clock, without clearance or other papers. and deeply in debt to parties IN this city. 1t is said that q number of persons had taken passage on the brig and had paid before hand. but the vessel sailed, leaving nearly all OF them behind. Capt. Hayes, however, carried of the wife and three children Of a gentleman who is one of those left. He also carried off q trunk belonging to a Mrs. ARM strong, and containing all that lady's title deeds to property in Sydney. Capt. Hayes, however, did not carry off his own wife, that lady having left town the day before he sailed. We learn that the following parties have been swindled by Captain Hayes: MIR. Morrison, $500; Mr.. Tchenor, $3.50; ship carpen- tiers, $500; victuallers and grocers, Sl2OO; vegeta- BILE dealers, $500; a gentleman, for borrowed money, $500; legal advice, 500; a bill which his lawyer promised to pay, $114; money borrowed from his lawyers, $50; plumbers, $500; aud a multitude or other liabilities of less note, making in all about $4,000. The fellow also managed to swindle MIR. Morrison out of some forty tons of beans. 1t is sup posed by those who appear to be best informed, that he will steer for Tahiti, where he will lay in a cargo of oranges for the Sydney market.-Herai The California papers do not however tell the whole story. We are informed that in addition to the articles above mentioned he carried offsome $4,000 worth of jewelry, bought on credit, and FIVE or six thousand dollars in cash which had been deposited in his hands on freight or for safe keeping by the passengers. 1t is worthy Of men ton, as a mark of the shrewdness of the rascal. that the greater part of his stores were purchased at suburban establishments-of grocers who would be very unlikely to hold communication with each other, and who would think it a great stroke of business to supply a ship with goods and a business as safe and profitable as it was unusual. After taking French leave of his San Francisco friends, and carrying off the wife and children of one of his passengers whom he left behind, Capt. Hayes next turns up in the Hawaiian Islands. He entered the port of Kahului, on the Island of Maui, on Thursday flast week, the 18th, with the design Of taking on board some fresh provisions, and probably of smuggling a few goods. on shore. Unfortunately for the carrying out of his intentions, the gallant Sheriff of that island, Peter II. Treadway, Esq, got an inkling of his proceedings, and ever on the alert when duty calls, FASTENED at once across the mountain to ar rest the rogue upon a warrant for the violation of the revenue laws. He arrested him on shore, on the afternoon of the 18th, but subsequently consented to accompany him on board that he might give certain necessary orders to his mate. Once on board, the Captain detained the Sheriff upon various pretexts, until it was too late to go on shore, and they arranged that he should sleep on board, and in the morning they would land and proceed together to Lahaina, while the mate remained to carry the vessel around by sea. Early in the morning, however, the Captain announced to the Sheriff his deter mination to resist the arrest, alleging that it was illegal and declaring that he should go to sea Immediately, and gave the Sheriff his choice to 60 ashore or remain on board. Being unaccom- panied by any force, he was obliged to submit, and having been landed, was subjected to the modification of seeing the EUenita squaring away before a fresh wind. Capt. Hayes forgot, before leaving, to pay for the supplies procured at Kahului, amounting to about 800. In allusion to this affair we do not wish to throw any discredit upon the Sheriff of Maui, who is an excellent oficer-well known and highly esteemed throughout the islands. Rogues rarely get to windward of him. In this case he has done what ninety-nine men out Of a hundred would have done, and under the circumstances he is not much to blame for the escape of one of the greatest rascals that ever weent unhung. Where Hayes will go next remains a problem. 1t is thought by some that he will touch at Kauai and complete the equipment which Mr.. Treadway in terrupted on Maui. 1t is hardly likely that he will eventually dare to show his face again in Australia or China. Possibly he will go to some South American port, touching perhaps at Tahiti on his way, and there, FORGETTING the vessel, will dispose OF her cargo and apply the proceeds, with the cash already in hand, to the accomplishment of further schemes. Hayes is a man Of little education and of but little talent except for rascality. He is very plausible and gentlemanly in behavior when he has an object in appearing SO, and seems to have the dangerous faculty of impressing strangers with the belief that he is an honest man. lie is minus one ear-said to have been bitten off in a fight. His most intimate friend and accomplish is a man by the name of Robert Parkinson, who ~navigates his vessel for him, and plans the rogue ries which Hayes carries out. Whatever may be said in extenuation of his crimes, he is now to all intents a pirate, and we trust may meet the re- ward his conduct SO justly deserves.

AurOra BOrealis. Z The indianapolis Sea1tael gives the fol- lowing description Of the appearance Of the Borealis in that city, on Sssaniay evening. The Lafayette and papers in other northern towns give us similar descriptions of its brilliant appearance. In these lower and benighted latitudes we saw nothing of it; 3, On Saturday night, we had the most gor- geous exhibition of electric fires in the heavens, ever seen in this latitude In sum mer, or, indeed, that we ever saw at any time. The day had been cool and moist after the rain of Saturday, and soon after sunset the heavy banks of clouds in the west gave way before silvery light that IL lumined the northern sky, and shot its trembling arches of dawning and of dying light far up into the heavens converging to the zenith, Early in the evening a sheet >of sparks seemed hanging ia the northwest, so closely resembling the effect of large fire distance of, that many persons could not be persuaded that the woods were not burning in tiat direction. The 6ery red appearance gradually died away in the west, and about nine o'clock a far more brilliant exhibition of the same nature was to be seen in the north and east. A belt of sparks of a smoky red appearance shot up, and rapidly spread over the eastern horizon, until two-thirds of the sky in that direction was wrapped in the fiery shroud. -r 1t. disappeared almost as rapidly as it rose and spread, and then the fantastic play Of what is well and commonly known as the Aurora Borealis or Northern Light, con- tinued, making one feel chilly, as if we could feel the frost on our bones as we watched the pale streaks of light fading as they CLEANED in their flight. At eleven o'clock and long after, a phosphorescent light shone in our windows facing to the north, by which we could read distinctly The most brilliant exhibition, however, was long after midnight, when every appear ance we have attempted to describe was heightened, and ghasly splendor overhung the earth that would defy the pen to describe or the pencil to paint. ..- The proverb in regard to these lights is backed by scientific authority, that they portend cold weather, but whether we are to have heavy frosts before the corn is ripe, or not, we are not prepared to say. .- We learned late last evening that in Mad ison and Upton counties, heavy frosts were experienced on Sunday night.

The Times gives the following interesting account of similar phenomena in times gone by, and the popular theory of the origin of the Aurora Borcalis; Pliny and Aristotle record phenomena iden' teal with those which later times have wit messed The ancients ranked this, with other celestial phenomena, as portending great events. The most popular theory attributes it to electricity, but that agent has been made responsible for everything which men did not know how TO account for otherwise. The late Prof Olmsted maintained that its origin was cosmica, or, in other words, that the earth in revolving on its orbit at certain periods, passes through a nebulous body, which evolved this strange light in more or less brillancy, as the bpdy was larger or smaller. He fixed the length Of these periods from 60 10 SO years, and if we remember Alright, named 1890 as the time when we might look for another appearance. The remarkable display Of Sunday night gives those who have so strongly contested this idea, a strong argument against it, and launches as tronomers who have anchored to it upon the sea of conjecture again. Time is gliding from its pre- sent Hopes that cluster around young life, that swell in the bosom of manhood, have fallen from around it like the forest leaves, when the frosts of autumn have chilled them unto death Ambition, with its hollow promises, and pride, with its lofty look, have vanished away. The world with It's deceltfulncss; pleasure, with its gilded temptations, are gone and alone, in utter destruction of all that time promised, il must start on its solemn Journey across the valley Of the shadow of death "Make no noise !' Let the tumult of life cease. Let no sound break the souls communion with itself ere it starts on its returnless flight. Trouble it not with ac- cents of sorrow Let the tear stand still on the check of affection, and let not the wailing of grief break the solemn silence of the death scene. Let it gather the accents that come from within the dark shadow of eternity, saying to it, come home. Afar off the music came floating to it in the air. 'Tis the sound of heav- enly harps touched by viewless fingers. Mar not the harmony by the discord OF earth. "Let me die quietly" The commo- tions of life, the strife and warning with human destiny, are over. Wealth .ac- cumulatcd must be scattered; honors won must be resigned; and all the tri- umphs that come within the range OF human achievements must be thrown away. The past, with its trials, its trans gressions its accumulated responsibilities, its clinging memories, its vanished hopes, is rendering up to the future account disturb not the quiet of that awful reck. oning. Speak not Of fading memories, of affections whose objects perish in their loneliness, like the fewers of spring, OF wither in a slow decay. Heaven is opening upon its vision. The bright turrets, the tall spires, the holy domos of the Eternal City are emerging from the spectral darkness, and the glory of the Most High is dawning around them. The white throne is glistening in the distance and the whitc-robed angels are beckonine the weary spirit to its everlasting home What is life that il should be clung &c longer? What are the joys of the world that they should be regretted? What has earth TO place before the spirit Of a man to tempt its stay or turn it from it' eternal rest.--Rcgistv.

This Sunday is very much Ike other days with Us here; although now We have the privilege OF attending Mormon meeting. l embraced the opportunity on Sunday-went with my bloomer dress and hat, with my revolver by my side. The Prophet Brigham and his counsellors, kimba and Wells, came in a back way, well guarded by soldicry The Lord does not always take care Of his Prophets, and they are little afraid Of their heads. The twelve Apostles were seated in this pulpit, which has a close panneled wall around it, four feet high. The men come into this Tabernacle at one end door, and the women at the other. On Sunday night and Monday morning there was an unusually brilliant exhibition OF the Aurora Borealia, which covered one half the Northern heavens, from East 20 West. This mysterious light has ever puz- z led natural philosophers, who have ad- vanced the most contradictory explanations Tor the phenomena. Some have ascribed ihem To the reiraction of the SUMS rays from Arctic ice bergs; others have believed that the refraclion is from Northern ice or snow, and the Iremulous motion to be caus- I'd by the perpetual vibrations of the earth's atnoSOhere; but The magnetic telegraph mas solved the prob i'm. On Sunday even ing, when the sky was perfectly clear, the stars shining and the wind still, the only unusual appearance being the reddening of lie Northern and Eastern heavens. one of the operators N the Harrsburyn Office chaaced to lodch the wire. and was thrown, by the viole nee of shock which he re- ceived, across the room. 1T :he; same time the Superintendent Of the Cansdiap lines Of telegraph informs US that the line betwe en- Quebec and Farther Point was in perle ct working order. Yet it was proved impos: Nsible to despatch the foreign news across the wires. BOo-hOO.ing. The Aurora Borealis, Douglas essay, Mr. Boyce's speech and the Blue Ridge Railroad are perfect God sends to editors these days. We hardly know what they would have done it these things had not turned up. Well, there are great diversity of opinions on all these subjects. Some they have run OH; (; some they can't. We recollect hearing an anecdote of an old gentleman by the name of Harper who had made q race Oh a sprlght- ly filly that he owned 1t so happened i'll the race, which was run in long lane, that hog, which was lying down in one corner of the fence, suddenly frightened by the run ming horses sprung out and boo.hoo.ed, there by causing Harper's tilly to throw her rider -Harper's son-whereby he lost the race. The old man was terribly outraged, swore that the Harpers were forever disgraced; SO To prove to his son that he was no rider, he told him to 20 off down the lane, get in one corner of the fence, when lie would ride the flly and see if he could boo-hoo him ott. The old man mounted his filly and put oit down the lane as fast as the animal could travel; Just as he got opposite his son, the lad sprung out, threw up his coat tail and boo-hoo-ed-when down the old gentleman tumbled, Now all of US are boo-hoo-ipg at Douglas, but we can't boo-hoo him oil the track, he rides we'll. It's true, gentlemen of the press, YOU have boo-hoo-ed off the aurora borealis, you have fairly run it OF. And some of you are trying to boo-hoo off the Blue Ridge Railroad. Well, you can boo-hoo and boo-hoo, and We tell you now you may get in the fence corner, throw up your coat tails and boo-hoo till you are hoarse, but you can't boo.hoo off the building Of the Blue Ridge Railroad. A ROMANCE. The traveller who has been fortunate enough to SIT beside an unknown beauty in railway carriage and had his conversational powers brought into play by her spirit of sociablity, comprehend the bliss of good looking bachelor whose car ad- venture we about to relate. This worthy gentleman was a passenger on the Central Railroad on Monday last, and happened to De IN the car that was pretty well stocked with humanity. lie had managed to retain a seat from the commencement of the journey, until the train reached stopping place, where fresh supply of passengers entered it, when he galantly surren- dered 1t to an old lady, and made up his mind to stand awhile. Now, it happened that young and stylish looking lady tced the act and so pleased was she to see an old woman treated politely that she at once removed her carpet bag from the end OF the seat she occupied, and invited the gentleman TO take Its place Nothing 10th, our hero accepted the modest invitation, and was soon engaged in a friendly conversation with the belle of the train They chatted in lively style until the "shades of night were falling fast when the lady's utter ances grew slower, then indstiuct, and then alto gether ceased, for she was asleep. Not being disposed to follow her example the gentleman amused hms If by watching his fellow passengers, and was reminded of his companion 5 presence by her head touching his shoulder. Nor pheus had her completely in his folds, and bv Sc rles OF graceful mods she unconsciously sought the support of her railroad acquaintance. The bachelor was delighted at the first gentle touch, but bis pleasure, when, in the sweet aban- donment of sleep, her form nestled down until its whole weight bore entirely upon him, battles de- serlptlon The better to support his lovely burden he placed his arm around her waist, and then gave himself up to the delirium of the moment. After passing the next station, gentleman en- tered the car containing the person above referred to, and commenced examining the faces of each oc- cupant, as though he was in search of some friend In the darkness of the hour he passed the sleeper and her supporter without noticing them and it was only when he returned to retrace his steps that the scene attracted his attention. In moment the shade of anxiety on bis features was succeeded by trown, and he stepped quickly to the side of the fair sleeper. As his hand descended heavily upon her shoulder she started opened her eyes and sprang to her feet "blushing celestial rosy red" Before the bachelor could speak, the new conner politely informed him that he would take care of his own wife, if he had no objections, and straightway led the lady to another seat The explanation that ensued unfolded the fact that the lady had been absent on a visit for some time, and was then returning to the faithful hus- band, whose impatience led him to meet her half way. Eager to meet her, he had entered the car only to find her asleep in the arms of a stranger Of course the stranger told how it happened; but the trown did not pass away from the brow of the husband until they left the car. AUTUMN OF LIFE. Before my door, 20 summers heat, Proudly the elms their branches spread; Cool verdure sprang beneath my feet, And shadows played around my head; Joyfully passed the sultry hour, And Knocked the suns meridian power But when, with whitening hand, the frost Shriveled the leaves, and gaunt and bare, Their naked arms the elm trees tossed, While Autumn tempests rent the air, ] mourned the Summers glories fed, And copious tears Of sadness shed. When Winter came, and cold and still, The ice-king forged his frozen chain, And over snow-olad vale and hill Midnight assumed her solemn reigni Forth looking from my window bars, Through the stripped limbs saw the stars Thus earthly loves, like summer leaves, GLADDEN. but intercept our view; But when bereft the spirit grieyes, And hopes are crushed and comforts few. 10 in the depths Of sorrows night Beams forth from far celestial light.

Cheering Signs. We received call, few days since, from an old friend, who some time ago concluded that he could not stomach Re- publicanism, negro equality. and all that; and therefore had taken to voting the Democratic ticket. He informed us that his eyes were opened, and that he is now with the Republicans. The white sui frage clause in the Constitution satisfied him of the falsity of the negro equality charge; and the vote of Democratic Delegate against making Kansas a Free State, and the vote of the entire Demo cratic Delegation in favor Of continuing Slavery in Kansas for one year after her admission, convinced him that the Dem ocratic party of Kansas is but the old Pro- Slavery, Border Ruffian party in disgnise-and in addition to this, their boiling from the Convention, and their miserable efforts against the ratification of the Constitution, have completely dis gusted him. He would prefer some 9th or party to the Republicans, like ourself but in Kansas, it is Democratic or Re- publican-Democracy, here. means Sla- very, and Republicanism means Free State; therefore, he must unite with the Republicans. He told US of number Of persons in his locality, some of them in fluential men. who had become lukewarm, or had been led astray like himself, but who have determined to come back to the old landmarks. and to use their in Guence to reclaim others. We hear Of number of persons, who we're first induced to unite with Demo Gratis upon local issues. and were then gradually drawn into the Democratic ranks, who have discovered that they were duped, and are returning to the faith. In Doniphan, where there was not q Republican vote cast at the June election, we notice that they have organized Free Labor Club. If the Club practice what they profess, they cannot vote the Demo cratic ticket. We notice the names Of several staunch Free State men in the proceedings of the Club. We think the local schemes down there, to aid the De- mOcracy. have exploded, and that hence forth men will vote their sentiments. The skies are Frightening everywhere. In this County. with an honest registry. and thorough Republican organization, we can win the day by decisive major ity. The Democrats only succeeded. in the last election, by specializing schemes; but such measures will not hold the same men together for two elections in success sion. Then, organize at once, and we will give the Constitution big majority, and elect our entire County and Legisla- tive ticket, in November, to say nothing of the several hundred majority we will roll up for Parrot

The Milky Way forms the grandest feature of the armament. 1t completely encircles the whole fabric of the skies. and sends its light down upon us, accord ing to the observations, from no less than ls,WO,OO0 of suns. These are planted at various distances too remote to be more than feebly understood; but their light, the medium of measurement, requires for its transit to our earth periods raging from ten to a thousand years. Such is the sum of the great truths revealed to us by the two Herschels, who with zeal which no obstacle could daunt,s have ex- plored every part of the prodiuious cir Gle. Sir William Ierchel, after accom- plishing his famous section believed that he had guaged the Milky Way to its low est depth, affirming that he could follow a cluster OF stars with his telescope, con- structed expressly for the investigations as far back as would require $50, 900 years for the transmission of its light. But, presumptuous us it may seem, we must be permitted to doubt this assertion, us the same telescope, in the same master hand, was not sufficiently powerful to re- solve even the nebule in Orien. Nor must we forget that light, our only clue to those unsearchable regions, expands and decomposes in its progress, and coming from point so remote, its radient waves would be dispersed in space. Thus the reflection is forced upon us, that new clusters and systems, whosebeaming light will never reach our earth, still thronc beyond; and that, though it is permitted to man to behold the immensity, he shall never see the bounds Of the creaton.- 4HarrcLs Of Science.

The little girl was a scholar of the "Beech Woods" School House, and on the 9th of July, in the absence Of the teacher at noon, some of the boys began amusing themselves by firing crackers and throwing torpedoes in the neighborhood of her seat. Being a child of aVery nervous temperament, she was so much frightened that she sprang forward and tainted under the teachers desk, but on being taken to neighboring house. soon re- Vived. Her parents, from that day, noticed perceptible change in her spirits-and al though she did not complain, she was no longer bright but languid, passing the great er portion of the time 10 sleep. Medical aid was summoned, to relieve her, but to no avail. JehersOn's Wedding and his Wedding Night The following pleasing picture is from the Early Days of Jefferson, in the New York Century: Belinda" (Jeffersons first Iove) had been married many years, and her old admirer was approaching thirty, when he met with young lady of twenty two, who produced strong impression upon him. She was little above the medium height, slender, but elegantly formed. A fair complexion, with delicate tint of the rose, large hazel eyes, full Of life and feeling; and luxurinnt hair Of rich soft | auburn, formed a combination Of attractions which were eminently calculated to move the heart of a youthful bachelor Ia addition to all this, the lady was admirably graceful: che rode, danced and moved with elegant ease, and sang and played on the harpsichord very swcetly. Add still to these accomplishments the possession of excellent good sense, very considerable cultivation, warm, loving heart, and last, though not least, notable talents for housekeeping, and it will not be difficult to un- derstand how the youthful Mr., Jefferson came to visit very frequently at the lady's residence, in the couny OF Charles City. Il was called 'The Forest, and the name Of the lady was Mrs. Martha Shelton. She was a daughter of John lies, an eminent lawyer, and had mar ried in her seventeenth year, Mr.. Bathurst Skel- ton, who, dying in l76s, left his young wife widow at nineteen As the thee years of mourning began to expire, the beautiful young lady found herself besieged at "The Forest" by numerous visitors. Ofthesethree were favor ties with the fair Mrs. Shelton, of whom Mr. thomas Jefferson was one. The tradition runs that the pretensions of the rivals were decided, either by the musical accomplishments of the young counsellor, or by the fears of his OPP ponents. The tale is differently related One version is, that the two unfortunate gentlemen encountered each other on Mrs. Skeletons door step, but hearing Mr.. Jeilersons violin and voice accompanying the lady in pathetic song, gave up the contest thencefOrth and retired without entering, convinced that the affair was beyond their control. Et Ea The other story is, that all three met at the door, and agreed that they would take their turns Mr. Jefferson entered first, and the tones of the lady in singing with her companion de- PTived the list 'Ders Of all bOpe. However this may be, il is certain that the beautiful widow consented to become Mrs. Jefferson; and on the first day of January, l772, there was great festival at "The Forest" Friends and kindred assembled from far and nenr-there was frclick- ing and dancing after the abundant old fashion and we find from the bridegroom's note book that the servants and hddleIs received fees from his especial pocket. Il showed without, but WAhnlu hiA was lulIlu anu euluyInenL IN the light and warmth Of the great log fires, roaring in honor Of the ceremony, the bridegroom and his bride set out in their carriage for "Monti- cello" where No. Jefferson had commenced building in 1869, Just before the destruction by fire of his patrimOnial house Of "ShadWel - The journey was not to end without adven- lures. As they advanced toward the noun talns, the snow Increased in depth, and finally they were compelled to leave the carriage and proceed upon their way on horseback Stop. ping to rest at "Blenheim," the seat of Col Carter, where they found however, no one but an OveTseer, they left it at sunset Tesolutely bent upon reaching Monticello before night II was eight miles distant, and the rode, which was rather amOuntain bridle-path than an hon. est highway, was encountered with snow three feet deep. We may fancy the sensations of the newly welded bride at the chill appear ance Of the desOlate landscape as she passed along through the snow; but she was a woman of courage and good sense, and did notlcare for inconvenience. 1t was late when they arrived and a cherries reception awaited them--or rather, thore was no reception at all. The fires we're all out, the servants had gone TO bed, and the place was as dark and silent as the grave Conducting his wife to the little pavilion, which was the only part OF the house habitable at the time, Mr.. Jefferson proceeded to do the honors. On shelf behind some books, part of bottle Of wine was discovered; and this formed the supper of the bridegroom and the bride Far from being annoyed or discounted by their re- eeption, however, it only served for topic Of jest and laughter. The young lady was as mer- ry and liz ht hearted as a bird, and sent her clear voice ringing through the dreary little pavilion as gaily as she had ever done in the cheerful drawing room Of 'The Forest" Thus the long hours of the winter night fed away like minutes, winged with laughter, merriment aud song. The vigil was mirthful incident rather than a trial OF their equauimity They were young--and they had just been married. 4 When hands are claspod, and hearts beat close together, there 10 very little gloom in darkness, and winter nights are not cold This little moral sentiment, will not, hope, he criticised as too romantic for che dignity Of history IL doubtless explains how . young lady and gentleman, both used to every comfort and lux ury, found the gloomy little pavilion In the midst Of three feet Of snow, neither dark nor cold, on that January night long ago.

CHEROKEE MARBLE-The marble of Cherokee is attracting attention in various sections and Justly So The white marble quarries of Valley River produce a superior article wherever the excavations have been made below the line of atmospheric influences 1t is fine grained and susceptible of very fine pol ish, and is of snowy whteness. This variety is fonnd along the range in great quantity. 1t ex- tends the entire county of Cherokee and into Georgia There is also found accompanying the white stratum band of beautiful clouded marble The ground is rather sky blue with the most deli cate shades, resembling columns Of smoke cloud; and is in our judgment, most beautiful article for ornamental work. There is also on the northeastern part of the marble belt a flesh colored marble of a very fine texture. This quarry is located within some eight or ten miles of the line of the Blue Ridge Railroad, and Judging from specimens We have seen dressed and secured we think it susceptible of fine and elegant polish. We have no doubt but that these marbles will make large item of freight should the Blue Ridge Railroad be pushed forward to completion. Some of the propreors of these quarres already erect ing machinery for dressing and polishing these marbles Franklin (M C) 0brercer. -

Air Voyage Across Lake Ontario. The successful voyage of Mr.. Steiner from Oswego, was attended with some incidents of peril. His voyage commenced on the 24th ult. at half-past four P. NJ, and in fifteen minutes the balloon attained an altitude Of five thousand feet, the wind carrying it in south easterly direction at the speed Of about thirty miles an hour. An hour later Mr.. thousand feet. In his narration Mr.. Steiner says: Heavy masses Of clouds to the north and narth- slowly accumulated, and in majes- tic silence foated eastward Into their secrets twas given to the aeronaut to inquire To the dwellers upon earth they appeared solid and dark, but from the side turned skyward deep caverns were discernible in each, filed with the suns rays, intensely, gloriously bright. But though their presence pleased the eye they chilled the atmosphere. The balloon began to descend, it required the discharge of consid erable quantity of ballast ere it was brought to stand. Still further to add to the difficulty of the situation, thick vapor rose up from the lake, which. gathering round the Europa, be- came condensed on her surface, and added very considerably to her weight. Tho balloon dropped down with the weight Of water comparatively near the surface of the Lake, and was kept ahoat by throwing over ballast. The Europa was thus lightened until she assembled higher than before. Tho narra- tive says: | The sun had gone down; darkness covered tho face of the earth. 1t was very cold, and an uncomfortable feeling seized upon the aerial wanderer. His feet and hands became be- numbed, his ears began to ache, and that hilar. ity, which all voyageurs describe as attendant upon ascent into rarified air, departed. By wrapping himself up, however, he managed to keep from freezing, and continued on his way And now came an event in the voyage which we'll nigh proved fatal. When the sun had gone down, Prof. Steiner had tied the neck oi the balloon to prevent any unnecessary flow oi gas, so that the ascending power might be re. tanned as long as possible. About eight clock and in the space of five seconds, he suddenly found himself in the midst of an immense mass of vapor. 1t was pitch dark; he could moi even see the balloon which bore him, but soon found he was rising with an immense speed His attentive ear was caught by the kissing sound of the gas, which was forcing its way through; and, instantly springing into the net ting, he felt that the balloon was disended tc her utmost capacity. 1t was but the work o. a moment to unite the string which confined the neck, and out came the hydrogen with { rush, which had nearly sutfocated the traveller The clouds disappeared as they had come, ant once more the Europa went calmly on he way. To the north and northeast clouds wer still dscernible, but elsewhere the star twinkled in the clear heavens. 1t was still very cold, but more gas having been discharged About half past nine o'clock, Prof. Steine neared the Little sOdus light, and shortly af terward he sighted Oswego.

CAUSE OF THE AURORA BOREALIS.-M. de IN Rive, the celebrated French astronomer, explains the production Of the Aurora Bore ais, in the following manner: s.When the sun, having passed into the Southern hemisphere, no longer heats our at mosphere, the aqueous vapors which have ac- cumulated during the summer in this part Of the atmosphere begin to condense the kind Of humid cap enyeloping the polar regions ex- tend more and more, and facilitates the pas sage of electricity accumulated in the upper portion of the air But in this elevated re- gion, and especially at this period of the year, the aqueous vap0rs must most frequently pass into the state of minute particles of ice or snow floating in the air, similar to those which give rise to the halos; they form, as it were, a kind of semi-transparent mist. These half frozen fogs conduct the electricity to the sur face of the earth, near the pole, and are, at the same time, Illuminated by these currents or electric discharges. In fact, all observers agree in asserting that the aurora borealis is constantly preceded by a mist, which rises from the pole, and the margin of which. less dense than the remainder, is colored the first and, indeed, it is very frequent near the pole in the winter months, and especially in those where there is an abundance of vapor in the air"

IEEEEPSON,S WEnnINC The following pleasing picture is from the Early Days of jefferson, in the New York Century: ''Beinda," (Jetferson's first love) had been mar ried many years, and her old admirer was ap- proaching thirty, when he met with young lady of twenty-five, who produced strong impression upon him. She a little above the medium height, slender, but elegantly formed a fair COM plexion with delicate tint of the rosc large hazel eyes, full of life and feeling, and luxurant hair of a rich soft auburn, formed combination of attrac- tions which were emipently calculated to move the heart of youthful bachelor In addition to all this, the lady was admirably graceful; she rode, danced, and moved with elegant ease, and sarg and played on the harpischord very sweetly. Add still to these accomplishments the possession of excel lent good sense, very considerable cultivation a warm, loving heart and last though not the least, notable talents for housekeeping, and it will not be difficult to understand how the youthful Mr. Jeer- son came to visit very frequently at the lady resi- dence in the county of Charles City. 1t was call ed ''The Forest" and the name of the lady was Mrs. Martha Skelton. She was daughter of John Wayles, eminent lawyer and had married in her seventeenth year, Mr.. Bathurst Skelton, who dying in l76S, left his young wife widow at nine teen. AS the three years of mourning begun to ex pire the beautiful young lady found herself besieg ed at ''The Forest" by numerous visitors Of these, three favorites with the fair Mrs. Skel ton, of whom Mr.. Thomas Jefferson was one. The tradition runs that the pretensions of the rivals were decided, either by the musical accomplish ments of the young counsellor, or by the fears eff his opponents The tale IS differently related. One version is, that the two unfortunate gentlemen en- countered each other on Mrs Skeletons door step, but hearing Mr. Jefferson's violin and voice accom- panying the lady in pathetic song gave up the contest thencefOrth ana retired without entering, convinced that the affair beyond their con- troll. The other story is that all three met at the door, and agreed that they would take their turns. Mr.. Jefferson entered first, and the tones of the lady in singing with her companion deprived the listeners of all hope. However this may be, it is certain that the beautiful widow consented to become Mrs. Jefferson, and on the first dav of January, l7T2, there was great festival at 'The Forest" Friends and kindred assembled from far and near-there was frolicking and dancing after the abundant old tashion-and we find from the bridegrooms note book that the servants and fdders received t, es from his especial pocket. 1t showed without. but within all mirth and enjoyment, in the light and warmth of the great log fires, roaring in honor of the occasion Soon after the performances of the ceremony, the bridegroom and his bride set for ''Monticelo," where Mr.. Jefferson had commenced building in 1769 Just before the destruction bv fire of his patrimonal house of "Shadwell." The jour ney was not to end without adventures As they ad- vanced towards the mountain the snow increased in depth;and finally they were compelled to leave their carriage and proceed ON their way on horseback. Stepping to rest at Blenheim the seat of Col Car ter, where they found however, one but over seer, they leftit at sunset resouely bent ing Monticello before night. 1t was eight miles distant. and the road, which was rather noun tain bride path than an honest highway, en- numbered with snow three feet deep. We may fancy the sensations of the newly welded bride al the chill appearance Of the desoate landscape, she passed along through the snow; but she was woman of courage and good sense, and did not care | for inconvenience. 1t was late when they arrived | and cherries reception awaited them-or rather | there was no reception at ALL The fires were all | out, the servants had gone to bed, and the place was as dark and silent ss the grave. Conducting his wife TO the little pavilion, which the only part of the house habitable at the time, Mr.. Jeer son proceeded to do the honors. On a shelf behinC some books, part of bottle of wine was discovered and this formed the supper Of the bridegroom ant | the bride. Far from being annoyed or discounted | by their reception, however, it only served for topic of jest and laughter. The young lady was al merry and lighthearted bird, and sent he clear voice ringing through the dreary little pavil ion gaily as she had ever done in the cheerful drawing room of ''The Forest Thus the long hour OF the winter night fled away like minutes, winged with laughter, merriment and song. The vigil wa mirthtul incident rather than trial of thei equanimlty. They were young-and they had jus been married. When hands are clasped, and heaI t beat close together, there is very little gloom il | darkness, and winter nights are not cold. Thi little moral sentiment will not, hope be criticized as too romantic for the "dignity of history" l doubtless explains how young lady and gentleman | both used to every comfort and luxury found tn gloomy little pavilion in the midst of three feet snow, neither dark nor cold, on that January nigh | long agO.

The Fourth OF July Thank God for " Fourth" that one can celebrate with sience-the religious silence of these deep solitudes yelling up from these vast voids like prayer for place where one can hear his own heart beat above the rant Of the citys hot and dusty day, and preach his own Grafton from the sacred text of history without comment or Interpolation TO be away out here, outside the smell and crash of your dirty gunpowder, beyond the re- hottest possibility of getting drunk, or the physical necessity of being so, to undergo the laryngial and thoracic infections of the days traditional ritual, is relief so mex preside that an aronaut, sitting in his balloon, in the serene heights of the upper air, at IA picnic of cheese and crackers, and watching the thunder clouds splitting their sulphur at you, could not feel more proudly above you and disdainful of you, than do now. A brisk morning ride of eight or ten miles ahead of the train, over naked rolling prairie, prepared my frie nd M. and myself, for delightful surprise, when, as we turned the summit of ridge, the picturesque val ley of the Otter Tail, with its green CULTS of wood, flashed along ahead of US, winding down from the north east between banks of considerable height, just here on the edge of the billy ranges through which it breaks, it passage. have called this river the o. ter Tail, out of Difference to an absurd usage of the early voyaguers; but in the inspira> ton of this moment, we spontaneously adopted the nomenclature of DIR. OWEN, N1CoLLEr, and othere, and with something of the feeling of Moses when he caught glimpse of the Jordan from the peaks of Pisgah, we involuntarily lifted the remains of our felt hats, and saluted the Red River of the North, with hurra which condensed in three cheers the enthusiasm of twenty anniversaries of National Independence. An hours lounge upon its banks, when M. must needs sketch 1.-THE cleaning rivers crescent curve" where itswaters broken and lashed by rapids, widened and parted to embrace wooded island that sat with fine effect of color against the picturesque bend of the massive banks beyond, while went to sleep over a pocket edition of BRYANT, and the horses picked up scanty foddering from the thin grass upon the sandy edge of the bluffs ; and then few minutes ride took US across the stream, over solid bridge of logs, to the nascent city of Dayton, and so by The length of that bridge behind us, we were upon new continent-the plateau of the Red Riv- er-as distinct division of the earth's sur face, in it's whole confguration, as if an ocean rolled between Us and the opposite shore. Dayton or Wassiota, as it's proprietor calls it, is situated about four miles below the mouth Of the Pelican, on the western bank of the Upper Red or Otter Tail river at the great angle where it changes its southern for westerly direction. The riv- er is about forty yards wide here, and runs with rapid current. broken by rocky shoals, between tortuous bluff banks, not less than one hundred feet high at the most elevated points. The rapids here are a continuation of the Pelican and other rapids which mark the descent of the stream from the PLATEAU of the Mississippi basin to that of the Red River. The river follows the edge of the billy ranges, and retains its precipitous banks to the point of its deflec- ton westward, when it takes the character istics of the Red River basin-the steep, irregular shores sinking to level bank, as smooth as the rim of bowl. AS, accord ing to all analogies, the main river carries its name to its source, it is difficult to see any just reason why the name of Red River should be cut off by the sharp point of its angle at Breckenridge. To retain, there. fore, all the convenience of different name for this portion of the Red River, and yet preserve its photographed unity, | would suggest the designation of Upper Red Rirer for the part of the stream above Brecken- ridge, and Lower Red River for the rest. The train had arrived and encamped on the opposite bank to spend the rest Of the Fourth-the boys were already smoking and sleeping out their siesta under the carts, when NJ. and j., feeling the pangs of hunger, entered the one unfinished log house which represented the architectural pride and pro- gress of the City of Dayton, alias Wassiota, and demanded something to eat. The log house, though not old, was venerable enough to embody the two eras of the citys growth the diminutive log shanty, at the rear end, which had satisfied the primary wants of shelter from the cold and rain, with just room enough within its mud-chinked walls for a bunk and a cooking-stove and the more pretentious modern addition, with its longer spaces, intended to fulfil the needs of domestic comfort and social decency, and which, when the chinks are plastered and the floor is laid, will make a stately dwelling for these parts.

The smile SO beaming, the cheek so bright, The eye so dancing with sunny light, I almost fancy my baby boy Is springing to me in his pride and joy; But tis only picture upon the wall- A silent picture-and that is all Only lock of silken hair Living alone in it's casket there! Where is the head that, in sportive glee, Was wont to toss it so careless and free? The baby head that upon my breast So lovingly nestled each night to rest? Only lock of it's silken hair 1fl Is lying alone in its casket there Only shoe that is soiled and torn! But where is the foot that that shoe has worn The darling foot, so dimpled and small, That made music merry in chamber and hall Oh, to catch of that little step one sound, How wildly now would my pulses bound! But there is only shoe thatis soiled and torn The foot comes no more that that shoe has worn Only these relics-and nothing more? Can naught to our arms the lost restore Must we hopeless yearn, as the years go by. For the bounding Step and the beaming eye? And of all that beauty, and life and grace, So fondly cherished, retain no trace Save these silent relics? Oh, nevermore Will the grave to our arms the lost restore Oh, woe for love, when from all its store It points to there tokens, and nothing more! When the vacant hall and silent stair But echo the groans of its wild despair , And from all the voices in the earth and sky Comes back no words to it's waiing cry, Save the mournful echo; "Oh, nevermore Will the grave to our arms the lost restore!' Oh, joy for love, when it yearns no more For that which the grave cannot restore! When it upward stretches it's dropping wings, And in darkness and sorrow still sweetly sings Of the brightness and bliss of that better home Where the lost are found and no partings come, Oh, joy for love, when it's priceless store There safe is garnered forevermore

TIE AURORA BORBALIs AND THE TELEGRAPH. During the auroral display of Thursday night in Boston, some curious phenomens were VII. messed in connection with the telegraph wires. The following conversation, says the Boston Traveller, between the Boston and Portland OPP erators on the American Telegraph line, will give an idea of the effect of the Aurora Borealis on the working of telegraph wires: Boston operator (to Portland operator.)- "Please cut off your battery from the line for fifteen minutes" Portland operstor.-Will do SO. 1t is now disconnected. Boston. mime is disconnected and we are working with the Auroral current. How do you receive my writiDgl" a.raF Portland.-"Better than with our batteries on. Current comes and goes gradually" Boston.-"My current is very strong at times, and we can work better without batteries, as the Aurora seems to neutralze and augment our batteries alternately, making current too strong at times for our relay magnets. Suppose We work without batteries while we are affected by this trouble" Portand.--"Very well. Shall go ahead with business 2" | Boston-"Yes. Go ahead" ! The wire was then worked for about two hours without the usual batteries, on the auro- raj current, working better than with the bate res connected. The current varied, increasing and decreasing alternately, but, by gradua- ting the adjustment to the current, a sufficient ciently steady effect was obtained to work the line very well. ~ This is the first instance on record of more than word or two having been transmitted with the auroral current. The usual effects Of the electric storm were also manifested, such as reversing the poles of the batteries, DC.
