The Remarkable Atmospheric Phe- nOncna, The New York Post, in describing the scenery of the heavens on the night of Sunday, the 2Sth ult., says: AT times it suggested mighty hand and an outstrctched arm, bound at the wrist with II bracelet of ruby and dia- monds, with the open palm held as if in bencdiction over the earth, while the fin gers of light reached almost to the dis tant horizon Soon, as Everett has beautifully spoken of somewhat similar scene, ''the hands of angels shifted the glorious scenery of the heavens" The mass of apparent red cloud to the east moved away southwark, gradually fading, while the corresponding red cloud on the west seemed to sink into chaos of dark cloud that, with fringe of blue, skirted the western horizon. While these chan ges were taking place in the cast and west, the wondrous crown above moved a few degrees and then gradually faded. Flashes of light covering many degrees slowly condensed into mighty luminous cloud, with its top near the zenith This cloud, gradually altering its shape, as sumed forms both singular and sugges- tive. AT one time it bore a striking resem- blance to an eagle, and then the slight est, almost imperceptible, change trans formed it into tortoise Then again it seemed to sweep across the heavens, pre- senting the appearance of confused procession of beings clad in ghostly shrouds, and reminding one of the dim heroes of Ossian For about half an hour these remarkable changes took place, and then the lights gradually disappeared. - In short time, however, they were re- sumed. Sheets of the same white lumi- nous cloud again illuminated the sky, producing about the same amount of light as the full moon, and the night became almost as the day. 1t must have been much like those de- scribed by DR.. Kane, Bayard Taylor, and other Northern travellers. OF tho extent of the phenomenon we have some idea from the fact that the telegraphic wires were affected by it in every direc- ton. All the operators on the eastern lines speak of this display of the aurora boreals as the most magnificent they ever witnessed. Certainly not since the APP pearance of the last comet have the hea- vcns declared the glory of God in sub liner manner, or the armament shown His handiwork in more gorgeous mani festations.

Thc Grand Aurorn norenlIs. The splendid Northern Lights on the night of the 2sth of August were seen and admired in both Hemispheres. In the South, as far as Cuba, the brilliancy was such as never before witnessed, and on the Pacific Coast the display was very remarkable. In the northern limits of Canada and the Lake Superior region, the exhibition, there common, was unusually grand; and there is no doubt the greater part of the North American continent was luminous with the flashing aurora The phenomena was seen in England on the morning of the Goth Of August, a time cores ponding with our midnight display of the 2sth The London Times correspondent speaks of the aurora borcalis as of great bnlliancy, "the in. tense glare of red, covering very large ex. TENT TO southwest, remaining fixed for twenty minutes, without that play of light generally to be observed, and in northeast direction rays of white light were playing in all directions, and at intervals black masses, their edges tinged with blood red, produced a sublime spectacle The aurora was also visible in Belgium, Holland, Germany, Russia, France, and Swift. zerland, but not so grandly in the South of Europe. Darkness has hed-with joyous tread Comes in the harvest day, And all things fair its joys to share Are making round our way, The king Of light 10 garment bright, Robes grove, aud stream, and plain, AS with glad song we haste along To cut the golden grain, A cheerful band of harvesters To cut the golden grain. The Saturday evening succeeding his solemn burial, we visited your beautiful little city. The storm howled most piteously the tyrants of the tempest were celebrating their orgies of the wind and rain; the elements seemed to be mock ing each other; not one vestige of the wonted cheerfulhess fingered around the spot endeared to me by thousand recollectons. Next morn ing, however, found the last nights wrath had died away, and the elements were at peace with each other. The Great King had sent abroad his emissaries of love, and when the next day came the golden sunlight trembled in the heavens, as the emblem of his smile. We repaired to the cemetery-the "city of the dead, upon one of your beautiful hills the shadows dwelt at its feet; while gazing up wards, its summit seemed decked with a crest of ! sunbeam feathers The ascent was arduous. Arriving at the sacred enclosure we paused, before entering its limits to refresh ourself upon a well-worn stile, and wonderingly contemplated the magnificent picture that nature had spread before me. The rolling torrents of the blue Delaware, just beyond the base of the old hill whereon we stood, reflected back the golden sunlight of the morning, and as they danced onward in their march to old Ocean, sang their morning anthems of praise to the Infinite One The mountains of sister State, pierced the danthS of tho aznrn doma ahoua than. uUb;Io the floating cloud banners of the morning, were flung athwart the radiant drapery of the Skies Peaceful homes and garlanded forests, crowned the lofty hills in the far off distance The gilt tering hosts of heaven had just retired before the coming of the morning light and the early star was not yet quite departed, but seemed re- splendent with the diamond dew drops OF the night, as it sank away from our view There was nothing in the rolling waves there was nothing in the grand old hills in the distance ; there was not emblem in the feecy purple banners o'erhead; there was nothing in the voice Of the genial winds that whispered of death. We saw nothing but life pulsating in everything But we turned from our Temporal ! ry resting place, and soemnly and silently di- rectly our footsteps to new made grave. We were there Can this be the grave of him whom we loved as brother ''Can it be-" we MUIR INJURED, that bosom friend lies beneath this dull, inanimate sod 2" Could it be that he OF the sprghtly step, of the cheerful voice, Of < the warm soul, the light of household, the bright star of affection to one in the future, has left it all Could it be that CHARLEY Gown 4 was dead That " He sleeps his last sleep 2" He was indeed, dead The last moments ever spent in his company, were in listening to re- : cital of his bright hopes of the future, and we grasped the hand then warmer and responded to his parting salutatons. What change The light had faded from his eyes the win :, dows of his soul were closed, and the golden CLEAN of the sunlight had been shut from the > chambers of his heart. The pulse was still; the blood had forgotten its well-worn ways in a thousand veins; the curling hair had forgotten its simple arts of cluster, and the lips were rigid y We pronounced his name, but no thrilling re- spouse arose from that sepulchre Then, in deed he was dead. We bid farewell to his tomb; we were not ashamed to do the homage of an earnest tear as we turned from his grave, and leaving the : cemetery, emerged amongst the living Peace to his ashes We shall ever preserve his memory, so long as ! we shall shall be privileged to enjoy our own "lease of life,' as fragrant as the breath of ro- ses and as sweetly as the melody of music throbbng its thrilling strains in the midnight air. We sympathise with those who were bound to him by thousand ties by the bonds OF consanguinity and kindred; with her to whom he was the sun of existence, with those OF his associates who shall listen in vain with ling ering ears, to catch the sound of his well known t footballs. May he sleep in peace, until the last great 9 clarion shall burst the bands of his grave and his spirit spring forth refreshed by its sumber, , never more to die and suffer; and his happiness 2 be as bright and brilliant as the starry lights o'erhead, that continually press forward with } their barriers of fire, in their endless marches , around the throne of the Great Eternal. We drop the curtain, conscious that no one will miss him more than I, his former respecter, associate and bosom friend. Gloucester Co., Sept. 26, 1859. The horse in the mid die is trained to run at trot, and the other two ION its right and lefty nevor, quit the gal lop The former trots with his head low, and is called the Snow-eater the other two prance with their heads loose, and are named the Furies. The whole equipment, thus directed in its course, presents the appearance of fan. A driver who can be we'll relied on conducts the troika To the back of the carriage young hog is at tached by cord, or, for more security, by a chain, between three and four feet in length. 1t is quietly taken in the vehicle to the entrance of the forest where the chase Is to proceed there it is put on the ground, and the driver incites the horses, which start off at a trot and gallop respectively, as we have mentioned; while the hog, little used to such an amusement, raises cry which soon degenerates into what may be called lamentation At this noise the nearest wolf shows it's nose, and sets itself to pursue the hog, soon followed by two, then by three, and ultimately, it may be, by fifty of its brethren They all make claim for the poor hog, and fight among themselves to get at it {; some of them stretching out to it a blow of their claws, and others endeavoring to bite it. From The Nc~ York Century, A"g"st 27.l The Wonderful power that Blond;n possess es of balancing himself, is the point Of curios- ity and amazement to the crowd. By cX planning little of the philosophy of this feat, we NAV lessen the establishment otsome pee ple, and perhaps remove the chief difficulty to u rational amount of selfculture, resulting in on improvement OF the nervous system. The common toy of man spinning on the point of a WIRE explains the whole matter The centre of gravity is lowered to the base and there it is easily preserved. The use Of the polc answers the same purpose. Blond ms pole is thirty-four feet long, and weighs forty six pounds. Held below the middle Of the body, it brings his centre of gravity suff- GENTLY near to the rope to be easily controll- ed. \ very slight elevation of one end and a corresponding depression of the other res torres the balance ofthe body. The skill to govern the position, by an exact movement of the pole to the required extent, and not an inch further, results from practice. Those who have seen " the infant phenomenon" Of tue Ravel troupe on the tight-ropc, must have observed the imperfect management OF the pole in less experienced hands. Philosophi- cally, Blondin and his pole constitute one body, andthe extension literally Gifts weight, is equivalent to lowering the centre of gray ity, or charging the base on which he walks. The most perilous exploit of NJ. Blondln is that of carrying man on his back: Here ne runs a frighttul risk, because he cannot command the nervous system Of another per- son. 10 this experiment he will fall avictim, if he persists in it, The slightest trcpidation of nerve in the carried body will imperil his centre of gravity and put it out of his COM mand in spite of the skill with which he adjusts the weight rest as much as possible on his hips, and rs little as possible on his shoulders. Travellers over mountains are warned by their guides to sit passively on the mule, without attempting to direct the ami NAL. This is what Il man must do who rides on Blondin' back, his own command OF nerve must be equal to that of his master, or he cndangers both. The fact of dismounting several times proves that it was so, and that he did not avail himself of any trick in shut ting his eyes from the abyss below. This is the whole explanation of NJ. Blond ms feat-his lowering of the centre OF grav- ity near to the base, and his amazingly skill full government oft We would not advise any one to try hazardous experiments; but the truth of this explanation may be tested by walking on the edge of a board firmly fixed in the required position on the ground or floor and by using or dispensing with the balancing pole, or other weight, to control the centre Of gravity.

The songs grew louder and the mirth more uproarious, until the most sober and circumspect of both officers and crew would gladly have ended the festivities; but Bill was now frenzied with liquor, and one of his drunken freaks was to compel every one else to drink, particularly those who tried to avoid it, and as we feared to arouse his anger by refusal, the result was that we were all, even to poor little Harry, soon in state either of helpless intoxication, or of drunken frenzy, What extravagances we committed while in this state cannot remember, but l fell into drunken stupor quite early in the evening, from which awoke some time after with raging thirst. / found the crew all lying about, drunk and helpless. The wind had greatly abated and all was quiet. "Having tried in vain to arouse some of the men, went down into the cabin and there found poor Bill lying on the floor breath ing stentorously and hard, his flushed face and relaxed limbs showing the futility of any attempt to ronse him. Ham and little Harry lay on deck close to the companionway ; the boy had, even in his intoxication, with the instinct of affection, nestled his head upon his brothers broad bosom, and his fair skin and bright golden hair contrasted strongly in the clear moonshine with Hams bronzed and rugged features, muscular throat and shaggy beard. Grieved and sick at heart at this sad picture of our drunken folly, and anxious about its consequences, l went forward and stretched myself on the bulwarks of the fore CASTLE leaning against the cat-head, and while looking over the moonlit waters, and the is lands, with their crests of dark waving trees, and fringe of white, sandy beach, and listen ing to the murmuring of the surf and the breathings of the dying norther through the rigging, fell into that state of dreamy tor por which every one sometimes experiences, and in which, although asleep to all intents and purposes, we are still in a great measure conscious of what is passing around us. In this state, our real impressions partake so much of the nature of our dreams, and in deed become SO much mingled with them, that often we are unable on waking to dis tinguish between them. l soon got into a long, rambling kind of dream, in which a small boat with two men in her, hailing us repeatedly, and then sculling quietly along. side, was the most tangible impression Next, Mobile-prizes-httle Harry-Missis- sppi - northers- drunken sprees brandy casks-immense boxes of specie--battle- blood, and long and earnest whispered con- versations with the two mysterious visitors, word of which did not understand, al though a confidential participant and adviser, were inextricably mingled In torturing con- fusion, while, to add to the chaos, an indie Unable sense Of some -horrid danger, some frightful catastrophe impending, peryaded all, and like a hideous nightmare, weighed down and paralyzed my system like noun tain of lead. Bill Wainwright's mother, her gray hair dishevelled, and muftled in a shroud, rushed shrieking from the cabin and commenced madly ringing our bell, the clang ing of which echoed through my brain like peals of thunder, and the huge volcanic cone Of Orizaba seemed suspended in mid air, di- rectly overhead, sending forth eruptions Of flame and smoke, and gradually descending like vast extinguisher upon U.S.. Through all this turmoil could still hear the mur- muring of the strange mems voices, and had an idea that somehow they were con- nectedr with it. When, however, would have demonstrated with them, as thought, they retired as mysteriously as they came, and could hear their oars, as they pulled softly away from the vessel. Then, all was for time blank and silent, and Twas con- scious of nothing but that vague foreshadow- ing Of danger, which grew more and more oppressive, and at length perfectly agonizing.

An EXTRAORDINARY PHgsoxENos, OF the celestial kind presented itself to this city and the surround ing country on Sunday evening, at about half past eight o'clock. The northern part OF the frmoment, from north. east to northwest, and from the horizon nearly to the zenith, became overspread with elearred light, through which the stars twinkled as merRy as from their accustomed blue. At intervals diverging rays Of white and yeow-ght stole softly across the red, and as softly retired The spectacle lasted shout half an hour, and was witnessed and admired and won dered at by thousands Of the population 1t had the appearance n all respects, Of an aurora boreals, the accustomed hsrbinger OF cold weather 80 frequently seen towards winter in the more north ern latitudes and we are satisfied that it was one But the sight Of such phenomenon as far south as New Orleans, and in the scorchng month Of August, TOO, was something well calculated to shake the public faith in its identity and to start all possible suggestions which might connect it with some neigh. boring terrestrial cause. Such suggestions. however. were at fault No steamboat burning on the lake, no blazing praries, no possible terrestrial blsses could | have produced any such an Opaque, widespread, claretcolored light with its glowing rays Of white and yellow. With many it was made matter Of joke and with the ignorant and superstitious it ated no little alarm. As for US, though we were not much frightened, we felt somewhat like the Tennessee farmer, who was nearly frightened to death by the great meteorc shower of twenty.six or twentyseven years ago. He ran out of his house, the grand celestial display of fireworks, and fell faintng over fence. Revying after little, he raised his head and saw neighbor standing and very cooly surveying the sight, with his pipe in bis mouth. For Gods sake, John,r he gasped, "tel me what this is-the world amt com. ing to an end is it?" John laughed and said, "No. don't feel as it the world was coming to an end Then what is this! what does all this mean ~ "Its phenomenon" responded John, putting away at his pipe. "Oh! funnomener!" exclaimed the fright ened man, coming to his breath again.; as long as the darnd things got name spose its all right ~ with which he went back satisfied to his bed. So | with US. Knowing the thing to be phenomenon, OF something with name, we afterward slept as well as ever. Seriously, we certain, from our own observation that the phenomena of Sunday night was an aurora boreals though the old folks say, forcibIy enough such thing was never seen in this latitude. A SOUTHERN AuRoRAL DIspLAY.-The Nj A SOUTHERN AuR0RAL DISPLAY,-The Mo- bile Advertiser has the following: On Sunday night we witnessed from Point Clear some electrical feats q little eXtraordi- nary for this latitude. A little after dark the attention of every one was directed to dull red light, which resembled that reflected from O burning building upon a cloud Of no great density. Gradually this light increased in intensity, and the cloud dropped down nearly to the horizon and assumed a hue Of the black est shade. Now, apparently from behind this cloud, commenced one of the most imposing spectacles it has ever been our good fortune to witness. Streams of light shot up all along the cloud from tho northeast to the northwest points, being the most brilliant on line due north. These streams were exactly analogous to the Aurora Of the North. 1T one moment they appeared exceedingly bright and we'll defined. The next instant would change the entire scene. A constant reformation of per- petually fading corruscations was kept up for half an hour, when change took place in tho | performances. As the streams gradually faded away, the cloud, which had before remained , perfectly dark, began to be illuminated with the ordinary forms of electrical flashes, which continued until we withdraw from the eau diencs." We wish we could have rung q huge bell at the time, that all might have seen tAf phenomenon which may not occur again In this latitude for century.

CAUSE OF THE AURORA BoRRALIs.-M. de Ia Rive, the celebrated French astronomer, explains the production Of the Aurora Boreas in the follow ing manner When the sun, having passed into the southern hemisphere, no longer heats our hemis- phere, the aqueous vapors which have accumulated during the summer in this part Of the atmosphere begin to condense, the kind ofhumid cap enyelopng the polar regions extends more and more, and facilitates the passage Of electricity accumulated in the upper portion of the air. But in these elevated regions, and especially at this season Of the year, the aqueous vapors must most fire. quently pass into the state Of minute particles Of ice or snow floating in the air, similar to those which give rise to the halos; they form, as IL were, kind Of transparent mist. These half-frozen fogs con- duct the electricity TO the surface Of the earth, the pole, and are at the same time illuminated by these currents or electric discharges. In fact, all observers agree in asserting that the aurora boreais is constantly preceded by mist, which rises from the POLE and the margins Of which, less dense than the remainder, are coored the first and indeed it is very frequent near the pole in the winter months, and especially in those where there is abundance OF vapor in the air.

"a Life for a Lifr,,--A sad STORY. M Graham, in New Orleans, has been given. lie is well remembered, as the person who Killed Mr. Loring at the st. Nicholas Hotel, in New York, and was sentenced to the State prison, but afterwards pardoned out on &C. count OF Ill health. A New Orleans corres- pondent OF the Charleston Courier, writing Of Inc event, gives a touching picture OF life MADE miserable, and at last destroyed, by the blight OF intoxication. He says; His reappearance in his old haunts here cre- aleu singular sensation. I never shall for get the hrst time met him. after his return iToh ms Nsrthern prison. He stood in front OF urng sOIe, that for many years was at the corner of St Charles and Common streets. and In which he had an interest 1t was a gathering place for many street lounaers and poiitlcians lie had been seen there year after year. When ne went TO New York, and while III prison, his portly form was much ruisseti;it was not known that he was going TO come back, and was fairly startled, r. hen. on turn. ing the corner one morning, saw him In his ola place, In MS usual easy attitude looking Just the same, cigar in mouth and small cane in hand-only a deathly pallor had replaced the usual healthy color of his face. The New ork scene of blood flashed over me: I ayerted my head, passed on. The same impression was no doubt pro. dueed vn the community generally, and for a long time this pallid faced man wa. as stran. ger in the community where he had lived SO him cordial grasp of the hand. He seemed prepared for this, had no doubt made up his mind to it, and perhaps had Il secret, defying pleasure in staying in his old haunts, and at tending, with silent pride, to the duties of his profession. Gradually a change of feeling came over the mass OF our citizens in regard to the man; we are warm hearted. sympathetic people if we are hot-headed; and the reserved nnobtru- sive course pursued by DR. Graham, his atten- non 10 MS profession, his avoidance OF his for iner weakness, after awhile induced many to forget what had passed, and the Doctor re- gained much of his old social acouain tance ana q large share of professional patronage. But the morbid craving for stimulus though once quehched In blood, could not be cured IL came back after awhile and it became known that DIR. Graham had occasional re- lapses into his old habit of intoxication. Still ne eontrlyed not 10 let this be seen about the streets and through the influence of his fami- fy ana friends, he was year ago eiee ted, by the American party, city physician. A short time ago, he lost the Office, at the ex- plratlon of the term, by the election of q DIR. Hart; and for fortnight, it appears, had been under the impression that Mr. Ernest TOleda- no. young man, prominent in the American party, had procured his defeat. 1t was known that he had expressed himself openly, for some days past in violent terms against Toledano, eursing him and avowing his purpose to shoot him at sight. These expressions and this re- solve were uttered whilst DIR. Graham was under the influence of liquor, which, il ap- pears, he had been since Thursday last; so much so as to be generally noticed. Last night, the Chief of Police Mr.. Adams who is related to Graham in some way, saw him at the Ruby Coffee house on Common street-a popular resort-and noticed that he was in liquor. He felt presentiment some thing was going to happen, should Graham remain in that condition in SD public place !; he went up to him and told him he must go home; if he created any disturbance he would arrest him and lock him up for the night. Graham insisted that bp w toXcated, but promised to go home soon. Mr. Adams left him to meet some police officers at his own private office. and a few moments af- ter was called ont and told that DIR. Graham had just been shot dead. The BODY OF the dead man was taken into the coffee e-house, the doors of which were closed, and physician was on the spot speed ily but his skill was of no avail The Chief OF Police then had his body taken to his pri- vate office, and there, stretched out on u table, / saw the unfortunate man. his large, hand some form stillened; his pantaloons and boots covered with mud; his coat, vest, and cravat of; his shirt stained with mud and 4 little blood; his arms crossed; his hands and wrists blackened, tied with his crayat; his shirt bo- som partly open; and his fine features white and fixed forever There was no expression of pain about the countenance; it was calm and serene. A physician Standing by showed me the wounds, three small black spots below the right breast, so close together that the hand could cover them, and one in the left arm. The last had seen of the man he stood at my elbow, chatting pleasantly, looking hand some, dlgnlfied and courteous, as usual; now he lay blood-stained. mud and rain-soiled corpse. DIR. Graham was unfortunate in being over come now and then with a craving a morbid longing for liquor; and when under the in1iu- = ence OF this stimulus he, otherwise calm, quiet courteous, thorough gentleman indenean- or and appearance, became obstinate, hothead- ed, quarrelsome, dangerous. His superior edu. cation and skill as physician, fine telligence pleasant manner, handsome dignified person and highly respectable and inf uentIal connec. tions here, made him very popular; and his grieyous weakness was borne with for his many good qualities, and the esteem had fol his family. Zens of New Orleans, including men of all positions professions and occupations in the community, of which for so many years the deceased had been member. The "Great Bore has reached depth of 2,O25 feet, and is progressing at the rate of fourfeet in TWEEN ty-four hours. The Ohio State Journal, Aug. 9Th J gives an account of some interesting exper- iments made in the well. It says: On Saturday, Professor I. G. Wormly made several experiments; the pressure per square inch, at the bottom, is 861 pounds, or $4,000 per square yard First Experiment.-Three bottles, two of them Theoretically sealed, were placed in the pump and sunk to the bottom of the bore. When withdrawn they were crushed to powder. The other, which was closed with a stsong cork, had it forced in and the bot. tie pulverized. end Experiment.-Two very strong cut glass bottles were used, one of them was crushed, the other, a very small and thick one, was forced half full of water-but not broken, and the cork remaining firmly fixed in the neck. The water forced into the bot tie at the great depth of 2,095 feet, or over & of mile, was as pure and limpid as the purest spring. Curious stones are brought, in limited quantities, from the the bottom, which, when polished, show minute stars, new moons, half moons, full moons, and suns, most regularly and clearly defined.

The Aurora Borealis and the Telegraph The Aurora Borcalis and the Telegraph During the late auroral display in Bos- ton, some curious phenomena were wit. messed in connection with the telegraph wires. The following conversation, says the Boston Traveller, between the Boston and Portland operators, on the American Telegraph, line will give an idea of the effect of the Aurora Borealis on the working of Telegraph wires: Boston OPERATOR" Please cut of your battery entirely from the line for if teen minutes" Portland OPERATOR" Will do so. II is now disconnected. Boston -" Mine is disconnected, and we are working with the Auroral cur rent. How do you receive my writ ing?" Portland -" Better than with our bat. teries on. Current comes and goes grad ually." Boston" My current is very strong at times, and We can work better without batteries, as the Aurora seems to neutral ize and augment our batteries alternate ly, making current too strong at times for our relay magnet. Suppose we work without batteries while we are affected by this trouble ?'' Portland" Very well. Shall 60 ahead with business ?" Boston," Yes. Go ahead" The wire was then worked for about two hours, without the usual batteries, on the auroral current, working better than with the batteries connected. The current varied, increasing alternately. but by graduating the adjustment to the current, a sufficiently steady effect was obtained to work the line very well. This is the first instance on record of more than word or two having been transmitted with the Auroral current The usual effects of the electric storm was also manifested, such as reversing the poles of the batteries, &c. We are informed also, that on the short line between the Cambridge Observatory and the store of Messrs. VIM Bond and Son, in Congress Street, which runs near ly East and West, the waves of electric ity displayed considerable regularity, be- ing from half minute to a minute in duration.-N. Y. Com.

Six years ago, young man, just entering life, under the influence OF rum committed crime against society, was tried In this city, convicted and sent to Wsupun, where he served out bis time behind the prison bars. Before his trial, a fair young girl had promised to link fortunes with him, aud cruel was the blow to her. But she loved him. All through the six long years did she wait and wait for the day Of his release. With true woman's heart, she believed him innoeent--innocent at least be- fore God-and, like the magnet, che held on her steady way her heart pointed ever to the future Long we're the years to him. Slowly passed the honrs-hours days-days weeks. weeks months-months years-and the years were like ages. Every tolling OF the prison bell struck deep 10 bis heart. and every sunset took another thread from his skein Nor were the hours less weary to her,. Hope. that bless ed angel, sat beside her by day, and reposed on her pillow by night. Some there were who laughed at her holy love-who sneered so meanly at her lover-a prisoner, miles away. Others might sneer-she remained true to her heart and to him. Others might laugl-she wept Others might point to man in prison Rarb toiling away from morn till night, with but one star to guide him on she saw but the honest soul that might be saved-or lost-and woman that she was nerved herself TO bear the gibes aud eers. Blessed words came to him in DIS lonely ceIl--WOTu5 Vi lONe, VI uOpSf vi ness; stronger grew the heart of him who had truly his better angel watching over his I'M broken future. Each word from her lightened the hours as they slowly went by, and larger grew the day on which liberty was TO come | Men visited him, and with careless word or speaking eye threw into bis cell maddening | thought on which bis soul must feed and trem- blingly shrink to the darkest corner of its liv- ing temple. Then letter from her would dash aside the Ozark curtain, and beacon him to spot of sunshine outside, and beyond his pres ent reach So passed the years. Friends died, and he wept over them. The Gin was long since atoned for, and at last the little spot of sunshine crept into his cell, and entering by the key-hole of the door, led him forth into the bright rays of liberty. He was conducted to to the Office of the prison by McGraw. and a citizens dress in place OF prison suit given to him, and led into an ipner room, where stood she who, years before, had promised before God to be bis. What a meeting! 'Tis not for US to speak of it. On the evening train the two arrived in this city, and were by one Of our di' vines Joined in marriage. We were a witness of the ceremony, and shall never forget it; nev- er forget the eye moistened with tears of hap piness nor the throbbing of hearts that had so long waited and trusted. Saved! Saved ! May the future be all the brighter for the dark cloud that has long hung over it, and true friends be ever ready to lend helping hand | MiL,Cdukie NetgS.

TIE MOCK PRINCESS. Il True Tale of Mobile, one century has gone by, and nearly half of another has followed upon its track, since the now rich and populaus city of Mobile was aroused to eager and intense curiosity by the advent of an ilustrious stranger, whose story created universal sympathy. This stranger represented herself as no less parsonage than the daughter of the Duke OF Wotenbutted and wife of Czaro- WITT Alexis Peter, son of Peter the Great ! OF Russia; and the reason given for claim | ing the protection and attention of the American citizens, was the i'll treatment of her illustrious husband from whom she had fled, at the risk Of unheard of calami. ties, and with innumerable har-breadth escapes. Such tale Of foreign tyranny, exemri- he'd on the very hearthstone Of a Russian home, and in the midst of imperial dignity was one of wonder and astonishment. Every honor and attention that could be bestowed upon the distinguished and un- fortunate lady, were freely given-not on y to her rank, but to her beauty, elegance and attractive manners. 1t was evident that however hastily her flight might have been at last accomplish ed, she had had sufficient time to make abundant plans for her escape before she attempted it. The richness and splendor of her dress, the immense value of her jewels, and the style with which she soon established herself in one of the finest man slons IN Mobile, were evidences that how ever terribly her illustrious spouse might have treated her personally, he had not touched her in that tenderest point with some women, viz, that of deprlying them OF the means Of adornment. If any doubts of the lady's story some. times arose in the minds of the cynical and prejudiced, they were speedily combated by the superior force of the believers The prevailing feeling in regard to her was that she was much abused wife, to whom all gallant and chivalric souls should and would extend the largest sympathy. The doubters were therefore obliged to be more | Gniet-muttering little, however, at the facility which rich people possessed of spreading " g amour' over the eyes of the multitude. Among the most ardent sympathizers of the cruelty treated princess, was the Chew alier d Aubant, a young Frenchman, who had travelled, and who distinctly remem- bered having seen the lady at the court of St. Petersburgh. Not that he recollected her as in connection with the czarowitz, in particular; but her face had left an impress sion on his mind, which always came up wildly when recalling any remembrance of the imperial family. 10 him, the wrongs and i'll treatment of the son of Peter the Great, towards his in nocent and beautiful wife, were as real as any incident in his own life; and with the generous faith and high toned sympathy of unsophsticated youth, before the world has left It's blighting brand of suspicion and unbelief on the page Of life, he deyot ed himself, like true cavalier to the SER vice ofthe unhappy victim Of Russian tyr. army. Not indeed that the lady showed any signs of a broken heart In D'Aubant's views of the case, she was one who kept all her sorrows within her own bosom, never allowing any trace of them to appear in her countenance, which was as blooming as if no breadth of wrong or injury had ever paled the rich glow. She entered freely into every plan of amusement, en- Joyed the freest exercise, the largest liber- ty of outdoor sports, and carried them all off with winning sweetness of manner, and an innocent gaiety of spirits, that were perfectly bewitching. Two or three years of residence in Mo- bile had rivetted the affection and rever- ence Of the citizens to their adopted daugh- ter, as they loved to term the distinguish ed lady. Nothing could draw the young ChevaIler d Aubant from bis allegiance to one so lovely and charming; and. one day when all circumstances of time and place were favorable, and the lady's confidence in him had been expressed in most un- equivocar terms, he made her an offer of his hand and heart and the somewhat en- numbered estates of which he WAS heir, and was accepted with undisguised satisfac- ton. "A most proper union was echoed from one corner of Mobile to another--the appreciation rising far above the significant "humphs." of the cynics, who always de- preciate everything to their own level. Madame was certainly free to marry. Her treatment and escape from tyrant was surely a sufficient ground for a divorce, and the absence of any stringent law in the State, afforded abundant privilege for a step of the nature 1nelita'ed by the lovers. a wedding, the magnificence Of which had never been equalled in America, and to which SO many were invited threw ad ditional glamour" over them all; and the pair left Mobile for Paris, followed by the regrets Of almost the entire community. At the French court, they resided in great style. No one knew or cared fOl the antecedents of the charming princess whose bewitching manners and rare per sonal beauty were indisputabe recommen dations in that atmosphere. 1twas enough that she was recognizable as the ton; anc for the rest-why, "glamour" was no needle at the French court. MY PSALM. NJ JonS 0. wnrrum. mourn no more my vanished years; Beneath a tender rain, An April rain Of smiles and tears, My heart is young again. The west winds blow, and singing low, hear the glad streams run; The windows Of my soul throw Wide open to the sun. No longer forward nor behind look in hope or fear; But, grateful, take the good And, The best of now and here. plough no more desert land, To harvest weed and tare; The mamma dropping from Gods hand Rebukes my painful care. break my pilgrim staff, lay Aside the toiling oar; The angel sought so far away welcome at my door. The airs Of spring may never play Among the ripening corn, Nor freshness of the flowers Of Nay Blow through the Autumn norm Yet shall the blue eyed gentian look Through fringed lids to heaven, And the pale aster in the brook Shall see its image given;- The woods shall wear their robes of praise, The south winds softly sigh, And sweet, calm days in golden haze Melt down the amber sky. Not less shall manly deed and word Rebuke an age Of wrong; The craven flowers that wreathe the sword Make not the blade less strong But shifting hands shall learn to heal To build as to destroy; Nor less my heart for others feel That the more enjoy. All as God wills, who wisely heeds To give or to withhold, And knoweth more of all my needs Than all my prayers have told Enough that blessings undeserved Have marked my erriDg track That, wheresoe'er my feet have swerved, His Christening turned me back That more and more a Providence OF love is understood, Making the springs of time and sense Sweet with eternal good That death seems but covered way Which opens into light Wherein no blinded child can stray Beyond the Fathers sight That care and trial seem at last, Through memory's sunset air, Like mountain-ranges overpast, In purple distancs fair That all the jarring notes of life Seem blending in psalm, And all the angels of its strife Slow rounding into calm. And SO the shadows fall apart, And so the west winds play And all the windows of my heart open to the day

The line was in most per, feet order, and well skilled operators worked necessarily from eight o'clock last evening until ten o'clock this morning, to get over IN an ineligible form about four hundred words of the report per steamer Indian, for the press, and at the latter hour, so completely were the wires under the influence Of the Aurora Borealis, TINT it was found utterly i'm possible to communicate between the tele. graph stations, and the line had to be closed. - The same difficulty prevailed as tar south as Washington.

Gu Wed es- day evening Blondin walked across the Mag ara river, from the American to the Canada shore, most of the way in darkness, two lights which he fastened to the ends of his pole, going out before he was half way across On his return he was surrounded with fire works, consisting of Roman candles, which gave pleasing appearance. He was literal- ly enveloped in blaze. When about mid way he laid down his pole, and stood up erect Inverted. Then he suspended himself below the rope by the heels, and there he remained drumming on his chest until his campfres were all extinguished There he was left, as before, in utter darkness. The same day, De Lave walked his rope across the Genessee Falls at Rochester, He had strapped on his back chair and salvcr, upon which were lot of small cakes which were to serve as his lunch. He immediately LOOK up his pole ant, started out When ahout the middle of the chasm he stepped and sat down. Taking the chair from his pack, he adjusted it on the rope, seated hin,- SCH Tn 1t, and composedly ate up the cakes rom the salver, which lay in his lap during .he operation. After delay of ten minutes ne started out again, till he got over the brink or the Falls, and then he carried out his pro- mise to lower himself down to the sheet of wa. ter and dpa draught from the flood. He ii. ea hIs balance pole to the rope, slided down and took drink and then returned to the ron. above with great ease

From about half past eight o'clock until after eleven, the northern heavens were iilumin- ated by an extraordinary display of the phe- nomenon known by the name of the Aurora Borealis, or Northern Lights. The first in dication Of it was light like that which precedes the moons rising or the dawh of day, palid rays or beams occasionally shoot ing from the horison towards the zenith with the rapidity of lightning g-fashes, and mountain ridges were palpably visible, as though moonlight were streaming over them, and banks of white vapor just rising from canon and gorge were distinct and slvery Gradually the sky flushed up with faint crimson hue, perceptible only to the right or left or just above the point where the lu- nar-like illumination was first observed and still continued to beam. Through this deli cately tinted mist rays of white light shot up at intervals and instantly subsidized Now the eastern horizon would blush and now the western. Finally there was a complete arch of crimson stretching nearly from east to west and extending about halfway to the zenith. The stars bedmed through it ruddy as Mars. 1t seemed like the reflection of burning praries. Streamers flushed through it, piercing it's circumference-now broad and fan-shaped, now narrow and spear-like, and like the slant rays OF sunshine in a dark wood, only quite paiiid. At this instant the scene was gloriops, yet somewhat awful, hushing all expression of delighted wonder An aerohte darsed across the arch, and the beholder was reminded of that line in Ham, let which speaks of " stars, aith trains of fire and deus Of blood" 1t is not strange that the ancients regarded displays of polar light as ominous of i'll. Little aid was needed from the Imagination to make an ignorant and su- perstitious people believe that in each mex plicable phenomenon they witnessed the evo- lutions and flashing swords of opposing squadrons mixed in sanguinary fray. 1t is one of the benefeent results of scientific re- search that cur modern wonder at sight of such phenomena is untouched with fear. While we gaze with most exalted imagina- tion and feelings Of delight, we also specu- late as to causes, inteligently, if not cor recuy. We see in the Aurora Borealis no prophecy of Ill to man, but simply beautiful manifestations of electro magnetism, re- sultng from peculiar condition of the at mosphere. In this view we are confirmed by the violent agitation of the magnetic nee die under the influence Of the polar light. AS it flies from point to point, obedient to the unseen power that compels its fealty, the mind is confounded by the vain attempt to fathom an effect as mysterious as life itself. But the broad crimson arch is fading, like the hues from sunset clouds. Now it melts in the center, yet family fingers still. Again it deepens, and the silver clouds lying on the breast of the mountains seem to reflect its color. 1t melts again--breaks-is scarcely perceptible to strainipg eyes-is gone entire ly. There beams the dawn, however, and there it beamed for hours, arrowy fashings going up from its focus as though God walked the earth and the glory of his brow filed the heavens. Thus briefly and ilnperfectly we have de- scribed a rare spectacle, projected by the Great Artist on the canvas of the northern sky. The few who saw it with us can never forget its resplendent beauty. In their mem- ories that crimson arch will stand forever. They viewed it frona the edge Of mountain, looking through tall pine across deep misty canons to long line Of mountains piled against the strangely illuminated frmament; /; and they turned their backs upon it at last as upon friend whom they might see no more.

Rrive, the celebrated FRENCH astrono. mer, explains the production of the Aurora Borealis in the following manner :-"When tho sun having passed into the Southern hemisphere, noonges heats our atmosphere, the aqueous va pors which have accumulated during the summer in this part of the atmosphere being to condense, the kind of humid cap enveleping the polar re-. gions extend more and more, and facilitates the passage of electricity accumulated in the upper portion of the air. But in this elevated region, and especially at this portion of the year, the aqueous vapors must most frequently pass into the state of minute particles of ice or snow float ing in the air, similar to those which give rise to the halos they form, as it were, kind of semi transparent mist. These half-frozen fogs con. duct the electricity to the surface of the earth near the pole, and are at the same time, illumi- match by these currents of electric discharge. In fact all observers agree in asserting that the Aurora Borealis is constan ty preceded by mist which rises from the pole, and the margin of which, less dense than the re mander, is colored the first and indeed, it is very frequent near the pole in the winter months, and especially in those where there is au abundance of vapor in the air.

All parties desire your approving smile, and therefore all are encouraged by your presence. I know that in the direct administration of po- litical affairs you have no share but yet, reisning as you do, supreme in The realm OF love, your influence often controls the desti. ny Of nations. Woman's love is the great lever which rouses man 10 action. The gen. era, as he plans the stra,egeiic combina- tions which are 10 insure victory, looks for ward to recompense dearer than The lau /. rels upon his brow; the soldier as he frud- ges along on the weary march, or mingles in the scenes of the battlefield, even with death around him, forgets awhile the carnage, and turns his thoughts 10 the fond girl he left behind him the mariner, tempest tossed, driven by the rude waves, sings merrIly aloit as he thinks of the little cottage by tho shore, where his wife and dear ones await him; the statesman, as he deviscs amid deep and painful thought, plans Of govern ment, which are 10 tell upon his own and his country's fame, never loses sight of the ! boys which await him when cabinet councils are over, and he nters the portals of home; the sentinel, as he PAGES his weary watch, loves the moonlight tramp, that he may look beneath its rays at the dear momento Of o mothers or a sisters love. The early impressions which the child receives from you outlive all the wisdom of latter days Sages may reason, and philosoph. ers may teach, but the voice, which we heard, in infancy will ever come to our ears, b caring mothers words and mo- theirs counsel. Continue 10 instil iEto your children virtue and patriotism. lmbue them with proper veneraion for the fathers of liberty. New York Letter, rAoAAA oui nCSuid 1NcW toTh correspondent. NEW YORK, Sept. 9, 1859. The soft skies of Italy offer no tempta- ton to one who can luxuriate in such eli mate as that of New York city at this sea- son of the year. Nights, glorious with moonlight, and days just warm enough to be cheerful, make UP the bill of fare which Nature offers, to draw back our wandering citizens to their own home. The summer has been one of health and prosperity. Hardly single case of epidemic disease has occurred among the proper inhabitants of the city; an almost unparalleled state of affairs of late years; of course, the milder epidemics have not been extinct, but the great unsubdued angels of death, cholera and yellow fever, have let us alone. Fortu- nately, too, for the quarantine troubles, there has been little occasion for quarantine. 1t is difficult to find any place so far out of the world that it will be induced by love or money to admit the State elephant within its precincts. Business is very active with the west and middle States. The dry goods jobbing streets are obstructed with boxes Of goods to that extent that corpulent traveller finds progress impossible except in the mid die of the horse path. Murray, Warren, and Chambers streets are very busy. Here all is drive and hustle, and a lady is rare sight, except an occasional wife or friend in pursuit of dresses "at wholesale prices" Time was, when fashionable promenades abounded in those regions. No city in the world, probably, unless some of our western cities, grows so perceptibly and changes so rapidly as Gotham. Ten years suffices to change locality of fashionable residence into retail market, and five or six more to convert it into a wilderness of wholesale warehouses. Business will be large in amount this fall, but the profits must be slim, owing to the great competition. The time has passed when mans pecuniary ability could be measured by the amount of business be does :; in these days Of extended credit, man may have the handling of vast amounts while he derives but limited income from his labor and invests little capital. The regular lines of business are paying less at present than certain specialities in which the compe- titiOn is small. But some men will make money, by industry and frugality, when others could only sink it. A case in point is that of cheap restaurant keeper near the Park, who has made fortune of over $4,000, it is said, out of subterranean place of refreshment, which he has attended to chiefly in person. Nowadays, having gained his fortune, the old gentleman does mot disdain to put on his apron and wait on SUGGESTIONS of men comparatively poor, all the morning; when afternoon comes, he goes home to drive out his wife and children with a span of fast horses, and an elegant turn out generally. Another man, in the same vicinity, is said to have made a very good competency, by selling bread and milk at sixpence per bowl. Other men have made large fortunes by the manufacture of articles of which one would suppose the aggregate sale to be too insignificant to deserve atten- tion. But all these little things "count up" The man who makes or sells an article appa- rently Insignificant generally clears a large per centage, while the "heavy man" of South or Front streets may have large sums of money passing through his hands, but very little indeed sticks to bis fingers. The pro- portion men ain business for themselves" who really make fortunes, is much smaller than is generally supposed and, in fact, the number of rich men is much smaller than the common estimate. People are judged rich according to the amount they spend, which is not safe criterion in this vincinity. 1t is affirmed by those who ought to know, that there are not more than twenty five millionaires IN the city of New York. s.. P. TOWNSEND has been counted very rich man, but has been obliged to sell his magni- icent house a Fifth Avenue, and is taking up again the manufacture of "Sarsaparilla." The Fifth Avenue mansion, which excited so much curiosity at its erection, is opened as branch Of the far-famed "Spingler In stitute." Mr. ABBOT, of the prolific family of ABBors, the well known principal, has made very profitable business of teaching the young ieea how to shoot" And, in truth, the fashionable boarding schools of this city "pa7" very handsomely. Several middle-aged ladies' of imposing manners and good family, have made themselves independent, after the death or failure of male supporters, by setting up institutions for the instruction of the children OF their fashionable friends. *x* Mr.. ms-A light, not Northern light, but one GS-A light, not Northern light, but one for q timc as difficult in its nature to UNDER stand, suddenly appeared near the landing, at the foot Of Broadway, at an early hour yester- day morning. It's sudden appearance, and the singular phenomena attending it, created a great Juror among the Policemen who hap pened in the neighborhood. 1t had the ap- pearance Of an animal enveloped in flames yet that suppositiOn was impossible. Could it be Satan in a diminutive form, visiting noe turnally this sublunary sphere? What could he want? Certainly he could have no business with our Police. Was it o comet? Some thought so, but Others, remembering the story of the New York meteors, declared it to be one Of the same character. While these copjec- lures were being freely expressed, the object began to utter the most doleful cries, and in a few moments it ceased to move. The fragments Of broken planets, the descent of meteoric stones upon our globe, the whiting comets welding their loose material at the solar surface, the volcanic sruptions in our own satellite, the appearance of now stars and dis appearance Of others, are all fureshadows Of that impending convulson to which the world is doomed. In the harbor of the last town the night was So bright that it was found almost impossible to fish for sturgeon, sport which is reneralI, most successful on a dark night, when bright light is carried in the bow OF the boat, and the doomed fish is caught mapping. Times gives glowing accounts OF the grand military fete which occurred in Paris on the l4th of August, in honor of the return OF the victorious army of Italy. 1t is stated that upwards of a million Of strangers were IN Paris on the occasion, and altogether 1t Is regarded as the most brilliant pageant OF the kind that has occurred since the reign OF Louis Napoleon. The number of troops IN motion was nearly 5000, with FIVE marshals, the Empe-or'S staff, &c. One writer says: The Place EendOme was by far the most interesting point Of the animated route through which the victorious army passed. The reader familiar with Paris, can easily imagine the spacious square, with Its noble Napoleonic column suggested 10y the Trojan pillar at Romeo surrounded by platforms reaching as high as the first floor, and cir cling all round the houses of the Place On the right and LETT of the Ministry of Justice were cons picuous tribunes occupied by the Empress, the Prince Imperial &c. Circling around the square were seats cal cu!ated to accommodate 10000 persons, and forming a vast amphteatre. At each cad of the entrance Of the Place were eight magnifcenrly gilt col umus, each supporting golden figure OF victory. 1t was here that the great military tSte found its centre of interest. The En- press, the Prince Imperial, and all the mem- bcrs of the Imperial family were in this elc- waited tribune; and surrounded on either side, and circlng all round the square, were seen cluster of elegantly dressed ladies and mil itary uniforms, presenting altogether Il most glittering and animated scene The Empe- ror on horseback, placed himself before the Imperial tribune, and there witnessed the troops file off before him amid the most deaf ming cheering. 1t was at this point that the great officers of State, the diplomatic corps, and in fact, the aristocratlc and fashionable members of Partisan society, were collected Those who witnessed this wide amphithcatre, containing 10000 persons, rs the troops, III an endless moving stream, passed through the seated crowd, will never forget the pic ture 1t was the event of the age. MAMIE AND THE MORNING GLORIEs, BY MARY CLEMMER AMEs. 1t makes me half child again, your laughter sweet and wild; Out in the dewy garden, you're picture more than fair, A little girl with morning glories wreathed around her hair Wee Mamie's mid the morning glories every summer morn, just as the young auroras on the rosy hill are born Just as the clinging valley mists AERIAL wings I'M furl, To leave the azure ether kissing our little girl And Mamie comes to breakfast with morning gIo- ries crowned, A band of purple bell-cups around her forehead bound; o. blossoms very beautiful your subtle spirit grace Adds hardly to the halo of the little soul-lit face And Mamie often says she loves the morning glory best =. And next the naiad lily which stars the waters My love- of all the flowers, whose ever-Iifted eye Looks learning toward the heaven for which sometimes sigh. Our lovely Morning Glory all your human fate The storm or sunshine waiting thee, alas! we may not see; Yet dim as shadows in lake, half seen, we know there lies A wondrous world of prophecy within our darling's eyes. We hardly dream her budding life will fade away too soon; That the glory of her morning will perish ere it's noon She may live to love, and suffer all woman's heart can know, To hold flowing life-cup till she marks its faded glow. THE ELECTRICAL LIGHT-The light seen in Borealis, was very vivid, and was an exhibition seldom witnessed in this latitude. A learned writer, speaking of this phenomenon, says The Aurora Borealis is a luminous phenomenon, which appears in the heavens, and is seen in high littudes in both hemispheres. The term Aurora Borelis Northern Lights has been applied to it be- the opportunities of witnessing it are, from the geographical character of the globe, much fire. quent in the northern than in the southern hemisphere The term Aurora Polaris would be more proper de- signation. This phenomenon consists of luminous rays Of various coorS issuing from every direction but convergng to the point, which appear after sunset, generally toward the NORTH occasionally toward the west and sometimes but rarely, toward the south. 1t frequently appears the horizon, vague and diffuse light, something like the faint sreaks which harbnger the rising and form the dawn. Hence the phe- nomcna has derived its name, the Northern Morning. Sometimes however is represented under the form of a sombre cloud, from which luminous jets ISSUE which often variously colorcd, and illuminate the entire atmosphere An exhibition so striking the aurora could not fail at early period attract the attention of scientific inqurers and to give rise to various theories. Some suppose be the refracton of the solar rays; others ascribed it to be the effects of the magnetic fluid. Euler identified it with the tails of comets. Effects of the Aurora Rorealfs. The superintendent of the Canadian Tele- graph COmpany's lines telegraphs as follows in relation to the effect of the aui ora borealis last night: 81 never, in an experience of fifteen years in working telegraph lines, witnessed any thing like the extraordinary effect of the aurora borealis between Quebec and Farther Point last night. The line was in most per- feet order and well skilled operators worked necessarily last evening till O'Clock this morning to get over in an Ineligible form about 400 words of the report per steamer Indian for the associated press, and, at the latter hour, so completely were the wires under the influence of the aurora borealiS, it was found utterly impossible to communicate between the telegraph stations and the line had to be closed. The same difficulty pre- vailed as far south as Washington"

EMANCIPATION Of the African Race. OF prayers unanswered, OF contumely patiently endured--ha7e convinced us of the truth. 1t must he spoken out, loudly and energetically, despite the wild mockiugs Of "howGng can't" The freed West India negro slave will not till the soil for wages; the free son of the ex slave is as obstinate as his sire. He will cultivate lands which he has not bought for his own yams, mangoes, and plantains. These satisfy his wants de does not care for yours. Cotton, and sugar, and coffee and tobacco--he cares little for them. And what matters it to him that the Englshman has sunk his thousands and tens of thousands on mills, machinery, and plants, which now totter on languishing es tate that for years has only returned beggary and debats. He eats his his yams and singers at "Buckra." We know not why this should be; but it is so. The negro has been bought with price the price OF English taxation and English toll. He has been redeemed from bondage" by the sweat and travail ofsome millious ofhard- work ing Englishmen. Twenty millions of pounds sterling-one hundred millions Of dollars-haye been distilled from the brains and muscles of the free English laborer, ofeyery degree, to fash ion the West India negro into "free and nde- pendent laborer" "Free and independent" G. nough he has become, God knows; but laborer he is not; and so far as we can see, never will be- He will sing hymns and quote texts, but honest steady industry, he not Only detests but despises We wish to Heaven that some peo- pie in England--neither government people, nor persons, nor clergymen--but some just minded, honest hearted, and clear sighted men, would go out to some of the islands-say Jamai ca, Antigua or Dominica--not for a month or three months, but for a year--would watch the precious protege oil philanthropy the free negro, in his daily habits; would watch him as he lazily plants his little squattng;woud see him proudly reject agricultural or domestic service, or accepts it at wages lud icrously dsproportion- ate to the value of his work. We wish, too, they would watch him while, with hide thick er than that of a hipopotamus and body to which fervid heat is comfort rather than an annoyance, he droningly lounges over the pre- scribed task on which the interpId Englishman, uninured to the burning sun, consumes his inn patient energy and too often sacrifices his life. We wish they would go out and view the ne gro in all the bazonry Of his idleness his pride, his ingratitude contemptuously sneerng at the industry Of that race which made him free, and then come home and teach the memorable les son of their experience to the fanatics who have perverted him into what he is.--Londo,s Times ! Nay, let the canting fanatic read and ponder, and let pc : litical demagogues blush with shame when they reflect how many honest and well-meanng per- sons have been led astray by their "cunningly devised fables" in regard to the "poor slave" But one word to those who, by false alarm, have been frightened from the democratic par ty, and have taken refuge in the arms OF black republIcanism You, once good and true dem ocrats of Maine New Hampshire, Connecticut, New York-what have you gained, or are like ly to gain, by joining the republican party?- What would you gain were that party to ac complsh what some Of its ablest and most in fuential leaders really seek to accomplish-the abolition of slavery in the South? or, in the event of failing in this, the dissolution OF the Union? Why take alarm at this demagogical cry about slavery? Why meddle with the sub ject? From the National Intelligencer, Sept % THE REPUBLICAN COURT. Observing in the New York journal of Com. merce few days ago complimentary illusions to the late George Washington Parke Gusts of Arlington, we were reminded that we had in our possession an unpublished contribution from his pen in relation to the social habitudes which prevailed at our Republican Court in the days of the first president. AS these re- miniscences may be deemed to have received new interest since the death of their writer has precuded the hope of any additional COM municatiop such as our readers were annually favored with on the 22d of February during the life of Mr. Gusts, we have concluded no longer to withhold from them the last contri- button penned by the "child of Mount Yer non" The REPUBLICAN CoURr IN THE DAYS OF THE FIRST PREsIDENT.-The Presidential Mansion in Philadelphia was the property of Robert Morris, and had been the headquarters of Sir William Howe during the occupation of Philadelphia by the British army in 1777-78. The situation was eligible, being in an airy and pleasant part of the city, with a consider able area of open space adjoining it, aud con tguOus to the public buildings Considerable additions and improvements were made to the original building with view to the accommo- 1ation of the Presidents household still the Doms were small, and the whole establish Aent but indifierently fitted for the purposes ->4uired. The equpage of the President were all pro- vided for, the stabling for twelve horses being extensive and commoaious, and the coach. houses large and convenient Washngton's unmitigated, untiring employ ment and labor made it necessary that lie should have some mode of public reception for the many visitors who were continually seek ing opportunities OF paying their respects and presenting their letters of introduction; hence the PRESIDENTS LEvEE. On Tuesdays, commencing at and ending at O'Clock AT these receptions there was no shaking of hands, the Chief receiving his visitors as President of the United States, and not as Gen. Washington. The foreign Ministers attended the levee in full costume, and often introduced persons of distinction embraced the opportunity of the levee to pay their respects to the Chief Magistrate. The President was plainly but handsomely dressed, his hair in full powder, and wearing dress sword. He was attended by his principal Secretay, Mr.. Lear, Major jackson, and the other gentlemen of his family. He addressed few words of courtesy to the visitors as they were presented. The company then formed in groups for conversation, and on the stroke of o'clock retired, the levee being at an end. THE DRAwING-RooM. When Mrs. Washington received company it was on Friday, commencing about and ending about 10 o'clock. Two rooms were thrown open. The furniture that was thought handsome in those days would be considered barely decent in modern times. The PRINCIPAL ornament was glass chandelier in the largest room, burning wax lights. The chair of the lady of the President was plain armchair, lined with green morocco leather The ladies visiting the drawing-room were always attended by gentlemen. 1t was not ~ n 10 nt the drawing-room, but only those of tie age when it is proper for ladies' to go into compa- ny. Upon the ladies being introduced they were seated, and the President, who always at tended the drawingroom, passed round the circle, paying his respects to each in success sion, and it was common remark among the chit-chat of the drawing-room that the Chief was no inconsiderable judge OF female beauty, since he was observed to tarry longer than usual when paying his compliments to Miss Sophia Chew, charming belle of Philadelphia in that time. Refreshments were handed round by SER wants in livery, and about that period first ap- peared the luxury, now so universal OF ice cream. Introductions to eminent personages and conversation formed the entertainments of the drawing-room. Cards were altogether un- known. But the leading and most imposing feature of the drawing.room was the men of mark, the "Revolutonaries," both civil and military, who were to be seen there. The old officers delighted to pay their respects to the wife of Washington, and to call up the "reminiscences of the headquarters and ofthe "times that tried mems souls" These glorious old chevaiers were the greatest beaux of the age, and the re- collection of their gallant achievements, to- gether with their elegant manners, made them acceptable to the ladies everywhere. They formed the elite of the drawing-room. Gen. Wayne the renowned "Mad Anthony" with his aide-de-camp Lswis and DeButts, fire. quently attended, with Mifflin, Walter Stew art, Col. Hartley, and many others. Indeed there was often to be met with at the mansion of the first President an assemblage of intellect and honor, public virtue, and private worth exalted merit and illustrious services, such as the world will never see again. Among the foreign officers of distinction, visitors of the drawing room, were the Vicom' to de Noailes, of the French, and Major Beck with, of the British armies. There was no etiquette in the drawing ROOM simplicity with dignity prevailed. There all was afability, with the polite and elegant man ners of that distinguished age. One privilege alone existed. The seat next to the Pres dents lady was always occupied by Mrs. Rob ert Morris. This was no matter by arrange ment, but was yielded to the excellent lady o. common consent. House OF REPRESENTATIVES, December 23d, 1858. ELOQUENT ExTRAcT.-The best thing yet written by Edward Everett in his Mount Vernon Papers, is an article on the late comet. After describing its approach to the earth and the beautiful picture it pre- sented, he says: Return, then, mysterious traveller, to the depths of the heavens, never again to be seen by the eyes of the men now living Thou hast run thy race with glory. Mil lions of eyes have gazed upon thee with wonder, but they shall never look upon thee again. Since thy last appearance in these skies, empires, languages and races OF men have died away-the Macedonian, the Alexandrian, the Augustan, the Parthian, the Byzantine, the Saracenic, the Ottoman dynasties, have sunk or are sinking into the gulf of ages. Since thy last appearance old continents have relapsed into ignorance, and new worlds have come out from behind the evil of waters. The Magian fires are quenched on the hill tops of Asia; the Chaldean is blind; the Egyptian hierogra- mist has lost his cunning; the Oracles are dumb. Wisdom now dwells in the farthest Thules, or in newly discovered worlds be- ,yond the sea. HAPPY, when wheeling up again from the celestial abysses, thou art once more seen by the dweilers of the earth, the Language we speak shall be forgotten, and science shall have fled to the utmost corners of the earth. But even there His hand. which now marks out thy wondrous circuit, shall still guide thy course ; and then, as now, Hesper smile at thy approach, and Arcturns with his sons rejoice at thy coming.

A STARTLING SURPRISE. curious circumstance has come to our knowledge. says one of our Western exchanges recently, which, though creating much talk among certain parties, has been hushed up as much ss possible, and a il does not seem like ly to proceed farther, we suppress names. A gentleman and his wife some time since settled in Rockford; shortly after their arrival they made, among others, the acquaintance Of young and beautiful widow who had the repu tatiOn of being great flirt. The gentleman up to this time, had been q most devoted hus- band, and though there seemed to be a mutual attraction between himself and the gay widow whenever they met, the wife, confident Of his affection, suspected nothing. Matters pro- gressed, how rapidly she did not know, until the beginning Of this week when husband wife and widow were invited to tea at the house of a friend 1t was an agreeable social party and the company were apparently enjoying Them selves highly, when the wife, vino had been chatting with friends on the piazza. entered the parlor and seated herself in the shadow of window, the heavy damask curtains of which separated her from teie-a-.stG which stood in arecess. The parties occupying the tCie-a-tPie were her husband and the fascinating widow ; and what was her astnn;shmeni when their low tones became fully sudible % her strained ears to hnd that they were arranging the prelimi- naries OF an elOpement, TO take place that very night, Matters were to be arranged so that ing, while the husband, in the most natural manner in the world, would offer to drive home the beautiful widow. Instead of going home however, they were to go Immediately to the cars, and leave on the eIevcn-o' clock train. The discovery was So unexpected and the shock so great that the poor wife almost faint ed. She was determined, however, not to be- tray her knowledge of the guilty scheme until the proper time came, and. recovering herself glided from the fatal seat. and tried to enter into conversation az usual Of course she was not greatly surprised when her husband shortly aIterward afectiOnately advised her to 90 home with Mr.. and Mrs. -. who were going their way, as he himself had TO go to his Office short ly. and might be detained till late. She made no objection, but putting on her bonnet and bidding adieu to her entertainers started for home, to the great relief of the guilty couple who had feared some trouble in getting rid of her. Immediately on arriving at home, the wife proceeded to pack a carpet bag with a pile of shirts, and other neces.aries and start ed on foot for the house where her husband still remained. She hid herself in the shadow OF the trees and waited, but not long. Soon her husband and the widow exchanged GOOD night with their hostess the latter remarkiny IN lively tone. that she should certainly tell his wife. They seated themselves comfort ably IN the vehicle. when the wife without bonnet or shawl, suddenly walked to the side OF the carriage and said quietly at the same time holding up the carpet bag, l ID, don't go without your shirts the mercy knows when you will get any mOre,' The blank astOnishment Of the two NAV be imagined. Hero We stopped for dinner at 3, p. m.. with two or three wagons of Pixies Peakcrs, from whom We obtained generous supply eff fresh bread and another Antelope ham, very much to the improvement Of our edible resources. may as we'll explain here that all the emf grants We met going into the Kansas diggiugs, had started from the Missouri, on the north side of the Platte, aud had failed to cross at Shinn's ferry, sixty five miles up that stream, supposiDg that they could do so at Fort Kearpey, or some other point below the forks; but in the absence of ferries, the high water had headed them of, and forced them clear up to Laramie, whence they we're now working southward, hav- ing lost fully two hundred miles by me- gleeting to cross the Platte where they might have done 50. In all this region, it is settled maxim that you must cross a stream directly upon reaching it, if your way lies across it, never camping before you do 30, lest sudden rise should obstruct your passage for days. Many have lost fortDight,s weary travel by failing to heed this rule in spirit with re- gard to the Platte. We moved again at 5, passing over ridge and into broad valley, with round ed hills on the west and a range of such precipitous clay-rock bluffs as / have tried to describe on the east. These bluffs were broken through at intervals, and the streams that came down on the hills on the west ran out at the brooks, after traversing the valley for two or three miles, and flowed away east to join Howard s Fork and the South Platte Our trail here bore considerably west of north, evidently to reach the mouth OF the Cheyenne Pass. We had hoped to make our next camp at that point, but night tell upon US before reaching it, and We stopped on little run where we found good water and grass, but close under the mountains, and in one of the loneliest spots ever beheld. Not tree nor shrub was visible, nor had been for miles; yet it was not difficult to gather dry sticks enough to cook our supper, proving what have elsewhere observed, that wood was formerly more common in all this region than now. We had all turned in by 9, and were doing very well, when rush by one of our mules apprised US that he was loose, having broken his lariat; but he was soon caught and made fast, and we all addressed ourselves to slumber again. In an hour, however, there was fresh alarm, and not without reason, for three or four of our mules had gone, we could not tell whither.-- The first impression was that band Of Cheyennes, who were known to be en- samped in the mountains very near US, had been watching our progress from their heights unsuspected by US, and had stolen down under cover of the deep dark ness, uDfastened and started of our mules with intent to run. them of. This was not an agreeable view of the case, as We could hope neither to recover nor replace bur faithful animals for at least week. However, little watching of the mule still fast convinced our conductor that the others had started back on the road We lad traversed, which was route the Jheyennes were most unlikely to take, while so near their hiding places in the Mountains. So two of our men started IN the back track, but returned in an ,our unsuccessful. Then the remaining mule was saddIed and bridled-and he lad to be thrown down twice before he would submit to the operation-when our conductor mounted him, expecting to be instantly thrown by the perverse beast. unused to the saddle, but he was happily disappointed, and started down the road N brisk trot. By this time there was moonlight; and he found all the missing mules little beyond the poibt to which lie had proceeded on foot, and brought hem back in triumph. 1t was now break f day, and we resolved to feed and break ast for once before starting. We did so, nd moved on at 6 a. m, reaching "Camp Volbach," at the Cheyenne Pass, in less han half an hour.
