Few persons who can reflect on the highly interesting and eevating subject Of the proba- bic uses in the creation of the vast rnyriads of heavenly bodies which we see, during our hours of darkness, sparkling in the distant armament above, and which we know, by the calculations and discoveries Of astronomers, 10 be spread over the illimitable universe, can entertain the narrow minded irrational idea that ell those visible and invisible globes are mere matter, floating in space, unemployed and uninhabited, while our little planet alone has been selected by the Almighty for the abode of intellectual beings. This idea is the embodiment Of selfconcet, vain glory, and presumption For, though We are told in the Scriptures that man is made " lower than the angels, we are nowhere as sured that no intellectual beings except man have ever been imbued with life and we have no warrant to pronounce that these vast lumi- naries we're called into existence for no other purpose than TO throw tide of useless splendor over the solitudes Of immensity."* Such is not, and has not been, the opinion of the greatest, the wisest, and the best. Many Christian philosophers and astronomers, as well as learned divines, have declared their belief in the theory of the sun, moon, and stars, being each and all inhabited worlds, or in prepa- ration to receive inhabitants. Faith" says one of these philosophers, whose grasp of mind may well claim influence, even for his specula- tons on this lofty theme - " faith associates with these bright abodes the future fortunes of immortal and regenerated man. 1t places there the loved and the lost it follows them into celestial bowers " and genius brings the charm of poetry to shed halo of beauty around the mystic scenes, which imagination fails to portray; There is place where spirits come, Beneath the shrine % live, mystic place, middle home, Which GOO TO them doth give. AURORA Recommendations Of the Grand River valley, as vol rs those in the more Eastern portions of the United States, have been favored with view of that beautiful phenomenon of nature, known as the Aurora Borealis, or "North- en Lights" scene very unusual at this season of the year, as il is well known TO all careful observers of natures operations that these grand and curious lights arc seen in their greatest brilliancy and per- lection during tho severe frosts and SHOWS of winter, and are hence sure index of clear and cool atmosphere; and thus it is nothing more than a natural conse- uncnee that severe frost should accom- pany this appearance. The cause Of this celestial brilliancy was for a long time a subject of much speculation to sages and philosophers. Some affirming that it was occasioned by the reilection OF llght from the immense fields and floating masses of ice far to the northward, and others that electricity was the primary cause; the latter idea now having gained the almost unanimous assent Of the learn ed, appropos TO which, it is stated by the Superintendent of the Canadian Line of Telegraph between Quebec and Farther Point, that during the night Of August 2Sth, when the Aurora Borealis appeared in great brilliancy during the entire night, five hours wero required by the best oper- ators to transmit four hundred words be- tween those two points-so great an ef- feet did the electricity, with which the at mosphere was so fully charged, have up on the telegraph wires.

She, in her modesty, holding volume of poetry in her dainty hands; hoping thereby to attract the attention Of her lover away from herself to the holy, thrilling, and exalted products Of master mind He, through polite ness, listens to the glowing theme; yet longing for her rosy lips to warbe the last word upon the glowing page. Rocking to rest in their sweet content, The birds their heaven taught vespers sung, And over our heads like gorgeous tent The crimson curtains of sunset hung. The lilies lifted their queenly heads And swayed with the current to and fro, And the wild flowers leaned DER their grassy beds And gazed at themselves in the wave below. Silently passed they, one by one, AS stars fade out from the sky above In the glorious beams of the rising sum- All, death were the end of earthly love!

Come, sit with me, dear reader, by the open window, for tits the hour +" When the Inst sunshine of expiring day, in summer twilight, weeps itself away" Watch those rosy, purple clouds, piled up in the golden west, slowly changing their gorgeous, sun-tinted raiment for the more sombre hue, be6tting the hour Of night; the noisy tumult of day is subsiding to a low, indistinct murmur an evening song now breaks on the ear, and anon the mellow notes Of tugle como floating Ger the water, broken now and then by the melancholy notes Of whippoorwill, filling our hearts with sensation of awe and dread. A star makes its appearance, now followed by another and another, until, as if by magic, the azure canopy, stretching far and wide above us, is dotted by millions of diamond lights, scintillating and cleaning on us, till we are tempted to believe they are the eyes Of those loved ones gone before, searching our Utmost souls, and when our pure and noblest thoughts meet their gaze, how they CLEAN and glitter with love and light; but, ali! when they gaze on the dark and sinful thoughts that sometimes sway our souls, how their loving light pales away, even as though they were blinded by tears !. Now the moons broad, red disc is slowly rising behind the trees, casting pale, mellow light over hill and vale; softening the rugged hills; bringing out in bold relief the white cottages against the dark, green trees bathing all the landscape in beauty. All, now her beams have fallen on the water, and glittering there, from magical golden bridge over the dark, blue river, on which you imagine you can see the fairies crossing and recrossing in el6n frolics. The south wind is whispering now his love-story to the listening leaves, who dance and tlutter in their joy; now, like a gay deceiver, he has left them how sad and motionless they hang-while he is wooing the flowers in the vale, or murmuring through the lonely pine. This is the hour l love best, and yet, tonight, ! am oppressed with sadness !; the world lies so calm, so pure, in the moonlight-can it be that aught Of toll should mar its loneliness yet, tits even so-how many homes is this golden moon beaming upon, where strife and discord prevail how many hearts filled with envyings and bitterness Aye, even in some Of the homes / have been this day, where all was fair to the outward eye, Joy and mirth seemed in every heart, but could l not see the dark shadow, that only seemed banished for a while, lingering near, waiting the opportunity to steal nearer and nearer, and envelope all in it's clouds? Who can tell the misery Of life in these homes, guarded by shadow, it may be, of sighted love, an angry or cruel word, a broken faith, or broken heart! Is not life Of loneliness like mine far preferable? Dear married friends, why will you not realize how much is dependent upon you in keeping these shadows from your own homes for once admitted, from ever so slight o cause, and they will never leave; you may Danish them for time, but, all +! they are:hoverng near and willreturn ere you arc aware oft. You, oh, husband, close the door carefully as you enter your home admit not that dark shadow with you to darken the brightness Of those happy hearts within 4 gentle, loving wife is there, wearied, perchance, by toll or pain, or those little trials so wearing to her spirits ; yet, as you enter her face is lighted with smiles to welcome you no trace Of pain or WEAKNESS can you see there, and cannot your very heart echo the words Of the poet CHANGER CA WIFI a Seinte Marie benedicte, How might a man have any adversitee, That hath a wifi ?" Your children, too, are there with Joyous hearts, and meet you with laughing eyes and rosy checks. Oh, guard them well, that no dark shadows may rest on them, chilling their joyous mirth and saddening their happy faces. And you, too, oh! wives, how much you have in your power to keep away all shadows +; your empire is there and yours the power to rule it wisely and happily !; to beautify and make your home SO happy that your husbands steps will, as he turns homewal d, involuntarily quicken, and his earth warm as he thinks Of his wife and little ones. And your children in after years, when they have left the roof tree and gone out to buffet with cold world, will look back upon their childhood's home as darkened by no shadow, and the lesson there learned will be a safeguard from all evil with the world. $50 fret net like an idle girl, That life is dashed with fieeks of sin, Abide-thy wealth is gathered in, Wien time hath sundered shell from pearl" Cousin KATY.

THE SAN JUAN DIFFIcuLTY.-Wa stiaqton. Sept. 25.-Colonel Rankin, Register of the Land Office at Olympia, in Washington Terri tory, has arrived here, from the island of San Juan. He reports that if the intentions of Gov ernor Douglas had been carried out, there would have been collision between the British and American forces, as the vessels Satellite and Plumper had had orders from him to fire, but Admiral Baype opportunity arrived and superseded him in command of the English ships of war, five in number. The original misunderstanding was with the Hudson Bay Company, the interests of which were represented by Governor Douglas. The island of San Juan had been in the occupancy of the Americans at least eighteen months, no body seeming to question their rights, and for a longer period was considered and treated in all respects as belonging to Washington Ter ritory. 1t was not until General Harvey applied to. and was informed by Boundary Commissioner Campbell, that our title to the island was clear and certain, that he dispatched troops thither, at the earnest request of the residents, who claimed protection from British aggression aud especially from the predatory incursions of Northern Indians, who had even taken and held possession of light house for three DAYS. and against whom private expeditions had re: peatedly been sent to chastise them. Colonel Rankin says the people of Washington Terri tory and of the Pacific States are unanimous for our retention of the island of San Juan. And such is their enthusiasm, that if the U. s. troops should be directed to vacate it, private parties, in formidable numbers, would imme- diately occupy that important position, aud not surrender without C severe struggle. But it is not supposed in this city that our troops will be withdrawn, as this would be considered as an admission that our title is clearly disputable. 1t may not be generally known that this Government has recently confirmed bluff of land, containing three thousand acres, for military reservation, if anything, further north than San Juan.

Who are sleeping Children wearied with their play For the stars Of night are Peeping, And the sun has sunk away. Who are sleeping Mortals. compassed round with wo Eyelids wearied out with weeping, Close for very weakness now: And that short relief from sorrow, Harassed nature shall sustain. Who are sleeping Captives in their gloomy cells; Yet sweet dreams are o'er them creeping, With their many colored spells: All they love-again they clasp them; Feel again their long lost joys; But the haste with which they grasp them, Every fairy form destroys. Misers, by their boarded gold; And in fancy now are heaping Gems and pearls Of price untold Golden chains their limbs cucumber, Diamonds seem before them strewn; But they waken from their slumber, And the splendid dream is TOWN. Who are sleeping Pause 4 moment, softly tread Anxious friends are fondly keeping YigilS by the Sleeper's bed: Others hopes have all forsaken One remains, that slumber keep: Speak not, lest the slumberer waken From that sweet, that saving sleep. They are sleeping. Who are sleeping? Thousands who have passed away, From a world of wo and weeping, To the regions Of decay. Safe they rest, the green turf under; Signing breeze, or music breath. Winters wind. or summers thunder. Cannot break the sleep Of death.

IL never in an experience of 10 years in working telegraph lines, witnessed anything like the extraordinary effect of the Aurora Borcalis between Quebec and Farther Point last night. The line was in most perfect order, and we'll skilled operators worked necessarily from eight o'clock last evening till one o'clock this morning to get over in an Ineligible form about four hun drcd words of the report per steamer Indian for the Associated Press. and at the latter hour the wires were so completely under the influence of the Aurora Borcalis, that it was found ut tcrIy impossible to communicate be- tween the telegraph stations, and the line had to be closed" The same diff iiculty prevailed as far south as Wash. ington.

E oQuent Extract, The best thing yet written by Edward Everett in his Mount Vernon Papers, y is an article on the late comet. After describing its approach to the earth, and the beautiful picture it presented, he says: = Return, then. mysterious traveller, to the depths of the heavens, never again to be seer by the eyes of men now living Thou hast run thy race with gIoryl Mil lions Of eyes have gazed upon thee with wonder, but they shall never look upon thee again. Since thy last appearance in these skies, empires, languages and races have died away-the Macedonian the Alexandrian, the Augustan, the Par. THAN, the Byzantine, the Saracenic, the Ottoman dynasties have sunk or are sink ing into the gulf of ages. Since thy last appearance old continents have relapsed into ignorance, and new worlds have Gene out from behind the veil of waters. The Magian fires are quencbed on the hill tops of Asia; the Chaldean is blind the Egyptian hicrogramist has lost bis cunning; the Oracles are dumb. Wis dom now dwel5 in the farthest Thules or in newly discovered worlds beyond the sea-Haply, when, wheeling Up again from the celestial abysses, thou art once more seen by the jewellers Of the earth the language we speak shall be forgotten and science shall have fed to the utter most corners of the earth. But even there His bands. that now marks out thy Wondrous circuit. Shall still guide thy course; d then, as now, Hesper will smile at thy approach, and Arcturus, with his sons, rejoice at thy coming"

MISCELL A N Y . A Sad Domestic Story. In the obituary column of the Palmer Mass Journal, we find tho following announcement: {: "Died--Mary, aged 20, wife of De Witt Clinton Packard, of Providence, r. l." In the editorial column there is sad and touching story, relat- ing to the announcement, which is given below 1t is a lesson from the tomb, to the young and thoughtless, and told so eloquently that it cannot fail to make an impression for good on readers of every age. 1t says: Sin another column we record the death Of q Young lady who died of a broken heart. We do not like to trespass upon the sacredness OF do mesto grief to unfold the details of her sad sto- ry; but when the privacy of atdiction becomes public feeling, it is not improper for the Press TO place the events on record. 1t is not neces- sary to repeat names or relate minute particu- lars. 1t is enough that we draw the outlines OF picture for the reader to paint with appropr' ate eolors Many months ago, in the neighbor- ing town of Belchertown, young man sought and received the promise OF the hand OF young lady, whose home was in the lap OF luxury, whose mental and personal attractions made all pleasant around her. Like too many conhdlng ones of her sex, she trusted mans unhallowed promise, and yielded all to him. From that hour he estranged himself from her, and soon removed to distant State. When It became evden, that he had exposed himself to the pen sty of the law, at the request Of her friends he visited her to fulfill the vows he had long before made. They were married in one OF those hasty, unceremonious ways, which occupy bnt little time or attention. Late iU the evening they re. turned to her fathers house, where he left her IN the street, promising to return in short time. Bur that promise was aever fulfilled. She wrote TO him. and received encouragement that he would soon provide home for her, but delay followed delay, till her letters and entreates were unheeded and unanswered AT length q pledge of woman's love for her husband came into the world to open new fountains OF attec- tion TO the Young wife. Still the husband and father came not. "The mother recovered from confinement; but, after repeated letters to her husband found no answer, the idea that she was deserted by him forced itself upon her, and she gave way TO despondency and despair. The child, partaking of it's mothers grief, soon died. There was nothing more that she could live for, and, though suffering from no disease, she sank upon dying bed Then the swift wing of lightning bore to the distant husband the intelligence that she was diving. He still hesitated, but at length set out to meet his expiring wife. Conscious that her hours were few, she only wished to live long q nough to see her husband; he was still all to her. Her last words TO her friends were: Tell him that still love him-that | died for him. When evening shadowed the earth, the husband came. As he approached the bedside of his in iured wife, he was recognized, and the words He's come burst from her lips. Already had the wing of the death angel cast its shadow over that dwelling, and she was entering the dimness of the dark valley. Next morning, in that room, lay the corpse of beautiful young wife, on which the husband had looked for the last time, and departed. "Lsst Sabbath afternoon, the funeral of the Young wife took place under her fathers roof | Her neighbors and friends, to the number OF five handred, were present; but the husband who had left her to die for him was not there. A deeply affecting address was made by her for rner pastor, and, just as the sun was sinking be- hind the western hills, four young ladies of her acquaintance, clad in garments OF white, bore her to grave in the garden, where the green turf was laid gently over her. Such is the story of one who died of broken heart. The grave is quiet place for the injured wife, but where | in ali the world can there be peace for him who would thus bring sorrow and death upon heri The story has its moral, but we will leave the reader TO apply it; it is full of warning, and we leave the young to heed it,"

Correspondence Of the Evening Postl NORTHWEST EXPLORING EXPEDITION there IS recorded some notable event, signalling every day in the year, and by whatever event July 18th is thus marked we celebrated it by arriving at four O'Clock in Pembna. On most maps with which have been familiar, Pembina is placed upon the east bank of the Red River of the North, opposite the mouth of the Penn pima river, at or near the forty ninth parallel the international boundary line. 1t is however, on the west bank of the river, just below q. c. north of the mouth of the Pembina, and therefore in Dacotah territory. The few Indian and halfbreed lodges which are upon the east side of the Red River, opposite Pembna, constitute the town of St. Vincent the terminus dd guem of the Minnesota and Pacific Railroad, and the place where, at election times, the present administration finds such valiant supporters, every man outnUmsering score of the ordinary kind. Two items more of geography, and will resume my itinerary at the point where it closed in my last letter, Alexandria. Thirty or hirtytwo miles west of here in st. Joseph another and larger half-breed settlement on the Pembina river, and about seventy miles north on the Red River, at the junction OF the Assinibone in British America, of course, is the Sekrk's settlement Fort Garry its centre. Less than hundred miles further north the Red River empties into Lake Winnipeg Our route, then, has been from the upper woters OF the Mississippi, northwest through the vail of one OF its minor tributaries, and across the lake region OF Minnesota to the head waters of the Red River of the North, and down its valley to the in ternational boundary line. An itinerary would thus divide itself naturally into three parasitic first pertaining to the Mississippi; the second to the lake region; and the third to the Red River valley. What has been told regarding the richness of the valley OF the Sauk river we found amply confirmed in passing from its mouth to its head waters Du- ring every days journey, of from twenty to twenty-five miles, we passed numbers of log houses surrounded by well-tilled fields and claims -shantes thickly dotted the intervening distances Perhaps some one may read those words who was as ignor- ant as was of their meaning. The pre-emption laws required of settlers making new claim the building OF house, actual occupation for a certain Perod, and the tlllage OF certain amount of land in the one hundred and sixty acres Honest and dishonest claimants fulfil the letter or evade the spirit OF the law by laying few logs four square, calling it house, and sleeping there few nights Tl1ese are claim-shanties. Sometimes the actual settler finds it more convenient to live in a neigh bor's house, but often the whole proceeding is an evasion of the law, by which spectators get hold OF the land, or others their choice of rich lands in different places, to the detrment of those desiring to settle and build at one These shanties however, serve the traveller good turn sometimes, by furnishing wood ready cut to boil his tea and fry his pork. The immediate vicinity of the Sauk is we'll wooded, though there wide reaches of open rol- ling prairie on either side of the stream before you reach timber again. We crossed the river twice boating the provisions and swimming our animals The soil is dark sandy loan, capable of producing splendid crops, and this added to the fact that it Is part of the Messrs. Burbank Co. s new stage and mail route from st. Pauls to the head of nav- CATION on Red river, makes it quite certain that its growing line of settlements will be one of the first and strongest links in the chain to connect South ern Minnesota and the east with the great north western areas. terrific thunder storm, in which we were caught one afternoon while travelling over the Sauk Prairie reminds me of the peculiarity of the Min nesota climate. The rains generally fall at night, and in the summer are accompanied by the most superb displays of electrical phenomena. The thunder to roll in terrible crashes around the whole circuit of the heavens, and the lightning to flash from zenith to horizon. At times half hem isphere of sky will be ilumined bv flashes of light through which, as it were of fire, the sharper lightning dashes with intense brightness and with every variety of line, from the straight and forked to the zigzaggedst. Minnesota is not only the geographical but also the hydrogropical centre of the North American continent. Within her boundaries arise the streams which afterwards flow into the northern and middle Atlantic and the Gulf of Mexico She is the centre of the three great river systems of the Continent or rather the point in which they meet that of Lake Winnepeg, Of the great lakes and Of the Mississippi. The waters of the Red River of the North, which join those of the Saskatchewan from the Rocky Mountains in Lake Wnnepeg and flow thence by Nelson's river into Hudson's Bay, take their rise but five miles from the highest point of the Mississippi and all interlock with the streams which flow into Lake Superior and the St. Law renee. This easily accounts for the innumerable lakes with which the whole area of Minnesota is dotted, and in which these various streams head They are indeed numberess and of every size from little ponds without any apparent outlet to the larger bodies of water which stretch over miles and miles of country Lake 0sakis, which is about halfway between the Mississippi and Red River, is fair example Of the larger lakes. In two days man might walk around 1t. 1t has white sandy beach for its en- tire circumference, sprinked with cornelian agate and other pebbles, and making perfect setting for its beauty, like the delicate line of cOrnea Just visi Bile around large blue eve. Four or five feet above its level is the level of the surrounding land which near the lake is covered with a thick growth OF timber of every variety. A sad gDo,nestic sdory, In the Palmer (Mass.) Journal of the Sd inst, in the obituary column, we find the fol- lowing announcement: Ded--On the 26th, Mary, aged 20, wife of De Witt Clinton Pckard, of Providence, R. l." We also find the follow. ing editorial paragraph, which, it would SEEM has relation to that announcement: " In another column we record the death of young lady who died of broken heart. We DO not like to trespass upon the sacredness OF domestic grief to unfold the details of her sad story, but when the privacy of affection becomes public feeling it is not improper for the press to ? ace the events on record. 1t is not necessary 10 repeat names or relate minute particulars. 1t is enough that we draw the outlines of pic ture Tor the reader to paint with the appropriate colors. Many months ago, III the neighborinc town OF Balchertown, young man sought and received the promise Of the hand of a Young lady whose home was in the lap of luxury whose mental and personal attractions made all pleasant around her. Like too many cenfidino ones Of her sex, she trusted mans unhallowed promise, and yielded all to him. From that hour he estranged himself from her, and soon removed to distant State. When it became evident that he had exposed himself to the pen atty of the law at the request of her friends he visited her to fulfil the vows he had long before made. They were married in one of those hasty unceremonious ways which occupy but little time or attention. Late in the evening they returned to her fathers house, where he left her i'll the street, promising to return in short time. But the promise was never fulfilled She wrote to him, and received encouragement that he would soon provide home for her, but delay followed delay, till her letters and entreaties were UNDECIDED and unanswered. At length a pledge of woman's love for her husband came into the world to open new fountains of affection to the young wife Still the husband and father came not. "The mother recovered from her conf nement but, after repeated letters to her husband found no answer, the idea that she was deserted by him forced itself upon her. and she gave way to dependency and despair. The child, parta> king OF its mothers grief, soon died. There was nothing more that she could live for; and, though suffering from no disease, she sunk upon a dying bed Then the swift wings of lightning bore to the distant husband the intelligence that she was dying. He still hesitated but at length set out to meet his expiring wife. Conscious that her hours were few, sho only wished to live long enough to see her husband he was still all to her Her last words to her friends were: Tell him chat still love him-that l died for him." When evening Swallowed the earth, the husband came. AS he approached the bedside of his injured wife, he recog- nized, and the words, 1" He's come - burst from her lips. Already had the wing of the death angel cast its shadow over that dwelling, and she was entering the dimness of the dark valley, Ne1 morning, in that room lay the corpse of a beautiful young wife, on which the husband had looked for the last time. g. Last Sabbath afternoon, the funeral of the young wife took place under her fathers roof. Her neighbors and friends, to the number of five hundred, were present, but the husband who had left her to die for him was not there. deeply affecting address was delivered by her former pastor, and just as the sun was sinking behind the western hills, four young ladies of her acquaintance, clad in garments of white, bore her to a grave in the garden, where the green turf was laid gently over her. Such is the story of one who died Of broken heart The grave is quiet place for the in ured wife, but where in all the world can peace be found upon her. The story has its moral, butwe leave the reader to apply it, it is full of warning but we leave the young to heed it,"

DOES METEOR EXPLODE !-Everybody who was not in profound slumber must have been startled this smorning by one of the most remarkable and thus far mysterious occurrences that has during a long period of time transpired in this section Of country. At about O'Clock, while the sky was perfectly cloudless, while not single indication prevailed of a natural commotion of any sort whatever, there was terrific, shocking, deafen- ing report, accompanied apparently by two sharp echoes. Hon. RCBT. ID. OWEN on SPIRITUALIsM.- We are informed that the work which the Hon. Robt. Dale Owen has in press is de- voted to the subject of spiritualism. What his convictions are upon the subject we have not learnt; but his talent for investigating abStruse and metaphysical subjects, and his ardor in searching for the cause of mental and physiological phenomena, have led him to very thorough consideration of the sub ject; whatever his conclusions are, they will be fearlessly declared. The work will contain facts and reasoning that will expose the modern spiritual theory as a humbug, or lead sober men to investigate its phe- nomena, in order to determine for them selves if it be something new in our philoso- ply of which they had not before dreamed. Its publication will be looked for with some interest in this part of the State, where the author is so well known.

COMMUNICATIONS. Written for the North Iowa Times. Conquest OF Thought. Summer has come with its leaves and flowers, With It's sunny skies and tie melting showers. IT'S summers day; shower has just re- freshed the earth. Even now the thunder rum bles mid the distant hills. In front of the window from which am gazing stands rose bush, its blossoms pertaining the air, and bloom ing in all their summer glory. How many re- collections are brought to mind BY this simple plant! Visions of childhood float before my eyes-ts pleasures, its little griefs, its sad in nocence. But, alas the thorns Of time have pierced me, driven away these childish feelings, and left in the wounds the selfish. heartless thoughts of womanhood. Beyond the rose lies the grass. The raindrops on the bosom Of each blade look like 20 many diamonds in settings Of green. Again my mind wanders and l dream Of the old homestead, Of the gentle father and loving mother who were wont 70 c.. ress me, but now lie clasped in the chilly en-. brace of death, beneath the green turf Of the village churchyard. Farther in the background the beauteous rainbow spans the heavens but as gaze it vanishes into air, reminding me Of the promises of hollow.hearted friends, which are made Of nothing but the sunshine of a mo- ment, beaming on the tear bedimned eyes Of hope, and which are forgotten ~ soon as made. But, beyond al. lies . range of hills. On their heads hang misty crown their feet bathed by the waters Of the Mississippi and robed in the green verdure Of the valley, leading my thoughts above them, up through the sky to that region where shall be crowned with etcr. nal glory, and lave my feet in the river Of life. Ii. FRANCES ELIZA ]. INoEasoLL. McGregor, Iowa.

AURORA BoREAL1s.-The heavens presented an unusual phenomena upon Sunday night The singularity of the scene, was caused by the Northern Lights, in rare and unusual state of brilliancy. They became visible soon after sun set, aud remained so until day break Monday morning. The efulgence, was in this latitude, the greatest from eight to ten Sunday evening, aud from two to three the next morning. The sight rivaled all power of description, that can give nn adequate idea of the reality Such an occurrence rarely takes place 10 this climate, but approached very near to the des- cription astronomists have given of the appear ance of the Aurora Borealis in ATTITUDES far to the northward. The effect upon Sunday night, upon the nt- mosphere, was so great as to prevent the work ing Of the telegraph for several hours, as the Cincinnati and other papers state.

AURORA BoREALIs.-All the papers North Of Richmond describe an Aurora Borealis, seen Sunday night, as magnificent. In this city it was but slightly perceptible, owing to the clouds. The Alexandria Gazette says: Itwas first observed quite early in the even- ing, presenting the appearance of q phospho- resent globe over the whole northern section of the heavens, and reaching from the eastern 10 the western horizon. In the course OF the next three hours it passed through diversity of changes, ending in splendid display Of rich roseate light in the east aud west, with coraScations of a paler tint shooting up from the phenomenon, during the whole evening, was such as to render our street lights com- paratiyely useless.

Immediate | " upon sinking to the earth it exploded, and the water above offering greater resistance than the soft earth and gravel below, the en- trance to the tunnel was at once cleared | Attempts to clear choked up shafts by taking hose and pipe into the tunnel with which they connect, has heretofore caused the loss of several valuable lives, and for this reason it is to be hoped the simple experiment we have described will be thoroughly tested THE New York Tribune speaks as follows of a new play entitled "Geradine; or Loves Victory" the author of which, is Mrs. II. The Crescent says of it: The northern part of the armament, from northeast to northwest and from the horizon nearly TO the zenith became overspread with a clear red light, through which the stars twinkled as mcrrily as from their accustomed blue. At inter- walls, diverging rays of white and yellow light stole softly across the red. and as softly retired. The spectacle lasted about half an hour, and was witnessed and admired and won dered at by by thousands of the population. 1t had the appearance, in all respects, of an aurora borealis, the accustomed harbinger OF cold water, SO frequently seen towards winter in the more northern attitudes; and We are satisfied that 1t was one. But the sight OF such a phenomenon as far south as New Or leans, and in the scorching month of August, too, was something we'll calculated TO shake the faith in its identity, aud 10 start all posi- BILE suggestions which might connect.t with some neighboring terrestrial cause. Such suggestions. however, were at fault. No steamboat burning on the lake, no blazing prairies, no possible terrestrial blazes, could have produced any such an Opaque, wide spread, claret-cOlored light, with its glowing rays of white and yellow. With many ii was made a matter of joke. and with the ignorant and supersttious it created no little alarm.

And now on the midnight sky look, And my heart gr ows full to weeping; Each star is to me sealed book, Some tale Of the loved one keeping. We parted in silence, we parted in tears On the banks of that lonely river, But the fragrance and bloom Of those bygone years VIII hang round its waters forever

The west winds blow, and singing low, hear the glad streams run, The windows of my soul / throw Vide open to the sun. No longer forward nor behind l look in hope or fear; But, grateful, take the good find, The best of now and here. plow no more desert land, To harvest weed and tare; The mamma dropping from Gods own hand Rehukes my painful care break my pilgrim staff, lay Aside the toiling oar The angel sought SO far away, welcome at my door. The airs of spring may never play Among the ripening corn. Nor freshness of the flowers Of May Blow through the autumn morn. Yet shall the blue eyed gentian look Through fringed lids to Heaven, And the pale astor in the book Shall see its image given. The woods shall wear their robes Of praise, The South wind sony sigh, tnt sweet. cafsf 94y 9 u! gcifeh rae Melt down the amber sky. Not less shall manly deed and word Rebuke an age of wrong; The craven flowers that wreath the sword Make not the blade less strong. But shifting hands shall learn to heal, To build as to destroy; Nor less my heart for others feel That the more enjoy. All as God wills, who wisely heeds To give or TO withhold, And knoweth more of all my needs Than all my prayers have told. Enough that blessings undeserved Have marked my erring track That wheresoe'er my feet have sweryed, His Christening turned me back That more and more Providence OF love is understood, Making the springs of time and sense Sweet with eternal good That death seems but covered way Which opens into light, Wherein no blinded child can stray Beyond the Fathers sight That care and trial seem at last, Through memory's sunset air, Like mountain ranges overpast, In purple distance fair That all the jarrng notes Of life Seem blending in psalm, And all the angels of is strife Slow rounding into calm. And SO the shadows fall apart, And so the west winds play; And all the win lows OF my heart / open TO the day.

In the obituary department Of the Journal, published at Palmer, Mass, we find the fol- lowing announcement: .Dnp.-Mary, aged 20, wife of De Witt Clinton Packard, of Providence, r. l." In the editorial column there is sad and touching story, relatingt to the announcement, which we annex below. 1t is a lesson from the tomb, to the young and t~houghtless, and told so ~eloquently, that !: cannot fail to make an impression for good on readers Of every age. 1t says: aIn another column we record the death Of a Young lady who died of a broken heart. We do not like to trespass upon the sacred ness Of domestic grief to unfold the details Of her sad story but when the privacy of affection becomes public feeling, it is not i'm proper for the Press to place the events on record. 1t is not necessary to repeat names or relate minute particulars. 1t is enough that we draw the outlines Of a picture for the reader TO paint with appropriate colors. Many months ago, III the n~eighboring town of Belch- ertown, n young man sought and received the promise Of the hand of a young lady, whose home was in the lap of luxury, whose mental and personal attractions made all pleasant around her. Like too many conf ding ones Of her sex, she trusted mans I'M halIowed promise, and yielded all to him. "a Rrau tbpt hon1. he AstlaNpsd q ft1Ifhscif to the penalty Of the law, at the request Of her friend he returned TO her to fulfill the vows he had long before made. They were married in one of those hasty, ways, which occupy but little time or atten. tion. Late in the evening they returned to her fathers house, where he left her in the street. promising to return in a short time But that promise was never fulfilled. She wrote to him, and received encouragement that he would soon provide q home for her. but delay followed delay, till her letters and entreaties were unheeded and unanswered AT length q pledge of woman's love for her husband came into the world to open new fountains of affection to the young wife Still the husband and father came not. The mother recovered from confinement. but after repeated letters to her husband found no answer, the idea that she was de- serted by him forced itself upon her, and she gave way to dependency and despair. The child, partaking Of its mothers grief, soon died. There was nothing more that she could live for, and though suffering from no disease, she sank upon a dying bed. Then the swift wing of lightning bore to the distant husband the intelligence that she was dying. lie still hesitated, but at length set out to meet his expiring wife. Conscious that her hours were few, she only wished to live long enough TO see her husband he was still all to her. Her last words to her friends were : Tell him that | still love him-that l died Tor him" When evening Swallowed the earth the husband came. As he approached the bedside Of his injured wife, he was recog- nized, and the words He's come burst from her lips. Already had the wing of the death angel cast its shadow over that dwelling, and she was entering the dimness of the dark val ley. Next morning, in that room, lay the corpse OF a beautiful young wife, on which the husband had looked for the last time, and departed. last Sabbath afternoon, the funeral Of the young wife took place under her fathers roof Her ~neighbors and friends, to the num. per OF i've hundred, were present; but the husband who mad leTt her TO die for him war not there. A deeply affecting address was made by her former pastor, and just as the sun was sinking behind the western hills, four young ladies Of her acquaintance, clad in garments of white, bore her to a grave in the garden, where the green turf was laiC gently over her. Such is the story of one who died Of a broken heart. The grave is Q quiet place for the injured wife, but where in all the world can there be peace for him who would thus bring sorrow and death upor herr The story has its moral, but we will leave the reader to apply it; it is full of warn ing, and We leave the young to heed it"

In fact, some Of our friends got up and dressed, sup. posing day had come. The same phenomenon was witnessed in other localities, though on different nights. The officers Of the John A. Fisher, a steamboat plying on the Cumber- land river, report to the Nashville Banner that strange, and to them, unaccountable pheuomenon was wit messed from the hurricane roof of the steamer. while aground at the shoals, on Monday night; which the Banner attributed, when tolJ Of it the following morning on tho steam. er, to the Aurora Borealis, and tha! opinion is strengthened from tie fact, that a similar phenomenon has been witnessed elsewhere, as it learns by its exchanges and by the tele. graph. The pilot of the Fisher, Mr. Harmon, states, that about 2 o'clock on Monday morning, the vessel was surrounded by kind Of phosphsres- cent light, so brilliant that objects might be easily distinguished upon the river banks, though but few moments previous the night was black as ink. The light lasted for several minutes and then SUDDENLY disappeared, aud all was dark as be- fore. The fog was very thick. and it may be, that the Northern Light" were reflected upon the misty vapor, creating light similar to the rehec- tion on dark night from a burn. ing building. Me Aurora Borealis vas also witnessed at Louisville on Monday night. The Louisville Democrat says it was an unparalleled phenome. non in that latitude at this season. The exhibition of the celestial won der began at about eight o'clock, be- fore the twilight had fully gone, and al twelve it was still brilliant. At the time it began, there were dense masses Of black clouds in the West, reaching half way to the zenith. The same beautiful spectacle was observed at Cincinnati. There we're dense clouds reaching from the West, which disappeared before the Au- rora,as it oyerspread half the sky, the arch eliminating, as the Aurora al. ways does when it covers The sky al the Zenith Of the Magnetic Dip" which phrase the Cincinnati Gazette thus explains: If magnetized needle be sus- pended in q vertical place on a ply OF, the northern pole will point to the Earth, but not in vertical line, and the angle of variation from the vertical line is called the "magnetic Dip The zenith of this point in the sky to which the south pole Of the needle points. The colors of the Au- rora were greenish yellow, andthe COM p!imentary shade OF red. When the Aurora was at its height the eolors were very brilliant. Later in the night the blush WAS confined to the north, and did not reach more than one-fourth the distance to the zenith. The Aurora is supposed to be caused by the illumination, through electrical Influences, Of PARTICLES of sleet, in the higher regions Of the at mosphere. We have seen it several times in summer, aud have almost always noticed that it followed a sudden lowering of the temperature after rain. NUMBER a. | GEN. HoUsToE TO THE WOMEN o. ITExAs.-The closing part Of General Houston's Nacadoches speech is one Of the most eloquent tributes to woman ever uttered: Ladies, I know that politics are all ways uninteresting to you, yet | believe you have in the general result an abid- ing interest. 1t is always gratifca- ton to me to behold my fair country women in assemblages like these. II is always a guarantee that their hus- bands and fathers and brothers are men fof intelligence and refinement, who ap- preciate their mental capacities, and desire their countenance in their I'M dertakings. Your presence exercises a calming influence upon these antago- nisms, which are to often engineered in the heat of political contests. All par ties desire your presence. / know that in the direct administration of political affairs you have no share; but yet, reign ling as you do, supreme in the realm Of love, your influence often controls the destinies of nations. Woman's love is the great lever which arouses man to action. The. general, as he plans the stragetic combinations which are to IN sure victory, looks forward to a recon- Ipense dearer than the laurels upon his brow; the soldier, as he trudgea along on the weary march, or mingles in the scenes of the battlefield, even with death around him, forgets awhile the carnage, and turns his thoughts to the fond girl he left behind him !; the mariner, tempest-tossed, driven by the rude, waves sings merrily aloh as he thinks of the little cottage by the shore where his wife and dear ones await him the statesman, as he devises amid deep and painful thoughts plans Of gov ernment, which are to tell upon his own and his country's fame, never loses sight Of the joys which await him when cabinet councils are over, and he enteIs the portals of fame the sentinel as he PAGES his weary watch, loves the moonlight tramp, that he may look beneath its rays at the dear memento Of | a mothers or a sisters love. Over man. in all bis relationships, the infu- lence Of woman hangs like a charm Deprive US of your influence, which dignifes and stimulates US to noble deeds, and we become worse than bar barians. Let it be ours, and we can brave the cannon's mouth, or face dan / ger in ten thousand forms. You stim- ulate vi to all that is good. You check US in ignoble purposes. You have also an important influence upon posterity. The early impressions which the child receives from you outliye all the Wis dom of later days. sages may reason, and philosophers may teach, but the voice which we heard in infancy will ever come to our ears, bearing a moth er's words and mothers counsel Continue to instil into your children virtue and patriotism. Imbue them with proper yereration for the fathers of liberty. Learn them to lore their country and to labor for its good, as the great aim Of their ambition. Bid them proudly maintain our institutions. Point them to the deeds Of their an cestors. Make these their escutcheon, and bid them hand it down to their children as free from stain as 1t came lto them. Do this, ladies, and your in Ifiuence will not be lost in the future Ii the language of the poet, it will stil be said: Woman il lovely to the sight, / As gentle as the dews of even, | AS bright as morning 5 earliest light, I And spotless as thesnows of Heaven.

Jack, although be mentioned it to no one, had entertained belief that gold existed in any quantity in the Wahsatch Mountains, aud it was his determination 10 visit them alone, and satisfy himself in regard to it For the purpose OF greater safety, however, he joined company OF emigrants, aud remained with them until shey had nearly proceeded as far westward as Pixies Peak. For the National Era. AUGUST 10, 1859. To GAIL HAMILTON; have Just laid down the Era, after reading the affecting story of your poor, dear, loathsome birds. Feeling great sympathy for you in your distress, hasten to acquaint you with my experience and success in caring for that curious genus of birds, the chimney swallow. l glance my eye at the date of your letter, July 25th ; OIL your unfortunate younglings will be dead ere this reaches you. But to my story. About two weeks since, on descending to the breakfast room, deafening noise met my ear, proceeding, as soon learn ed, from the fireplace of an adjoining room. In surprise inquired the cause of this tumult !; M answered, "the swallows have fallen down the chimney" There had been a heavy fall Of rain during the night, which had caused the descent of their domicil. The fireplace was hid by an iron fre-board, so we could in no wise conjecture the number Of our visiters, but, from the noise that issued from thence, they might be numbered by scores. The great trouble was, would the mother bird flor / am inclined to think the "pater would not mourn their loss much, as ne would thus get rid of feeding them) find them in their low home? / stationed myself near, to be satisfied as to the state of affairs. Hours passed, perhaps FIVE, when the lowering sound of wings coming near and nearer, and a fresh and more Joyous burst from the habitants of the fireplace, announced the approach of the old bird. All she had found them at last. The propping open of the fre-board to admit light was not necessary in this case, as there was an aperture in it (which had once been filled by the stovepipe) that suf fciently lighted their otherwise dark abode By the way, we too have acat, not delicate city bred cat, but one that has breathed the free mountain air all his life, that might had he the gift of speech boast of eleven pounds Of cat-hesh-in short, cat of consequence. We soon had reason to believe, from small tufts Of hair to be seen on the edges of the aperture, that he had explored the fireplace; but, as the noise still continued, we concluded all safe. Our noble cat touch dirty, sooty chimney swallow! Not he-he had too much selfre- spect for that; so we had no more fears from that quarter. But perilous times were in store, which these poor unfortunates little dreamed of. There are some individuals possessed of q peculiar organization, which causes them to be extremely sensitive to the least noise. 1t is not uncommon for persons of this description to lie half of the night philosophizing on mat tiers and things, and the other half trying to court sleep, or listening to hear if possible, breathings Il dare not say ssorings) from dis. tant part of the house. 1t so happened that the "master Of the house " was one this class.

written for the Yorkvile Enquirer. "rHERE's NO SUCH WORD AS FAIL" 0THERE'S NO SUCH WORD AS FALL BY SAMUEL L. HAMMOND. Many faint hearts, when great deeds lie before them, and difficulties present seemingly impassa- BILE BARRIERS instead of going to work with patience energy and fixed determination to surnnount them all-grcw pale, tremble and give vent to, "but if we should fail! ?" or, 81 can't" and such like puerile expressions This feeble spirit the immortal Band of Avon deservedly rebuked, though I regret that it fell not from other lips than those of the blood stained Lady Macbeth; who, when her husband having determined to murder the kind old Duncan snd seize upon the kingly crown, grew faint, and asks ssif we should fail :" exclaims with an energy de- serving of better cause: "We fail! Screw your courage to the sticking point and De'H NOT fdiH' Perseverance and Determination are unacquain- ted with the word the bright lexicon Of Youth contains it not, and Manhood and Hope acknowl- edge no such monosylable as fail! But deter mine upon success, have the will to attain il, and a way will be found by which it can be achieved. Rain falls from the variegated curtains Of the mellow tinted sky, in sparkling globlets, one by one, and yet, almost within the waning of moon in that short space, the little golden span of time which eacompassed the rising and setting of the sun for two.score times, the fresh, green valleys, the sturdy oaks, the stately pines, the the tall and graceful waving cedars of Lebanon, and all the luxuriant beauty Of the forrest the little hills and giant mountains, the mighty cities with their lofty spires and towers, all-were sub merged. The world, so glorious and bright, with all its natural grandeur and sublmity, and the superb splendor of its artificial magn6cence, was completely inundated. Save the lone Ark, which rode upon the trouble waters in solitude, bearing under the guidance of Noah, two of each of the different tribes and species of the animal kingdom, which the AIl-wise had reserved from universal destruction for the workings of the future naught met the eye at every turn, but an immeasureable expanse of water below, with the blue vaulted and star be-spangled heavens above Not one green leaf; not one bud, or flower remained, on which the weary eye might rest and become refreshed from the continued upheavings of the waters, and the oppressive loneliness of the scene-the end less seeming monotony of sky and sea. How wise, all-powerful and yet mysterious to man, seem the works of the great Creator. Here is set an example; for as rain falls little by lit tie, so may we accomplish the most difficult task if we but set about it with determination to per- severe until our efforts be crowned with the glo rious wreath of success! And as each falling drop-each crystalline rain-jewel descends and swels the waters, increasing their depth, so will each good action of our lives swell the store of happiness and increase the depth of our joy.

And hear amid songs Of, welcome, From messengers trusty aud feet, On the starry floor of Heaven, The patter of little feet.

THE AURoRAL LIGHTS. The auroral phenomena of the night of the 18th of August, and of the morning of the ID of September have probably attracted more general attention among learned and scientific men than was ever given to such phenomena before. The display on Friday morning, though less marvellous in its manifestations than that of Sunday night, we think far ex- celled it in beauty. AT the time of our obser- walton, between one and two o'clock A. NJ, there was bright, rosy light between the east and northeast, stretching upward to the zenith. On either side the colors melted imperceptibly into yellow, orange, and, in some places, a del icate violet hue. The whole heavens, eXcepta small portion in the north, were sutfused with the most pleasing of tints, which though ap- parently motionless, were evanescent and changing, even while the eye was upon them. There were no indications of disturbance and storm, as on Sunday night; no streamers, shooting arrows, brilliant corruscations, or waves of light. If we did not know it already, the electric telegraph would show us the intimate connec- ton between these auroral displays and that mysterious, all-peryading something which we call magnetism. Some very curious effects of the aurora were observed Thursday even ing by operators of the American Telegraph Company. On the wires between Boston and Portland, the auroral waves in the atmosphere were substituted successfully for the batteries, as we learn from communication relating to the matter, published in the Traveller. The immediate effect of the aurora has been to dis turb the wires. On Thursday evening, when the phenomenon approached the height of its flashing briliancy, the following conversation took place between the operators at Boston and Portland = "Boston Operator to Portland Operator please cut off your battery entirely from the line for fifteen minutes Portland Operator-'Will do SO. 1t is now disconnected Boston-'Mine is also disconnected, and we are working with the Auroral current. How do you receive my writing 2 Observation-Disclosures than with our batteries on. Current comes and goes rapidly Boston-'My current is very strong at times, and we can work better without batteries as the Aurora seems to neutralize and augment our batteries alternately, making current too strong at times for our Relay magnets. Sup pose we work without batteries while we are affected by this trouble Portland-'Very well. Shall l go ahead with business! Boston-'Yes. Go ahead.'" And they report that the line was worked more than two hours without the regular bat teres, the auroral current being superior to them, and quite as successfully managed. The Traveller states that similar phenomenon were observed on the telegraph line between Boston and Cambridge. 1t may not be uninteresting to our readers to recall some of the accounts given of similar displays OF auroral light in previous years. Correspondence pac. Commercial AdvertIser.l Hawaiian Smperstition. The natives have many superstitious ideas still clinging about them which the public never hear of. But their superstitions are not, after all, more un- reasonable than those of many European nations, and not at all surprising when the very recent period is remembered since when civilization first dawned on the Sandwich Islands. Thirty or forty years is surely short notice for a barbarous nation to divest itself Of the traditional hobgoblins of centuries: and we should not, therefore, be surprised to hear that there is, among the more ignorant, a lingering reve- renee and fear of the goddess Pele, about whose an cient exploits they have SO copious an unwritten history--more especially. as every year or two they see before them the manifestations of her mysterious power. Like every other superstitious people, the Hawaiians have a good deal of respect for the sayings and doings of 'sdaft'' folks-the harmlessly crazy. This was exemplifed recently at the beach at wailoa, where the eruption of Mauna Loa is running into the sea. A crazy man from a neighboring hamlet took up his residence alongside the lava stream, and for weeks together, walked up and down with rapid steps, talking loudly all the while to Pele. 1t seemed as though he never rested, for wake Mt whatever hour of the night you might, he was still jabbering away, and his gaunt form was always to be seen fitting about the burning rocks in the baleful glimmerinps of volcanic light. No one ever knew him to eat, but whatever he got in the shape of food, he carefully preserved. and with much ceremony presented to the goddess, expressing great satisfaction when the fiery stream rolled over and consumed the fish and poi which he had placed in its path. The natives gathered about him in crowds, some-the younger, and more travelled, jeering at him-hut here and there was one who looked upon him with reverence as an inspired priest of Pele. This feeling, combined with the natural awe inspired by the wonderful scene, had such an effect on some few, that I am credibly informed they sacrificed pigs. sugar cane. bananas, etc., to the spirit of the volcano. 1t was not, however, done openly, but slyly. with every at tempt at concealment. 1 heard at Kailua, a deacon speak of it in church. As a fact which he was ashamed to have to acknowledge. In the old times, before the abolition of ido,atry. the common people were liable at any moment to be knocked down and dragged off to be sacrificed to the gods. But whenever a new heiau, or beathen temple was to be consecrated, some one was sure to disap- pear neutrality-suspicious. a child or youth, and the only explanation found was that they had been taken by the .Mu. as the executioner of the priests was called. Strang ely enough, the simple natives of to-day. ignoring in this respect the traditions of their anccstors-or. it may be. arguing from them-have fixed this custom on the foreigners. and firmly believe that whenever a new church is built a human being is sacrificed Without this, they say, the pule,-.he worship,-will be ineficacious. Cause OF the aurora BoreaIls. M. de la Rive, the celebrated French astron. mer, explains the production Of the aurora borealis in the following manner; When the sun, having passed into the southern hemisphere, the aqueous vapors which have accumulated during the sum mer in this part OF the atmosphere begin to condense, the kind of humid cap enve- Looping the polar regions extends more and more, and facilitates the passage of the electricity accumulated in the upper por- tions Of the air. But in those elevated regions, and especially at this season Of the year, the aqueous vapors must frequently pass into the state of minute particles of ice or snow floating in the air, similar to those which give rise to the balos they form, as it we're, a kind of semi-transparent mist. These half frozen fogs conduct the electricity to the surface of the earth, near the pole, and are at the same time llumi- mated by these currents or electric discharg- es. In fact all observers agree in asserting that aurora borealis is constantly preceded by a mist which rises from the pole, and the margins of which, less dense than the remainder, are colored the first; and indeed it is very near the pole in the winter months, and especially in those where there is an abundance of vapor in the air.

~ A contemporary says there should be harmony in the Democratic party in relation to the selection of an United States Senator, to succeed or to return Mr.. SLlDEEL. That's a good idea! We doubt much if the same thought ever entered another EDITORS mind. But can they be harmonious? Will perfect harmony ever reign in the bosom of that once happy family? Pshaw, will oil and water mingle and unite as one? Some good genius should be invoked to preside over such happy deliberations and bring about this devoutly to be wished consummation.- 1t is a crying shame, SO it is, that the happy fold Of John SLlDELL & Co. should be distur- bed by an unreasonable set of men desiring off :e, or who are so imprndent as to think differently with the 8 old man" upon the true definition of Democracy. Was the like ever heard Does not our contemporary know that Democracy in this State is personitied under the form Of King john" and that he is sovereign in all that relates to Democracy? How then can some men be so imprudent as to forget it We marvel much that some extraordinary phenomenon does not take place to demonstrate it 70 all and everybody, such as occurred the night before Caesar was killed, or Glendower was born! Perhaps the Aurora recently seen was gotten up ex- pressly for that purpose. Who knows!

These | plains are not 'deserts,n but the, opposite, and will in future add much to the empire Of COM merce and industry now being exerted on this continent. Their position and extent may be easily understood. in stating that they are comprised within the meridian line on The west side of Louisiana, the boundaries OF Arkansas, Missouri, and Iowa for their eastern limi', and the Rocky Mountain crest for their western, with Texas at the south, and the Arctic coast on the north. embracing longitudinal paral- telegram of somewhat less than 1000 miles in width They have gentle slope from The west | to the east, abounding IN rivers, running al lertly in the Missouri. Mississippi, the st. Law renee. and to the Texan coast. They are of homogeneous formation, slightly undnlating and continuous, without timbered space or lake. The soil, though compact. is fine cacareous mould. producing an abundance OF herbage peculiarly adapted to the climate. During temporary prevalence of moist atmosphere, al in the spring, the delicate "Gramma" and "Buf- | falo' grass flourish. and are cured into hay | upon the ground by the gradual returning | drought. 1t is upon this longitudinal belt OF perennial pasture that the buffalo finds his win ter food, subsistng upon it without regard to latitude and here, are found vast numbers OF wild horses, the antelope. the elk. and numer- Gus other animals peculiar to the continent. As the larger portion of 'he Great Plains" lies within the temperate zone, the position with respect to climate is favorable TO intellec- tual and physical development, health, and longevity. The seasons are comparatively rainless. except during the melting OF the snow | on the immense mountain masses beyond, when the rivers swell like the Nile, and yield cop- ous evaporation in their long courses, causing the storm-clouds to gather oil the sumiis. roll down their 1anks, and discharge themselves over the earth in vernal showers The atmos phere is almost perpetually brilliant with an azure sky, tonic. healthy, and inspiriting to the tempere, corresponding to, if not surprising that of the historic climates Of Arabir and Sy- ria, whence we have inherited all that is ethere' oil and refined in our system of civilization. The order of vegetable growth in many respects being reversed by the aridiiy of the atmosphere, what appear above as mere shrubs insinuate themselves deep into the earth. ! and form below an immense arboscent growth. Fuel of wood is therefore found by mining. or digging, instead of telling trees. Freestone, | Limestone plaster. clay and sand occur to an unlimited extent. The large and economical adobe brick hardened in the sun without fire, supercedes other materials for walls and fences in these arid regions, and, as in Egypt aud Sy' ria, for centuries resist decay. THE AURORA BoREALIs.-Most of our contemporaries got sight of the northern heavens all aglow" on Thursday of last week. They have given us most eloquent account of the affair; among the rest we think Brother Avery takes the premium His description 'mpensates us in some measure for the loss of the sight our selves. But we woula have been graf ified to see the "lumen boreale," if for no other reason than to discover how far high-wrought political tempera- ment makes burning worlds out Of northern lights.

MORE PIECES OF THE AURORA BoREALIs.-The idea-the first advanced by the philosopher Merriam, of Brooklyn Heights-that tho northern light was the result of the phosphorescent, fbrous silky sub stance which oated in the atmosphere, but as far as such fact is demonstrabe, was perfectly solved in the city of Covington, KY, during and since, the recent remarkable display Of the luminous freaks of the aurora in the northern sky. The attention of Mr.. Adam Kiger, of Covington, on stepping into his lawn on Friday morning, was lying scattered at hapbazard upon his shrubhey and grass Upon touching tress or portion of it, he re- ceived very sensible although slight shock of cleo tricity or gslvanism. His attention being thus arrested, he Immediately summoned his domestics, and they proceeded at once to gather considerable quantity Of the dew spangled fibre, which Mr.. Kiger found by actual weight after desiccation to be two ounces. seven grains, some of which he bottled for future inspection and experiment, and some he made into skeins of silk. [Cincinnati Enquirer. We don't doubt that Mr.. Kiger may have found some singular substance in his lawn but he does not explain, any more than Philosopher Merriam did, his reasons for believing it part and parcel of the North ern Light.

The light appeared in streams, sometimes of pure milky whiteness and sometimes of light crimson. June l6, 1859, AS you learned from my last letter from Faribault, Minnesota, l left that point for Frazer River on the Goth OF July last. At Fort Garry and Fort Edmonton | wrote again, though there was no certainty that you would receive the letters. Up to the latter point, which is Hudson's Bay Fort, the main post of the Company on the Sas- katchewan River, we experienced no difficult ty in our progress. At that place, however, it became necessary to take a guide, both on account of its being the last point before entering the passes of the Rocky Mountains, and because there was no trail any farther. We had considerable difficulty in procuring guide, as it was late in the season (OctO- Der 49, but finally succeeded in hiring a half breed named Rossette, to take US across the Rocky Mountains by the Kotonais Pass, (about 800 miles from Fort Edmon- ton, in southwesterly direction,) to Hud- sons Bay Company's post on the other side of the mountains. For this we agreed to pay him 94O-G2O down and the remain. ing EGO when we reached the Fort on the other side. We were told by every one that it was dangerous undertaking to cross the Rocky Mountains at this season of the year, bat as we learned, that if we did not cross this season, we would be compelled to wait here until the following August, we made up our minds to attempt it. Three of our party gave up the undertaking, and entered the service of the Hudson Bay Company. The rest of us-ten in number, started on the 10th of October. On the the 25th we came in sight of the Rocky Mountains. They were indeed formidable looking obstacles. That evening our guide tried hard to make us give up our purpose of crossing that sea- son. He recounted the most dismal tales of Indians and hunters being lost in the passes of the mountains during the winter months, and assured US that the probabilities were strongly in favor of our all losing our lives should, we persevere in our present rash determination. All this however Though we subsequently learned that he was only telling the truth,) fell upon our deaf ears, and the consequence was that the next morning, he abandoned US on desolate prairie without the semblance of a track, and full two hundred miles from the nearest abode of white men. This, however did not dlscour- age US, and we took straight course for the mountains. On the 3lst of the month we encountered some friendly Indians of the Assineboin tribe, from whom we procured guide who for gun, some blankets and various other articles, agreed to take US through the "Sinclair Pass near the entrance of which we then were. The " Sinclair Pass is about one hundred and twenty-five miles to the north of the " kottonais Pass, the one by which we had originally intehded to cross. On the End of November we entered the mountains and for several days encountered no snow. We then began to have very bad weather, high peaks to cross and deep snow, but we surmounted all difficulties, and on the 9th of the month, came out, las we all thought,) on the other side. The next day the guide left us according to agreement, having previously shown us trail which he said.w ould lead US in three days to the noun tain Fort of the Kottonais." We trav- eled on, and the next day to our great dis may, saw drove of Buffalo; by which we knew that we were still on the Eastern side of the montans. To add to our discomfort, it commenced showing heavily and was soon from one to two feet in depth. Three days from the time he left US, to our great sur prise, our guide came back to US. For this / have never been able to account 4; under his guidance we pursued our travels, and on the 10Th of the month re-entered the noun tains at the " Kottonais Pass, our original destination. On the second day we ascend the first peak, There are two peaks to be crossed in this pass) and camped on the summit. The cold was intense, and the snow from ten to fifteen feet in depth. Wehad to keep guard over the animals all night, to prevent them from going back again to the valley we had left, which was dreadful work. We could only stand for about quarter of an hour at time. Morning, however, came at last, and with the earliest glimpse of daylight we started. The wind was blowing ire menduously, and the drifting snow nearly blinded US. With great difficulty we man. aged to reach the top of the peak by about 10 o'clock, when we commenced the descent This was comparatively easy, though rather headlong work, as it was terribly steep. The the level valley below, when by contrast the weather was like summer. We wandered about this valley till the oath, when our guide left US once more, and this time finally We were now in pleasant predicament in valley, surrounded on every side by noun tains covered with snow without any track, and about four feet of snow on the level. We determined however to proceed, and the next day commenced the ascent of mountain, where we thought we had discovered signs of an old pack trail About four o'clock in the afternoon, we arrived within about half mile of the sum- NIT, and myself and two Others went on ahead to see what were the prospects for the descent. Never shall forget the mingled sensations experienced, as the magnificent, but to us heart sickening prospect, burst upon our view We stood upon the edge OF perpendicular precipice, hundreds Of feet in depth, the snow on which we stood being SO deep, that good sized pine trees resembled brush, only their tops being visible while in every direction, far as the eve could reach, nothing was to be seen but snow capped mountains with their interest ing valleys running in every direction. THE KING OF SARDINIA AT MILAN-HIS 1RIUMPHAL RECEPTI0N / Correspondence Of the London Ne,oSl MILAN, August S.-Mian being now free Italian town, the national tri-coor flag greatly contributed to the magnificent appearance of the popular festi- val of yesterday. myriad of such flags were waving in the streets, from the palace of the rich nobleman to the humblest dwelling of the poor workman. 1t hoisted on the top of every spire on the roofs of public buildings, and on the lace like minarets OF the cathedral Underfoot there was complete carpet of flowers. Above there was an enormous number of flags waving against the deep azure of this unrivalled Italian sky. In one word, it was the spontaneous demonstration of a free people welcoming its beloved King after long desired deliverance As the day the activity of the upholster- ers and flower girls increased for both were anx- iouS to finish their work before the bells of the Du- ONO began to ring their merry peals. In every corner of the town these people were busy entyin- ing wreaths and hanging out draperies, but it was IN the Corsa de Servi and in the Piazza del Duomo that the greatest activity prevailed sort of tent mad been erected in front of the principal entrance OF the famous church. 1t was dispraceful dispIav of hanging rugs which had been ordered bv the town council of Milan and intended to offer shelter to the King on his arrival The splendid front of the magnificent church, erected in 1886, by order OF Giovanni Galeazzo was thus not only spoiled bv the squareroofed official barrack but the linen and the fringes with which it had been adorned were so shabby and dirty that they would have dsgraced the meanest church of an Alpine village. More over 1t appeared that the draperes of the tent had been used on former occasions that is to saw when the Emperor Of Austria and the Archduke his brother used to go and thank God for the love and hdellty of their happy subjects. You will agree with me that the famous tent could not but awaken painful recollectons and such was as YOU will see the opinion of the Milanese mob. 1t was about O'Clock in the morning when the crowd collected on the Piazza began to express its Indignation against the upholsterers engaged in putting together that disgraceful heap of rugs The tumult soon became serious, and alarm was naturally spread amongst the workmen, who has tened to leave the scafold. Impreeations of every sort were directed against the Mayor and the conn cillOrs of the Broletto for not providing better tent. The popular wrath was thus increasing, and 1T was easy to perceive that the gend' 'armes who were present would be unsuccessful in restoring order; and so it turned out for in a few moments the pavilion pulled down, and the rugs torn to pieces. The Mayor was obliged to apologize and the disturbance which had originated in an hon orable feeling of affection towards the gallant King ended, when new and more elegant tent was erected on the spot. | have thought it nv duty to relate this incident, which marked til great fes- tval of yesterday, for should not wonder lift was turned luto regular cmente by the press devoted to Austria and by the too numerous Cassandras of the French official journals. The tumult on the Piazza del Duomo was but the expression of public indignation, and if the means employed were not very orderly, they are fully excused by the cause which gave rise to them. Even this little disorder is striking proof of the attachment of the Lom- Dards to the worthy sovereign who has been chosen by the general and free will of the country Inc OlHclal proclamation OF the MaYOr had al ready informed the people of Milan that his Males ty would arrive at the Porta 0rientale at O'Clock IN the afternoon, and from there proceed to the Cathedral through thcsplendid streetof the Corsia AT twenty minutes past six the merry peals of the church bells announced to the assembled crowds that the royal cortege on its way towards the Duomo had hired a window at the corner of San Babila Lion, from which | could distinctly see the Corso as lar as the bridge of San Damiano. 1t is impos- sbe for my pen to describe the enthusiastic mani festations of the people the King on his splen- dld bay charger, proceeded towards the cathedral The cheering and the vociferations were so unani- nous and spontaneous that one would have thought they were but the effect of one stentorian voice. The road along which the King and his brilliant staff were proceeding was kept in good order by a double row of French soldiers, who Joined their cheers 20 those of the crowd. Prince Carignan riding on the right of his Majesty who was closely followed by General Della Rocca his first aide-decamp, on the left. Behind the royal staff came the state carriages of the ministry and those OF the high digntaries of the kingdom About sixty other carriages had been allotted to senators and deputies, who had come from Turin to accom- pany Victor Emanuel. A great many eduipages of the Milanese nobility had also joined the roval cortege. Amongst the deputies and senators recoonized Counts Mamian Valerie, BrofTerio, Marquis Sierra, Paolo Farini, and the patriotic and able Cavalier Plea. At a few minutes before seven o'clock, his Majesty made his entrance into the cathedral where Bishop Caccia, temporary rector of the diocese was waiting at the head of his chapter After having received the benediction of the bishop Victor Emanuel entered the largest nave of the church amidst the crowd of official people, and took his seat on magnificent velvet throne which had been erected on the right of the central altar The report OF twenty guns announced to the crowd ed town that the Te DeuH had begun. As soon as the service of the Catholic Church was over four bands OF the city and two of the French mingled their harmones with the sounds of bells and the accIa- nations of the people. 1t was then that Victor Emanuel made his appearance on the Piazza del Duomo; 1t was then that the greatest manifestation OF popular feeling | ever witnessed took place be- meath the unclOuded vault of the Lombard sky From the cathedral his Majesty rode to the roval palace, three months ago the splendid dive ling of an austrian archduke. Count BelgiojosO, the Mayor OF Milan, and the town councillors received the hlng at the great stairs of the palace who was also met by Cavaiere Vigliani, the governor of the Lombard provinces The assembled crowd did not disperse till eleven at night, and Victor Emanuel was obliged to ac- knowledge four times the cheering of the population by showing himself at the principal balcony of the palace. MAHlN: I promised to let you ant !" my friends, through your paper, know some thing in relation to my trip to and arriva in Californis, which will now do. After visiting awhile in st. Louis and Indiana, proceeded to New York. where l arrived or the lst of July, and on the 9Th, at 9P. r., took passage on board the steamer Northern Light for this destination. Nothing worthy Of note transpired that evening, except that we hailed pilot boat and put Of two pas. sengers who had bogus tickets. 6th-Westher cool, with good breeze; sea tolerably rough while crossing the Gulf Of Florida. 7th-Weather still cool and sea rough, with head winds. Weather COOL. 9h-PssssnEers getting over their sea- sickness. The weather pleasant. ..a 18th Weighing baggage and getting ready for Aspinwall in the morning. 14tA-Arrived at Aspinwall at daylight. About 9 O'Clock took the cars and run across the Isthmus to Panama, distance of Al miles, in four hours. Took the Lighters and run out into the Bay some four miles to the large steamer Orizaba, on which we took passage. Gun has fred-we are off 15th-Our steamer, the Orizaba, is good and well. arranged ship. Weather pleasant for so far South and not q cass Of sickness on board. There has been but little sea- sickness. Running in sight of land all day. 16th-Out Of sight Of land making good hsadway. The good breeze we get here on this wide "prairis" makes the weather very pleasant. 18th, Sunaay-We had two sermons again by the Rev. Nj. Clark. 1Sth--Iu the Gulf of Tehuantepec. Saw large schools Of black fish. Weather warm. l9th-Runing in sight of mountains on the coast Of Mexico. Weather pleasant. 20th-Arrived at Acapulco at P. N. Went on shore and walked through the town, to zee the curiosities. Our vessel ran clear into the Bay, which is small. 1t is a beau tiful harbor, surrounded by mountains. We have to take in coal and water here to last us to San Francisco. 2lst-Left Acapulco this morning, at s O'Clock run near the Mexican shore all day. Weather pleasant. 22d-Still running near land; saw large schools Of porpoise and flying fish. Weather pleasant and no sickness. 23d-Crossing the Gulf of California, to-day, out Of sight of land. Weather quite cool. 24th--Passing the Marguerite Islands this morning in sight of land all day. Met the Golden Age this morning. Had two sermons on board to-day. Weather cool enough for overcoats. Still in sight of land. The Sonora running close to Us all day: She is one of the opposition line vessels. Saw several whales and q great many sea-birds. Passengers in good spirits. We4ther cool. 26th-Out OF sight of land all day. Heavy head sea; weather cool. 27h-Passed St. Nicholas Island this morning. Saw eighteen OF twenty whales. Passed Point Conception. Heavy head sea but oil on board in good spirits. 98,h- Running close to the California shore Wild oats on the mountains and cat tie ranches in sight. Saw one small Island half covered with sssls also great number of whales. We will soon enter the Golden Gate, q few miles this side of San Francisco. 29th-Arrived at San Francisco last night, at 10 o'clock. Left the ship this morning and may now be found at the American Exchange, all right. Family, also, all we'll and in good spirits. We had a pleasant trip and not . particle of trouble since we left Museatine. have not yet wished 10y self back. Our passage from New York cost us $13750 for each grown person, my boy going free, and 90 my favorite terrier. There being an opposition line. things on shipboard were made especially agreeable to US. We will leave for the mountains next Monday. lmet my brother in good health. find this the best vegetable and fruit market l ever saw. like the city very much. Yours. G. N. COLLINS.
